title: Falcons Must Rediscover One Key Part of Their Identity to Save Season
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons entered the bye week in a skid. The 3-7 squad has lost three straight games and five of their last six. The season isn’t completely lost yet , with the division still within reach, but the margin for error has nearly disappeared.
If the Falcons hope to reach their goals, it starts with getting back to what they do best: running the ball and stopping the run.
Head coach Kevin Stefanski spent his time away locked in his office, watching play after play and working to get his team’s season back on track. He said he identified some areas that they can improve and continue to address as a team.
From there, it’s a “big lift” for the position coaches to convey that information to the players in bite-sized form to avoid mental overload.
“All of our coaches have a specific area that they’re in charge of, quote unquote,” Stefanski said. “They do their self-scout in that area. Then, in our own ways, you go back, and you just watch games; and then you also go back, and you watch the run game, and then you cut it up; and you watch the wide zone and the duo and the perimeter run game, et cetera.”
After 10 weeks of games, the Falcons needed the reset, both offensively and defensively.
The Falcons are No. 23 in scoring offense (20.1 points per game), No. 18 in total offense (327.4 yards per game), and No. 27 in EPA per play (-0.16). They are No. 24 in scoring defense (25.8 points per game), No. 29 in total defense (358.2 yards per game), and No. 20 in EPA per play (-0.02).
There is plenty to improve, but fitting it all in a week away is a massive undertaking.
“I think it's the age-old as teachers and coaches, we should be able to handle a lot of that. And then what you give your students – what you give your players, maybe is not as much of that,” Stefanski said. “I often think about the playbook. The playbook's this big, but you don't need your players to know all of that. A lot of times that's for the coaches to go back and reference.
“We need our players to know the game plan… You definitely take the players through the key things and the bullet points, if you will. But as coaches, you do a deeper dive so that you have the whys and the what-fors behind all of it.”
The time away helped them identify their own trends, specifically what has been working against them on the ground.
Through the early weeks of the season, Atlanta was among the NFL’s best. They allowed 48.3 yards per game and piled on 181.0 yards of their own. Despite some starts from Cooper Rush that doomed the offense in two of those games, the Falcons rode the ground dominance to a .500 mark and 24.0 points per game.
Since then, the numbers have dwindled. The rushing offense has dropped to 101.8 yards, while the defense has plummeted to 166.3 yards allowed.
“It’s never one thing. If it was one thing, that’d be easy,” Stefanski said. “It'd be a short self-scout meeting. But it's never one thing.
“We're looking for a level of consistency that we haven't reached enough.”
Injuries have certainly played a role, with the Falcons missing key contributors in linebacker Divine Deablo and running back Brian Robinson. The week off should help both players get healthier, but their return will only be a small part of fixing a regressing facet of this team's self-proclaimed identity.
But focusing all of their attention on a single facet of their team would come at a cost.
“You have to make some decisions on what you want to do moving forward, because, like anything, it’s about what you want to attach your time to,” Stefanski said. “There’s a cost to everything. Every change you make or every investment in a scheme, there's a cost to it. And there's cost in terms of the meeting room and the practice field. So, I think a lot of the conversations with the coordinators, especially, are all these learnings: where do we want to streamline this so that we can maintain or find a level of consistency?”
That is what happens when a team loses its identity halfway through a season. With similar shortcomings in the passing offense and secondary, the Falcons have no time to lose if they want to snap out of this skid.
Stefanski didn't specify what he found, but his comments on streamlining suggest the Falcons will simplify what they ask of their run game and defense. That will be tested right out of the gate.
Three straight games against playoff-caliber opponents in the Vikings, Lions, and Browns await them after their time away, plus a trip to Washington and three division games to finish their season. How they manage these games will dictate how this season is remembered and whether this team can snap out of an eight-year playoff drought.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: The Ravens Did Nothing To Boost Their Offense In The Offseason, And It's Showing Every Week
full_text:
The Ravns have no discernable strength as a football team right now.
The defense is the biggest issue, by far, alleged $60M “closer” Trey Hendrickson has instead been a colossal bust and the entire defensive class of free-agent additions have been a total nothing burger this far with little hope for that changing anytime soon. Rookie head coach Jesse Minter was supposed to be savant on that side of the ball with his years of experience calling a defense.
The fact that all of the real resources from outside the organization were going to his side of the ball seemed strange. And with rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle struggling mightily and unable to score points in the second half of games and with the entire offense crumbling when Lamar Jackson got hurt in the pocket – defenseless – again – there are very real questions that need to be asked about what the Ravens did and did not do to address obvious deficiencies at every position group on offense.
Perhaps, it’s not as devastating as what’s happening on the defensive side of the ball ( total disaster ) considering how little, on scale financially, was put into the offense this offseason. But the results are just as pathetic and continue to make the obvious case for why failing general manager Eric DeCosta needed to be fired when head coach John Harbaugh was in January
Here’s what they did to add to the offense prior to the season, and how little it’s provided in return:
Key Stats: 23 Pressures Allowed (4th most); 16 Hurries (13th most)
This contract never made any sense for a below-replacement level guard and especially guaranteed $5.5M into 2027 is utterly foolish. He was pretty good for the Ravens a few years ago but not special physically and with real issues in pass protection and he has been a complete disaster here. If this team was serious about winning and serious about building for the future, he would have been benched by now.
He has helped to undermine whoever was throw next to him at center. He has been repeatedly thrown back into the quarterback, no matter which one was starting a game (there have been four already, in no small part because the line is a joke). The inside run game has gone nowhere all season with Simpson a big part of that to the where under-center runs averaged 2.7 yards per carry since Lamar Jackson went down.
If Emery Jones isn’t worth a looksee now, then they better draft like three offensive linemen at least.
Key Stats: 6.6 yards/attempt, 95.5 passer rating, 6.2 air yards/attempt
Could have been a total loss with him having to learn a new system and with a new coaching staff when Baltimore opting to bring him back after his second stint with the team went okay a year ago. The idea that he profiles as anything close to Jackson in terms of movement and athleticism is silly and he refuses to throw the ball downfield.
If he did not suffer a serious toe injury this offense was going to be a very tough watch him at the helm. Jacoby Brissett is multiple levels above him and upgrading at back-up QB should be on the table. Huntley is not going to age well, but he did win that game in Atlanta in OT and he works cheap.
Key Stats: 4 Games, 120 Snaps
They actually did add someone who had played in an offense with Doyle before. Of course, they didn’t add nearly enough in that regard and they silly games they played at the center spot (read below) truly tore the guts out of this offense. Smythe was doing great work helping the ground game go and aiding pass protection (much needed) and elevating the team’s offensive Expected Points Added when on the field.
But he suffered a season-ending injury a month into the season, replacement Nick Vannett is not nearly as versatile or impactful and Smythe’s loss proved huge. It was naïve not to try to impart more players with ties to this system. His presence would have really helped take things off the plate for these rookie tight ends, especially with Mark Andrews cooked .
Contract : $3.3M/1 year (Pinter)
Key Stats: 171 total snaps
The idea that DeCosta was smarter than everyone else and didn’t need a real center was so dumb them tried to dig out of a self-inflicted hole by trading for two centers – one who isn’t any good and one yet to play - at the trade deadline. This was ridiculous in real time and not drafting one in the second round will haunt this desperate front office.
Pinter couldn’t play regularly on a mundane Colts line and ditto Gwyn in Atlanta and Pocic was still recovering from a late-season Achilles tear when they signed him. This was all far too cute and far too risky, and Doyle desperately needed a legit center in his building while he installed an offense for the first time.
DeCosta has been a D-level GM, at best and being generous, since Jackson’s second MVP and he was a total failure with everything he touched this offseason. Most of the moves looked DOA in real-time and the only reason more isn't being made about his surrender with the offensive roster is because it’s not the financial atrocity he committed with the defense.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: 10 Winners and 7 Losers From Ravens' Deflating Loss To Panthers
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens dropped their sixth straight game this season in Week 11 on Sunday because they weren't able to come out on top of the middling Carolina Panthers in a gut-wrenching 35-33 defeat.
They entered this game as understandable underdogs after losing to the last winless team in the league the week prior on a quick turnaround. Once again, they were their own worst enemy with costly and untimely turnovers and an inability to get stops or points when the game was on the line.
With the loss, they fell to 4-7 and remain in last place in the division and still have better odds of earning a top 10 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft than they do returning to the postseason with six games left to play.
Here are several Ravens players and coaches who stepped up and showed out, and others who made some costly mistakes from coaching and execution standpoints.
With four-time Pro Bowl veteran Marlon Humphrey deactivated for this game, and watching it from back home in Baltimore, he might've gotten a good glimpse of his eventual replacement as the third-year pro capitalized on his most extensive action on defense of the season thus far. Tampa didn't get the starting nod but ended up playing 56 percent of the team's total defensive snaps with 40 and finished as the Ravens' highest-rated player according to Pro Football Focus , with an overall grade of 90.5.
Tampa was impressive in coverage throughout the game, with the exception of one costly lapse when he was late coming over to cover a tight end on a trick play that scored. His best two plays came on the same drive deep in the red zone, with the first being an excellent pass breakup and the second being a drive-ending interception. Both came while tight coverage of the Panthers' top wide receivers and showed why Tampa is deserving of even more playing time moving forward.
The underutilized speedster is another third-year pro from the same draft class and round as Tampa, who showed out in this game. Walker made big plays in two phases in his homecoming to North Carolina, finishing with a career-high 245 all-purpose yards after recording a 34-yard reception and racking up 211 on kickoff returns, with a long of 86 yards that he took all the way back for a touchdown. As a result, he earned AFC Special Teams Player of the Week honors and is the only player in the league who has recorded a catch of 30-plus yards and scored on a kickoff return in the same game this season.
The second-year pro stayed hot and capitalized on the extra attention paid to the four-time Pro Bowler on the opposite edge, recording his second straight multi-sack game and raising his team-leading total to 7.5. Green didn't waste any time making his presence felt, logging his first sack of the game and first career safety on the Panthers' opening possession to put the Ravens on the scoreboard first. His second sack came one play after another; the soon-to-be-revealed winner recorded the first of the season, giving the Ravens two on back-to-back plays to come up with a key fourth-quarter stop and keep Carolina from getting into field goal range after starting with the ball at midfield.
After being held to a measly season-low 10 rushing yards on 10 carries in last week's embarrassing loss, the five-time Pro Bowler bounced back with his third-most productive game of the season and best in a month and a half. He fell just shy of reaching the century mark on the ground alone with a team-leading 94 rushing yards and went over 100 yards from scrimmage by recording four catches on five targets for 17 receiving yards.
The second-year pro made a pair of clutch plays between two different phases of the game late in the second quarter. On a third-and-short, he made an impressive tackle in space for no gain on Panthers top wideout and 2025 Offensive Rookie of the Year Tetairoa McMillan
, who is six inches taller and weighs nearly 50 pounds more than Martin. In doing so, he forced a punt to get the ball back to the offense for a chance to potentially extend their lead before halftime. On the ensuing punt, he was in the right place at the right time to prevent another muff from falling into enemy hands for a turnover.
The Ravens' two-time Pro Bowler had his most productive game in nearly a month as his connection with his fourth different starting quarterback, leading the team with 11 targets, eight catches, and 97 receiving yards. He picked up several key first downs, gained consistent separation and finished as the team's third-highest-graded player on offense with an overall grade of 81.
The Ravens needed the fifth-year veteran nose tackle to step up in more ways than one in this game with two-time Pro Bowler Nnamdi Madubuike out with a hamstring injury, and he delivered. In addition to leading all the team's interior defensive linemen with a season-high eight total tackles, including five solos and a team-high three run stops, Jones also recorded a pair of pressures, a quarterback hit and his first sack of the season on 16 pass-rush snaps.
The eight-year veteran continued to carve out more of a role for himself in the offense as more than just a pass protector, as he recorded his highest scrimmage yardage total of the season with 96 yards on 10 touches. Hill recorded the second-most rushing yards with 69, the fourth-most receiving yards with 27 and would've had his first multi-touchdown game had it not been for a costly fumble at the end of a 36-yard run that resulted in a touchback.
The sixth-year veteran was the Ravens' second-most targeted pass catcher with eight, and even though he finished with just two catches, both were highly impactful and came on scoring drives in the first half. His first capped off the offense's third drive with a 52-yard touchdown on a well-designed and executed trick play. The second was a 15-yard gain on their next possession to get the ball past midfield on a drive that ended in a short field goal to put the Ravens up 12-0.
A week after being bullied and embarrassed by the Chargers' defensive front and managing just 16 rushing yards over the course of four quarters, the Ravens' starting blocking unit rebounded in a major way. They racked up 157 rushing yards with an average of 7.1 yards per carry and held up well in pass protection for the most part, outside of some key high-leverage moments.
There was no bigger loser coming out of this game than the underwhelming second-year pro because his poor performance literally cost him his spot on the team, as he wa s waived on Tuesday after muffing a pair of punts in the second quarter. Prior to his first, the Ravens had just taken the momentum back after Hill's fumble with a swift three-and-out, and Wester gave the Panthers the ball right back at the Baltimore 23-yard line, and it took them just three plays to get into the end zone and take their first lead. He squandered his chance at redemption and sealed his fate by failing to corral a punt just before halftime that was, fortunately, recovered by one of his teammates.
The third-year pro didn't get beat for a touchdown, but he gave up too many key snags on pitch-and-catch conversions in high-leverage situations on third down. He was either in tight coverage and didn't trust what he was seeing to make more plays on the ball or he wasn't communicating with his fellow defensive backs to effectively pass off routes post-snap. Wiggins was targeted seven times and allowed four receptions for 54 receiving yards and broke up one pass.
End of half game management
The four turnovers committed by the offense and special teams, nor the missed assignments and bad eyes by the multiple defenders in key moments, deserve to be laid at the feet of first-year head coach Jessie Minter. However, his decision-making and management of the clock at the end of each half were mind-bogglingly poor and are where he is deserving of the most blame.
At the end of the first half, he opted to put the offense back on the field for a Hail Mary attempt instead…

title: 3 Changes Jesse Minter Must Make Immediately To Curb The Ravens' Six-Game Rot
full_text:
It would be nice if Jesse Minter could understand the situation he and the Ravens are in.
If he didn’t look glazed over and run over (by his players) on the sidelines every Sunday, that would be a nice start. If he found a way to win a football game and not allow most teams to hang 33-plus points on his defense, that would be fun for a change. If he found a voice and offered real accountability and didn’t come off as an overwhelmed functionary of the personnel department, that would be a welcomed wrinkle.
Any signs of growth, development and awareness from as an NFL head coach would be great. It might also, of course, force him into some tough conversations with failing general manager Eric DeCosta , who wanted him under his control but has undermined Minter, miserably, with this roster– both at the start of the season and by failing to get real at the trade deadline.
Minter’s job security must be in question and with this team likely to win no more than a game – two seems a stretch – from here on out, the rookie better find other ways to suggest and connote progress. The standings are not going to be his friend, and the people who hired him should have been fired years ago, but there is also mounting evidence to suggest this owner takes the easy way out and path of least work. In this case, that’s simply firing a coach and leaving the rest of his failing organization in place like this past January. Owner Steve Bisciotti has co-signed this aimless and feckless losing in a profound way.
"I'd probably keep a lot of the conversations between Steve and myself private,” Minter offered on Wednesday. “He's great. He's very supportive. Talk a lot; talk about a lot of different things. So I always appreciate our conversations. Leave it at that."
With the season running thin and nothing pointing in the right direction with this football team in any aspect, we have some suggestions for Minter on things to change ASAP, for this week at Houston, even before the looming bye:
If Adam Randall and Elijah Sarratt are not worthy of getting single snap, even on special teams, then it’s an indictment of everyone. The Ravens can’t beat anyone with their aging and bloated roster but also mastermind alleged-genius kid coordinator Declan Doyle can’t find any use for these players with an offense that is garbage as soon as he exhausts his early-game script?
There is no role in the screen game? Nothing? Team this bad doesn’t even need to get a look at a fourth-round pick or a fifth-round pick at the same time whatever is left of Mark Andrews continues to out-snap both rookie tight ends?
Doyle had the audacity to default to “player development” in taking vital blocking tight end Durham Smythe off the field in the home opener as Baltimore blew another big lead in defeat, and now the team is a laughingstock but the kids don’t need to be a point of emphasis? Make that make sense.
If you want to really have the bottom fall out as the weather turns and the stadium is about to be empty, mess around and become a joke stopping early down runs.
If you manage to run a defense that not only cannot stop the pass all season but then wilts in a massive way up front the first time you face volume on the ground, you are hastening your own demise. And, yeah, it’s going to mean you are slashing the role of some guys your bosses grossly misplayed but that’s coaching.
Trey Hendrickson on the field on early downs in divisional games against Pittsburgh and Cleveland will be brutal. Tampa will run all over him to. Houston will just throw the ball all over the place. But we know the hard-hat mentality that comes from December AFC North football and if Minter isn’t willing to adjust his run front and find ways to hold up without Tavius Robinson (IR) or the rest of the season and maybe without Nnamdi Madubuike (hamstring) for a while longer, it will definitely get uglier in Owings Mills.
He is utterly disconnected from this product and from reality up in the booth. He was supposedly gong to be willing to tinker and alter and be malleable as a first-time play caller. But the moment he looked good in the preseason opener that was enough to convince himself that being upstairs was the only way?
He seems to have little clue when his quarterbacks are being maimed up there. No idea how badly his offensive line is being whipped. He has the worst second half offense in the NFL by several metrics, and appears totally detached and says he wants to script the entire game.
Get him out of that comfort zone, get him interacting with players in the moment, on the sidelines, as humans – you know, looking in their eyes and all) – instead of cogs in part of his machine. Try something different to shake up how horrible your football team is after the half.
If this staff wants to curb the chatter about being one and done, and not answer questions about their job security and being on the hot seat down the stretch , then something new and different in their approach better show up, quickly.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The One Raven Truly Benefitting From Jesse Minter's Arrival
full_text:
The Ravens defense isn’t big on feel-good stories.
It isn’t big on anything good at all, at the core of the team’s six-game slide that is quite likely to run to seven against the potent Texans passing game on Sunday in Houston.
Head coach Jesse Minter has been totally overwhelmed to the point where his job security is being called into question and at the very least he should have divested himself of play calling duties (don’t worry, it’s coming) .
The highest-paid players have been failures by and large (especially alleged “closer” Trey Hendrickson) and now Kyle Hamilton is regressing, and Roquan Smith and Marlon Humphrey have been sunk costs for years. Oh, and the entire group of free agents brought into the $150M defense have been a collective and individual failure and the draft class hasn’t offered anything, either.
But there are strides made.
Linebacker Trenton Simpson has come along quite well and proven himself as an everyday player ( who needs a contract extension ) and perhaps could displace Smith next year. And one defender has made a true leap, threatening to thrust into a different stratosphere – 2025 second-round pick Mike Green. More than anyone else on this roster, he is making a significant breakthrough in his second season.
Green was asked to do way too much on early downs last season and was overextended as a raw rookie; exposed far too much against the run in a bad defense. Somehow, Minter’s defense is significantly worse than Zach Orr’s from 2025 despite all the resources poured into it. But Green is looking like the best young pass rusher the Ravens have produced since Terrell Suggs and certainly at least since Matt Judon.
He can’t anchor like Suggs and that isn’t a fair comparison, but Green has tapped into his strength and pliability and versatility this season, getting loose for inside pressures on twists and at times with pure tenacity. He has been focused and slippery and playing his best football now while so few around him seem to know what to do or where to be (especially in the second half).
Green is going to run away with the team lead in sacks and, with 7.5 already (no Raven had more than five last season), is on pace for a rare double-digit season in these parts. Since Suggs posed 11 sacks in 2017, Kyle Van Noy (12.5 in 2024) is the only edge defenders here to surpass 10.
“I'll say just first and foremost, just approaching every day with a clear mindset,” Green said Wednesday when asked what has helped him take the leap. “There's a lot going on for everybody in this building and what I try to do is to make sure that I'm just controlling what I can control and putting my best foot forward. So, just having that kind of mindset going into each day ended up helping me out a lot."
Green has more than twice as many sacks as anyone else on the team and has out-snapped Hendrickson the past two games, rightfully so. Green has more juice and energy and despite the proclamations about Hendrickson closing games he has no fourth-quarter sacks and just five pressures. Getting 50 snaps on Sunday was a nod to his development.
“It's been helping me out a lot,” Green said of the rising PT. “Even just from my first year, I think I played a good amount. I feel like once you get in a good rhythm and you get in a good flow of just how the game's going and the tendencies that your opponent typically does and things like that, it sets you up to play a little bit better. So, I think just overall just being able to go out there and play more snaps kind of gives you the confidence, and it gives you a little bit more time to be consistent."
Green registered two sacks against the Panthers on Sunday and had two less than a week prior, against the Chargers. Hendrickson has two in his Ravens career (he still trails Tavius Robinson, for second place, despite Robinson going on season-ending IR weeks ago).
Green ‘s average time to sack is extreme (4.16 seconds) and speaks to his motor and effort. He also has been fresher late in games. He leads the team with two fourth-quarter sacks and three QB hits in the final quarter.
He is far and away the most efficient edge player on the team. Green has those 7.5 sacks on just 23 pressures, an elite finishing rate (Hendrickson has two on 31 pressures. Green leads Baltimore with 13 QB hits; tackle Nnamdi Madubuike is second with nine.
He’s the rare positive this coaching staff can point to on any level, and he and Robinson should be the bookend starters next season despite Hendrickson’s bloated salary. Green is also one of the few players making defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver look sage. Weaver’s bold predictions about Humphrey and Smith from the spring are going to fall well short, but his prediction of 10-plus sacks for Green is looking pretty good.
“He shares his experience and what he thinks is going to work and things like that,” Green said of Weaver. “I like it a lot. He's played in the league. He's been to places that we're trying to go, and he knows a lot, especially on the defensive line. So, it's been great to have him around, and we appreciate him."

title: Ravens Waive Struggling Return Specialist LaJohntay Wester After Final Straw
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens announced a pair of roster transactions on Tuesday, and neither came as a surprise for different reasons.
The release of third-year quarterback Kedon Slovis, who had been serving as the emergency third quarterback for the past two weeks, might've resulted in him being re-signed to the practice squad had he not been claimed off waivers. The same can not be said for former starting return specialist LaJohntay Wester.
We have waived WR LaJohntay Wester and QB Kedon Slovis. https://t.co/cnZ4NuE7Sn
The Ravens parting ways with Wester comes off the heels of a disastrous outing by the second-year wide receiver in the team's 35-33 loss to the Carolina Panthers , in which his struggles fielding punts persisted in the worst way with two muffed attempts.
After the defense forced a three-and-out early in the second quarter, the first was recovered by the Panthers at the Baltimore 23-yard line, and it only took them three plays to get into the end zone for a go-ahead touchdown and then first of several lead changes in the back-and-forth affair.
It came as a huge surprise when the Ravens trotted Wester out for another opportunity later that same quarter, only to see him make the same mistake, but this time, he was fortunate that nickel cornerback Keyon Martin was able to fall on the ball at the Baltmore one-yard line before a Panther could recover it.
Those two colossal gaffes alone were at minimum a 10-point swing, and potentially a 14-point swing, in a game the Ravens lost by just two points. The Panthers scored as a result of the first, and the Ravens had to cover more ground on their final drive of the first half, which ended in a failed Hail Mary attempt from the Carolina 45-yard line, rather than a more manageable field goal or a closer shot at reaching the end zone.
Wester's short-lived tenure as a Raven began with a lot of promise after the 2025 sixth-rounder flashed explosive playmaking potential in his preseason debut as a rookie when he returned his second punt return for an 87-yard touchdown .
Through the first 10 games of his rookie campaign, he was still bringing the juice to the return game that Baltimore special teams has missed since the departure of All Pro return specialist Devin Duvernay. However, his decision-making and inconsistency when it comes to fielding punts have been a noticeable detriment to the team since he committed his second career muff in Week 11 of last year, which resulted in a lost fumble.
LaJohntay Wester 2025 Weeks 1-10 rookie season: 16.3 yard punt return average 1 fumble 0 fumbles lost Wester 2025 Week 11 - 2026 Week 11: 7.9 yard punt return average 5 fumbles 3 fumbles lost Wester never regained confidence after muffing a couple of punts at Cleveland. https://t.co/0Qmv3vyhRn
Wester was benched after the second muff, and the Ravens were bailed out from starting a later drive from inside their one-yard line a second time after second-year safety Malaki Starks failed to field a punt that rolled deep inside the 10-yard line and was downed by a gunner whose heel was luckily touching the goal line.
According to reports from the portion of Wednesday's practice that was open to the media, the Ravens had over half a dozen players fielding punts, and head coach Jesse Minter expressed confidence in their in-house options moving forward.
"I think we have a pretty good idea, but we'll kind of see how this week shakes out and see which direction we decide to go by the end of the week," Minter said. "It's always tough when stuff like that happens, but you just got to do what's best for the team."
Wester cleared waivers and officially ended his tenure with the Ravens after 28 career games in which he logged five receptions on six targets for 58 receiving yards as a pass catcher, 321 punt return yards and 625 kick return yards.
Moving on from him could open the door for fourth-round rookie Elijah Sarratt to finally be a regular active member of the roster on game days moving forward as both an option at punt returner, which he saw some preseason action at, and as a depth slot receiver option behind two-time Pro Bowler Zay Flowers.
In the same game in which multiple punt return gaffes cost them dearly, the Ravens got a much-needed boost from a different young receiver as a kick returner. Between Wester's muffs, underutilized third-year pro Devontez Walker took his third-career kickoff return opportunity 86 yards to the house for a go-ahead touchdown.
The incredibly clutch play accounted for over a third of Walker's 211 kick return yardage in the game and earned him the first AFC Special Teams Player of the Week honors of his career.
Touchdown Tez is the AFC Special Teams Player of the Week 🔥 @DevontezWalker pic.twitter.com/g9ZseaetE3
While that was the highlight of his performance against the Panthers, it wasn't the only impactful play of note. Walker added a 34-yard reception on his lone target of the game, giving him a career-high 245 all-purpose yards and making him the only player in the NFL to record 30-plus receiving yards and a kickoff return touchdown in a game this season, according to the Ravens communications department.
For inexplicable and blatantly inexcusable reasons, the 2024 fourth-rounder hasn't been regularly featured in the offensive game plan since entering the league, despite possessing game-breaking speed to take the top off of opposing defenses. Walker has shown explosive playmaking ability in limited opportunities with 12 catches on 21 targets for 22.2 yards per catch, five touchdowns and 266 receiving yards.
"When you get an opportunity, and you take advantage of it, there's definitely a path for more of that," Minter said.

title: Mark Andrews' Last 20 Games Have Been Nothing Short Of Disastrous For The Ravens
full_text:
In Week 10, with the Ravens playing on Monday night, out of nowhere during the broadcast came a report about Mark Andrews and a broken hand.
The tight end, who was leading all players at his position in false start penalties and had the highest drop rate as well, went on to have his first productive game, honestly, since September 2025, his first game over 50 yards receiving since then, and the hand, so the story went, has now good to go. Of course, Andrews has not shown up on an injury report and he hasn’t been wearing anything protective on his hand.
Maybe he was feeling better and maybe he wasn’t going to just go on being one of the most overpaid players in the NFL. Maybe, with each passing week, the ridiculous decision to extend his contract last December would look like an utterly foolish decision by a general manager, Eric DeCosta who has made such failures his brand .. Surely, Andrews was never going to look like half the player ex-Ravens tight end Isaiah Likely is week after week for the Giants, but at this point merely string together two 40-yard games would amount to significant progress.
… And nothing close to that came to pass..
Sunday’s debacle in Carolina was simply more of what ever week is for Andrews. A confounding display where he is asked do more than rookie tight ends Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas , and he offers precious little. It was another game where he simply did not show up in the passing game at all, he cannot do anything downfield, and he finished with two catches for two catches for 14 yards. The eight grabs for 82 yards vs the Chargers was the outlier, and it may prove to be for quite some time.
Andrews continues to exude rampant positivity in the face of a disaster season, but thinking he has the answers and can actually influence this offense would be silly at this point.
"I'm just fired up, man," he said after Sunday's setback." I am ready to go. I think for me, just playing with my heart, playing all I can and doing anything I can to help this team win is the main thing. And just being there for everybody. I just want to be able to do that."
This is no slump for Andrews; it’s the end of his tenure as a move tight end in the NFL. It’s been over and it is over, only the Ravens are going to be stuck paying him next year anyway with another $5M guaranteed on his deal (top seven at his position in average salary). He was paid like a top 10 tight end, but those days are long gone.
Andrews is going to end his career without every registering a playoff touchdown. Certainly his Ravens' career, with this team not sniffing the postseason anytime soon. And even with back-up quarterback Jacoby Brissett funneling the ball to tight ends, Andrews can’t do anything after the catch and he moves the chains on check downs and short passes and that’s about it.
Over his last 20 games, he's averaged three catches for 26 yards. Gulp.
He has just two touchdowns in his last 20 games.
He averages 2.1 yards after the catch in that span, and for the last two seasons , which is hard to fathom. He has caught just 63 of 91 targets in those games, despite his routes being pedestrian and high percentage by and large. He is averaging just 8.3 yards per reception.
He'll probably play more snaps and run more routes than anyone else at his position again Sunday. Nothing much ever changes in Owings Mills, and they refuse to get real about who they really are and how deep their personnel issues and coaching issues run.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Trey Hendrickson Isn't The Only Ravens Offseason Addition Failing To Deliver. He Has Company
full_text:
The Ravens are stuck with Trey Hendrickson.
They missed any chance to pawn him off before the trade deadline, and they will regret it , and they are stuck with another $30M fully guaranteed coming his way next season after getting nothing out of the $30M invested in him during this lost season. General manager Eric DeCosta has a failure offseason continuing a three-year debacle that should have cost him job in January when head coach John Harbaugh was fired.
He got nothing right, his offseason was doomed from the moment he pulled out of a Maxx Crosby trade and The Football Gods or karma have been kicking up every week since (or, well, it’s mostly just that he isn’t very good at this whole evaluating, negotiating, leadership thing). And no one, from an on-field standpoint, is going to embody this 2026 disaster as much as Hendrickson, who should honestly be doing far more standing on the sidelines as he gets attacked in the ground game with the weather turning.
They called him a $60M closer, and he hasn’t shown up in a fourth quarter all season and after six straight loses with rookie head coach looking overmatched all along, nothing Hendrickson does this season even really matters, now. Sad. But true.
With Hendrickson’s malaise getting more and more attention around the NFL, it’s as good a time as any to reflect on all the players brought in from outside the organization by DeCosta for this much-hyped defense and evaluate the evaluator. Hint: This ain’t pretty.
The defense is the biggest failure in the franchise and Minter can’t seem to do anything about it. His side of the ball was handed the preponderance of resources in free agency, and Minter is an alleged mastermind. so this should be keeping owner Steve Bisciotti up at night, and jobs should be on the line.
Key Stats : 2 sacks, 5 pressures in the fourth quarter, 12.7% pressure rate late five weeks
Verdict – F: He was supposed to be the guy who ended the fourth-quarter rot and turned this defense around and stopped all the blowing of fourth quarter leads. Doesn’t have a signature moment or game and has been increasingly invisible lately, except when getting exposed in the ground game. His "revenge" game vs. Bengals could not have been more of a dud.
Key Stats: 1 sack, 1 batted pass, 6 solo tackle, 28 snaps/game
Verdict – D: Hard to see him play out his age 40 season on a joke of a defense in a franchise hardwired to lose. Going to post close to 500 snaps if they keep this pace up, but with so few playmakers around him, the impact has been muted. He is an all-time great leader and exemplary human, but this DL has not been strong and now they are getting run on.
Key Stats : 6 GP, 1 Pressure, 16 tackles, 137.5 Passer Rating
Verdict – F: Will probably be out until the bye. Has not connected with any of the fellow safeties and communication issues are rampant. Showed up against the run and pass game with the Patriots but this has been brutal. Picked on when they do throw his way. Part of one of the worst secondaries in the NFL.
Key Stats: 103 Coverage Snaps. 97.9 Passer Rating
Verdict – D: Compared to last year, where he provided excellent bang for the buck, it’s an F. But, hey, he hasn’t been picked on as much as $19M corner Marlon Humphrey and he hasn’t needed Mayor Brandon Scott to rebuke him for offensive remarks about Baltimore, so we have to grade on a curve here. Even with Humphrey getting carved up, Minter hasn’t wanted to play him much and he’s fallen behind TJ Tampa now, too.
This was a total joke by the front office. Across the board. Every level. They got absolutely nothing out of the draft on defense – Zion Young (second round) has no pass rush and barely plays; Chandler Rivers hasn’t’ seen the field on defense in weeks – and you won’t find a bigger collective bust of new defensive coordinator plus lack of production from the players brought in during the offseason.

title: The Ravens' 5 Biggest Needs For 2027 (Excluding QB, Fingers Crossed)
full_text:
The Ravens refuse to acknowledge the depth of their problems.
Whether it’s failing general manager making silly buy-side trades at the deadline (and some that thankfully didn’t happen) and failing to unload contract of players who have no meaningful future here, or an overmatched rookie head coach dismissing calls to stop calling plays on defense in hopes he can grow into being an NFL head coach. Whether it’s refusing to bench underachieving veterans on bloated contracts who are hurting their product ($60M closer Trey Hendrickson, for instance) or choosing to make rookies healthy scratches every week despite the need to start seeing what they can.
It’s a woefully misguided organization and with six-straight losses and counting, it’s only getting worse. The biggest issue, of course, will be convincing two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson to stick around in 2027, and given what Lamar Jackson Entertainment has put on social media lately, that’s an uphill climb to say the least . It’s daunting all around, the head coach keeps talking and acting like someone who should be one-and-done, and this roster is in decay and needs an overhaul.
Even if you take quarterback out of the equation – which is impossible, but let’s do it anyway – there are glaring and massive needs facing this team in 2027. As it stands right now, here are their five biggest needs outside of QB, in reverse order:
Trading for Cam Jurgens was a failed stopgap measure . Thinking he is going to hold up for 2027 and play well while doing it would be based on pure folly; not game film here or in Philadelphia and not based on his medical history. Paying him $17M next year is a self-inflicted error but that’s GM Eric DeCosta’s brand, and this trade will haunt them.
They played a comp pick game picking up veteran center Ryan Neuzil, who has been riding the bench. Finding a long-term solution is vital; offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has been undermined by the rotating guards and shuffling offensive lines. Rookie guard Vega Ioane is still the best center on the roster, but they want him to focus on guard.
You can find plug-and-play starters on the second day of the draft.
Malaki Starks cannot handle deep duties in Minter’s defense and if he is married to split safety concepts , he better find a few guys who can do it. Free agent Jaylinn Hawkins has been a bust. Kyle Hamilton is a SAM linebacker.
It’s a pass-happy league and the Ravens have not been able to defend the middle of the field - short, intermediate or deep – since coordinator Mike Macdonald left after the 2023 season. This needs desperate attention and probably needs to be a proven veteran type if at all possible; this franchise stopped drafting or developing defensive backs with ball skills a long time ago.
Finally, Marlon Humphrey will be gone next season, along with a bunch of other cooked veterans on ridiculous contracts. But he’ll leave behind a $12M cap hit. Nate Wiggins has zero ball skills, Chidobe Awuzie won’t be back, and rookie slot corner Chandler Rivers never sees the field on defense despite Baltimore having the worst slot defense in the NFL … So yeah, this might be low because they need a handful.
Nice to see TJ Tampa finallly get to play and come up with their first pick by a corner all season, but this staff has shown no conviction in him.
This was allegedly a superpower for the Ravens and their wunderkind head coach . Oh well. More folly.
They tried to patch it up by keeping run-stuffer Broderick Washington around on a team-friendly deal and bringing back Calais Campbell for a second stint, despite being 40. They crossed their fingers that Nnamdi Madubuike would return to All Pro form after a neck injury negated almost all of his 2025 campaign.
And, worst of all, despite this being a lingering need DeCosta completely ignored it in any meaningful way in consecutive drafts that were loaded with DTs – one of which will go down as potentially generational. Madubuike as this point is a good player but might not be consistently great anymore, and he is only signed for one more year. Travis Jones is a nice rotational player but nothing more. This defense has lacked a spine for years, we already covered free safety, and Roquan Smith has been a marginal-at-best middle linebacker for years.
Better fortify the middle in a big way at the point of attack if this defense is ever not going to stink. (at least some youngsters are emerging on the edge).
Ronnie Stanley had a great career but he’s not going to be here by June 1 if this franchise has a clue. They should have drafted his successor by now and he is on borrowed time physically and is committing penalties in droves and the pass protection is going south. It’s time to move and this needs to a substantial commitment in terms of assets.
Not some hope-and-pray late round pick. If they don’t think enough of Carson Vinson to give him a run in a garbage season with journeyman Jacoby Brissett back there, don’t start selling parables about his potential and upside in the offseason. And the idea that Roger Rosengarten is a two-contract right tackle is in doubt; he can’t help on the blind side.

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis: Biggest Winners, Losers and Role Changes From Week 11
full_text:
The Ravens results do not change.
They lose, week after week, as questions mount about just how overmatched this front office and coaching staff appear to be . It’s six straight games and counting and given the piercing issues in all three aspects of play there is no reason to expect that to change anytime soon. This franchise refuses to embrace its obvious rebuild and continues to keep players like Adam Randall and Elijah Sarratt inactive, while abstaining from letting youngsters like Carson Vinson and rookie tight ends Josh Cuevas or Matthew Hibner play as much as they should .
There were definitely some noteworthy trends with the snap counts however – that always tells the story of what coaches really think beyond what they say – and hopefully a thorough youth movement is unleashed amid this lost season in which the job simply appears too big for Jesse Minter; well, both jobs: head coach and defensive coordinator .
The questions are coming regularly now about Minter relinquishing play calling duties and, around the league, the chatter about him perhaps not being cut out to be a head coach is mounting. The Ravens faced some new personnel scenarios on defense with corner Marlon Humphrey suspended by the team for the game and top defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike out with injury.
TJ Tampa : Minter has been slow to embrace this former mid-round pick despite his body type seemingly a better fit in his zone-heavy schemes than other boundary options. Minter barely played him in the first half (six snaps), preferring veteran Chidobe Awuzie, but with the secondary starting to get lit up in the second quarter he made the switch to the youngster.
Tampa played 39 snaps on defense, by far his most under Minter and his most, period, since Week 5 of 2025. Tampa responded by getting into excellent train coverage on Tet McMillan and picking off a pass in the back of the endzone for the first interception by a Ravens corner all season. Even with Humphrey coming back, it would take a truly cowardly organization to sit him for Humphrey, but with Eric DeCosta in charge, well, don’t hold your breath .
“I thought T.J. took advantage of the opportunity to play more,” Minter said.” I thought, man, the play two plays before the interception, great play as well, particularly where they're at and just trying to throw like the run-pass option slant there. Great play by him there.”
Mike Green: The pass rusher is having a true breakthrough in Year Two, he’s headed for double-digit sacks, and he is out-performing $60M alleged “closer” Trey Hendrickson in a big way against the run and getting to the QB. Green out-snapped the big-ticket free agent again and v astly outperformed him.
Green played 50 snaps – tied for second-most of his career and most since Minter took over. He produced five tackles and two sacks and two QB hits and will continue to pace this edge group in snaps. He and Tavius Robinson should be the starters next season, but good luck dumping Hendrickson’s contract.
“He gives you everything he's got from a physical standpoint,” Minter said. “He strikes people in the run game. There are times where he's taking on a lot bigger bodies, and he's holding his own, and then he does things in the pass rush game where he works well with other guys. He works well within games.”
Ja’Kobi Lane: Receivers DeCosta drafts almost always stink, and the learning curves tend to be steep . The heady days of rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle being called a genius this summer and Lane being a preseason superstar seem long ago. After a very rough game against the Chargers Lane’s passing snaps were slashed from 36 to just 23 against the Panthers, he continues to struggle to find his way in this offense and we suspect the shift to more 12 and 13 personnel is on (more tight end emphasis). He did not have a target in the game.
Matthew Hibne r: The rookie tight end was the big beneficiary of Lane’s slashed role; but it didn’t turn into much. Hibner went from 22 snaps against the Chargers to 33 against the Panthers, but he isn’t really separating and the big-play potential hasn’t shown up since before Lamar Jackson got hurt in Week 4. He had two receptions for 12 yards and unlocking his YAC is a must. Jacoby Brissett loves throwing to TEs and the have to get this cooking.

title: Ravens Rookie Head Coach Jesse Minter Still Resisting Calls To Divest Play Calling Duties
full_text:
Ravens rookie head coach Jesse Minter, struggling mightily to manage games and on-field situations, while also suffering as a defensive play caller, nudged a bit on Monday when probed about his failures as a coordinator.
For the second time in his 12 regular-season weeks on the job Minter was asked at a Monday press conference about his willingness to relinquish play calling duties of what’s becoming one of the worst defenses in franchise history. And unlike the first time, he offered an actual response.
Two weeks ago, he blurted out, “No,” when the topic was first broached and now, with his team holding the worst second-half scoring differential in the NFL (-98) and his defense giving up 33 points or more in four of the last five games, Minter (4-7) deigned to show some understanding of why he was being questioned about Anthony Weaver potentially taking over play calling for him.
“Everything crosses my mind,” Minter said when asked about considering a change on the headset, “but I’m always going to try to do what I think is best for where we are right now.”
So, that was still a no, but not quite as resounding. And with a lot less sass.
And if the Texans smash Minter’s defense on Sunday for a seventh-straight loss – and there is every reason to expect that to be the case – he will invariably be asked about this again before Baltimore takes its Week 13 bye. His highest-paid players continue to fail at their jobs and players now speak openly about the lack of “trust” and “execution,” while Minter himself was already begging for “leaders” to emerge in his locker room by October.
Minter’s tone changed when asked about having arguably both the NFL’s worst second half offense and defense (30-year-old offensive coordinator Declan Doyle suffers mightily once off his early-game script). "clearly everything,” was his response in terms of what needs to change in that regard.
In general, Mnter has been short of specifics and devoid of corrections but heavy on trite colloquialisms about “sticking together” and everyone “in it together,” that are straight from the John Harbaugh/Jim Harbaugh playbook.
Now that teams aren’t just throwing the ball all over the field on an overmatched secondary that was supposed to be one of the best in the NFL, the run defense has become a significant issue. Minter’s alleged $60M “closer” Trey Hendrickson not only offers no late pass rush but is getting attacked in the ground game. Expect that to continue, with Minter unwilling to bench overpaid veterans to this point (struggling $19M corner Marlon Humphrey will return to practice to this week, Minter said, after being deactivated Sunday for disparaging remarks about Baltimore on his podcast).
The Ravens entered the season boasting about a defense that should be among the best in the NFL, propelling the team to its self-purported Super Bowl expectations, but the best Minter could muster Monday about where that standard is now was:
“We can be a serviceable, productive defense, but right now it’s too inconsistent." Good luck sending out those season-ticket renewals off that.
Minter did take blame, in a more straightforward sense, for botching a two-minute drill at the end of the game, keeping two timeouts in his pocket with back-up quarterback Jacoby Brissett under assault and wasting close to a minute of precious time.
In hindsight “banging” a timeout after a QB sneak would have been the better decision, Minter offered, as he weighed the need to save a timeout for a potential sack or negative play later in the drive. “You always want to try to keep one for that,” he explained.
The Ravens have lost seven straight games in a season just once before, 2007, when Super Bowl head coach Brian Billick was fired. Minter’s defense has a lot in common with that one , and he continued to carry the look of someone who might not be cut out for a second year on the job.
“We haven’t played the level of defense I think we’re capable of,” Minter said.

title: Bills Show What NBC Didn't Want Viewers to See During Thanksgiving Halftime
full_text:
NBC network programming executives apparently took Johnny Rzeznik's lyrics literally.
In the Goo Goo Dolls' late 1990s smash hit "Iris," Rzeznik famously sings "And I don't want the world to see me, 'Cause I don't think that they'd understand."
With Rzeznik and Robby Takac ready to rock at halftime of their hometown Buffalo Bills ' Thanksgiving night game against the Kansas City Chiefs, NBC pulled the plug on the performance in favor of an interview with coach-turned-analyst Mike Tomlin about the Aaron Rodgers saga.
Rather than show the 10-minute performance live, NBC forced more Pittsburgh Steelers drama down the throats of viewers. The broadcast minimized the legendary rock band's halftime set down to a 30-second highlight clip.
After noticing the outcry on social media, the Bills' organization posted the entire performance across multiple channels, including X and YouTube.
Rather than the rain-soaked field, the Buffalo-born rockers set up shop on the Bills' Legends Deck at the new Highmark Stadium.
They opened the mini concert with back-to-back singles off the 1998 record Dizzy Up The Girl. Starting with "Slide" before breaking into "Broadway."
Despite the cold, wet conditions, the Goo Goo Dolls, led by the 60-year-old Rzeznik, captivated the soggy crowd by delivering a beautiful rendition of "Iris." The moment rivaled the band's iconic Independence Day performance in Niagara Square on July 4, 2004 when they played through a driving rain.
"Buffalo, show the whole world who we are tonight," said Rzeznik to the crowd after playing the final chord on guitar.
Bills' kicker Tyler Bass appeared to take the closing line to heart as he braved the challenging conditions to nail two long-range field goals in the fourth quarter. His 57-yarder broke a 10-10 tie at the gun, sending the fans into a frenzy.
Bass, who missed the entire 2025 season, has been the epitome of resilience , closely resembling the city he plays for.
The Goo Goo Dolls were initially thought to be the perfect fit to play the halftime show for the inaugural Highmark Stadium game on September 17.
Instead, the Bills and Prime Video opted for the Canadian-born Bare Naked Ladies , who, to put it mildly, failed to inspire the fans in attendance and the millions watching the Thursday Night Football show. The organization, however, made amends by inviting Rzeznik and Takac to perform at the first-ever Thanksgiving home game in franchise history.

title: Andy Reid Unhappy With Controversial Ruling in Bills-Chiefs Clash
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills outlasted the Kansas City Chiefs during a rain-soaked showdown on Thanksgiving Night.
Buffalo secured a 13-10 victory thanks to a 57-yard field goal from Tyler Bass as time expired. That clutch kick might not have happened if not for a controversial reversal that took place on an earlier Kansas City drive.
With fewer than two minutes remaining in the game, the Chiefs appeared to convert a first-down on third-and-10 when Patrick Mahomes hit Rashee Rice for an 11-yard gain, which could have been the spark they needed to pull off a game-winning drive of their own. Their excitement ended quickly as an official replay reversed the call, ruling that Rice bobbled the ball as he hit the ground, calling it incomplete.
We already saw Brittany Mahomes lose her mind on social media over the call. Now, Kansas City head coach Andy Reid sounded off, although he was far more measured than Mrs. Mahomes. Reid said he believes the replay was not clear and obvious, saying he didn't agree with the call.
“Not one that I agreed with, but they said it came from New York,” Reid said. “It’s not from these guys, our guys called it a completion — the guys who were working the game," Reid said after the game . "I’m not sure what they saw. I saw he had control of the ball, then his elbow hit, then the ball hit, but he had control. Normally, in those kind of situations, it’s got to be clear and obvious. And to me, that was not clear and obvious.”
To Reid's credit, he was simply giving his opinion and didn't seem to be willing to pin the loss on that single play.
That was a far different tone from Brittany Mahomes, who said they " can't play football without getting it called against us ." That's a rather interesting statement when the Chiefs are typically the ones who receive the benefit of the doubt with the refs.
The Chiefs also had a chance to redeem themselves after the play. Their defense forced a three-and-out and Buffalo had to punt the ball away. They gained no yards on three plays and had to punt it back to the Bills, which allowed them to set up the game-winning kick from Bass.
It was a strange turn of events down the stretch and both teams had several missed opportunities. This play was huge in deciding the game, but it was far from the only factor.

title: Three Thanksgiving Game Balls for Bills' Consequential Win over Chiefs
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are now 2.0 full games ahead of the Kansas City Chiefs in the conference standings following a last-second head-to-head win on Thanksgiving Night.
The Bills (10-1) remain atop the AFC playoff picture, but it could be easily swung in the opposite direction during the Week 12 holiday matchup. Not to mention Bills' quarterback Josh Allen struggled mightily in the elements, passing for only 81 yards.
Trailing by a 10-7 margin heading into the fourth quarter, Buffalo needed two long-range field goals from Tyler Bass to secure a 13-10 win .
"T-Bass just being T-Bass," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady . "He bailed us out. I mean, that was outstanding in those conditions. Extremely impressive."
Naturally, Bass gets one of On SI's three game balls for his role in the highly-consequential regular season victory.
Here's more on the kicker and the two other game ball recipients . They'll have a mini bye's worth of time to enjoy their Week 12 plaudits. Buffalo returns to action in n December 6 at the New England Patriots.
After missing the entire 2025 season due to a core muscle injury, Bass has been nothing shy of spectacular this season.
He leads the NFL with 108 points scored buoyed by a remarkable 26-of-27 clip on field goals.
"I've worked really hard since November, just when I was out of my surgery and just really grinded. All I had to do is work out and just train and train and train," said Bass postgame.
First, Bass nailed a 54-yarder on a cold, rainy night in Orchard Park. Then, with 00:04 remaining in regulation, kicking off a worn grass field, he cleared the crossbar on a 57-yard bomb.
"Just going out there, I just really just trust my preparation, trust my teammates. We worked really hard all week," said Bass.
The reigning NFL rushing champion appears to be running harder and harder as the weeks go by. In miserable weather conditions, Cook carried the rock 32 times for 117 yards and one touchdown.
It was the true definition of grit, and it was the only offensive success the Bills were able to muster up against the Chiefs and defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo.
“Josh Allen has 80 yards passing [and we win], kind of speaks to our football team. And it speaks to who James Cook is, and the O-line and the guys not giving a damn about anything else, besides just finding a way to win a football game," said Brady.
Cook extended his NFL record in the Week 12 win, rushing for 75+ yards and 1+ touchdown for the 10th game in a row. Hall-of-Famers LaDainian Tomlinson and John Riggins did it only eight consecutive outings.
"James is playing really well. Every one of those yards was really hard to get, you know, especially going against that defense and that scheme," said Brady.
We know there's still a lot of football left, and it's too early for a victory lap, but special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers deserves to take a bow .
Much like the Bills did on the road against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 5, the special teams units completely out-classed the opponent on Thanksgiving night, and it's goes well beyond the excellent field goal operation .
Seventh-round rookie punter Tommy Doman dropped three of five attempts inside the Chiefs' 20-yard line, twice backing them up during the final 2:00.
Then, there's return specialist Greg Dortch, who continued to display his trademark decisiveness when fielding the Chiefs' final punt and setting Bass up for the game-winning attempt.
Rodgers is likely responsible for Dortch landing with the Bills. He coached the undersized speedster while serving as Arizona Cardinals' special teams coordinator.

title: Bills' Weird Thanksgiving Night Win Has Apparently Broken Brittany Mahomes
full_text:
Apparently, it was the sixth consecutive regular season loss that set her off.
The Buffalo Bills posted a victory over the Kansas City Chiefs and heavily-decorated quarterback Patrick Mahomes for the sixth year in a row, winning thanks to a 57-yard field goal by Tyler Bass at the gun on Thanksgiving night.
Following Buffalo's 13-10 triumph that sent the Chiefs to 8-3 overall, and 2.0 full games behind the Bills (10-1) in the AFC standings , Brittany Mahomes used her Instagram account to go scorched earth on NFL officiating for apparently deliberately penalizing her husband's team.
"HAHAHAHAHAHA WHAT A JOKE," said the text overlay on Instagram story slide posted by Mahomes, whose @brittanylynne account boasts 2.1 million followers.
The angry football wife's primary point of contention stems from Kansas City's second-to-last possession with about 1:50 remaining in the fourth quarter.
With the Chiefs backed up to their own 9-yard line, facing a 3rd-and-10, Mahomes uncorked a liner over the middle to wide receiver Rashee Rice just beyond the first-down marker.
Rice appeared to make a contested catch with Bills' safety Amani Hooker delivering a hit as the ball arrived. As the Chiefs' receiver went to the ground, the ball appeared to move slightly and clearly made contact with the turf.
After a booth-initiated replay, the on-field call was reversed as the pass was ruled incomplete. As a result, the Chiefs were forced to punt it back to the Bills without being able to flip the field position and the score tied, 10-10.
Buffalo was unable to cash in, going three-and-out and subsequently punting back to the Chiefs, but it retained crucial field position advantage that eventually allowed for the long range game-winning field goal.
"Guess we can't even play football without getting it called against us... not sure what an actual catch is after that I guess? I don't wanna hear s--t anymore from anyone," said the three-time Super Bowl champion quarterback's ranting significant other in the first of seven straight slides referencing the game's officiating.
Brittany Mahomes posts a complaint on Instagram about the Rashee Rice no catch call https://t.co/wv4W21LApj pic.twitter.com/YTeDZaKeqW
Mahomes followed with five consecutive slides questioning the overturned incompletion, and she ended with a photo showing head referee Alex Kemp using a warning station on the Bills' sideline. The photo, which was part of a shared social media post, included the text "This would be front page news if he was on the Chiefs sideline."
Apparently, Mahomes does not remember the 2024 AFC Championship Game when her husband was the beneficiary of an outrageous call that the Chiefs cashed in for a touchdown on the way to winning by three points.
With Kansas City holding a 14-10 lead over the Bills late in the first half, wide receiver Xavier Worthy was awarded a catch down to the Bills' 3-yard line despite the ball hitting the ground as he jostled for possession against safety Cole Bishop.

title: Five Winners & Two Losers From Bills' Last Second Win Over Chiefs in Week 12
full_text:
The weather played a huge factor on Thanksgiving, just as we thought it would. The Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs both struggled to find sustained success on offense, leading to a low-scoring affair between two of the top teams in the AFC.
Following a slew of great plays from their special teams, Buffalo pulled off the 13-10 win as Tyler Bass drilled a 57-yard kick with no time remaining in the game. The Bills improved to 10-1 on the year and have a firm grasp on the No. 1 seed in the AFC.
There were a lot of highs and lows in this one for both teams, and here, we look at which Bills stood out as both winners and losers in their latest victory.
Josh Allen had two interceptions in the red zone and the second could have been detrimental to the Bills since they were trailing 10-7. That wasn't the case, however, as the defense held and forced a punt on a three-and-out. They were aided by Kingsley Suamataia who drew an unnecessary roughness penalty, setting up a third-and-16, but Greg Rousseau ended the drive.
Rousseau, who entered this game with a career-high 10 sacks and added to that total by recording his 11th sack to force a fourth-and-23. That was Buffalo's only sack on Patrick Mahomes, but it came at a pivotal moment.
The Bills had a chance to put this one away with roughly 1:30 to play. Allen hit Khalil Shakir for an 11-yard gain, moving the ball to the Chiefs' 36-yard line. From there, they could have begun forcing Kansas City to use timeouts while trying for better field goal position.
That play didn't stand, however, as Dalton Kincaid was called for offensive pass interference on the play. The Bills never recovered on that drive and had to punt. They were fortunate to get the ball back, otherwise this penalty would have looked far worse.
Special teams matter and for the second week in a row, rookie Tommy Doman Jr. came up huge. In Week 11, he had a 30-yard completion on a fake punt. This week, he reminded us all the real reason Buffalo used a seventh-round draft pick to bring him in.
Doman had five punts on the day and pinned the Chiefs inside the 20 on three of those, two of which were during the final minutes of the game. His ability to flip field position was huge, and the Bills may not have won without him.
It wasn't pretty, but James Cook topped 100 yards on Thursday, adding to his already impressive yardage total for the season. He also scored his 11th rushing touchdown of the season, a feat he's accomplished four consecutive seasons now. Cook had 32 carries for 117 yards and a touchdown, giving the Bills just enough in this gritty win.
The weather was bad, but that's not an excuse for some of the issues Josh Allen had on Thursday. It was his worst performance of the season as he had just 81 yards passing and threw two interceptions, both in the red zone. Allen said after the game that he needs to be better going forward , and vowed to make that happen.
Kansas City punter Matt Araiza has a cannon for a leg and was set to unleash it with 15 seconds to play. With the Chiefs pinned at their own 11 (thanks to Doman), Araiza was trying to flip the field and force overtime. Buffalo Joe Andreessen had other plans.
The hometown hero was able to get a hand on the punt and while it wasn't a full block, it slowed the ball down as it traveled 45 yards and into the arms of Greg Dortch. The Buffalo return man did the rest as he returned it 17 yards to the 39, setting up the game-winning kick.
Tyler Bass isn't afraid of bad weather. Bad weather is afraid of Tyler Bass.
The veteran kicker made history on Thursday as he became the first player to ever hit a game-tying and game-winning kick of 54-yards or more in the same fourth quarter.
Tyler Bass is the first kicker in NFL history with a game-tying 54+ yard FG and a game-winning 54+ yard FG in the 4th quarter of the same game. pic.twitter.com/AVRnDqoluO
Not only did Bass drill a 54-yarder to tie the game up at 10 early in the fourth quarter, but he then hit a 57-yarder as time expired to deliver the win. The clutch kick was never in doubt either as Bass drilled the ball through the middle of the uprights.
TYLER BASS CALLED GAME!!!!!!!!!! 📺: NBC pic.twitter.com/OXGtrPBFRE
Bass was rightfully named the MVP of the game after that performance and it's safe to say the Bills would not have won without him.

title: Four Biggest Takeaways From Bills Ugly Win Over Chiefs on Thanksgiving
full_text:
We knew the weather would be bad , but somehow, it seemed worse than expected. The Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs squared off on Thanksgiving Night and while there wasn't much offense, the end was exciting.
The two teams played a field position game and in the end, the Bills found a way to escape with a 13-10 win as Tyler Bass hit a 57-yarder with no time remaining on the clock. That win improved the Bills to 9-1 and should slow down the complaints about their soft schedule . For the Chiefs, it dropped them to 8-3 and makes their path to the No. 1 seed in the AFC incredibly difficult.
It was another fun chapter in the battle of Josh Allen vs. Patrick Mahomes, even though the star quarterbacks had very little to do with the outcome as it was a game led by defense and special teams. Let's look back at the game and check out a few big takeaways from the victory.
The Chiefs scored a touchdown on their first drive in the third quarter of the game, giving them a 10-7 lead. It also ended a sensational streak for Jim Leonhard's defense. Buffalo had not given up a touchdown since the opening quarter of their Week 8 victory over the Baltimore Ravens.
By keeping Kansas City out of the end zone until the second half, the Bills tied the 2008 Ravens for the longest streak without giving up a touchdown over the past 20 seasons. Buffalo had gone 46 drives, including three consecutive games.
The #Bills have now tied the 2008 Ravens with 46 straight drives without allowing a touchdown, the best mark of any NFL team in the last 20 seasons. https://t.co/WHBw9zqvzs
That's an impressive feat, but the critics will still have plenty to say about it. Not only did they play against backup quarterbacks throughout that stretch, but even slowing down Mahomes will come with an asterisk. The weather was clearly a factor as both teams were struggling to move the ball the way we're accustomed to seeing, evidenced by a 7-3 halftime lead for the Bills.
Of course, the Bills can't help who they face, all they can do is handle the assignments. The same is true of the weather. They have no say in the conditions, but can only control how they respond. In this game, they responded perfectly by holding the Chiefs to 10 points, but they need a few more big performances to truly shut down the criticism for good.
Josh Allen is one of the best players in the entire NFL and he gives the Bills a chance to win every week. We can acknowledge that while also admitting that he has had a problem with turnovers as of late.
Allen had two picks in the red zone against the Chiefs. One of those will be excused because the ball bounced off the hands of Khalil Shakir, but it still was an ugly pass that Shakir might not have bobbled if it was accurate.
With these interceptions, Allen has now thrown an interception in each of the past five games and has seven during that span. We can attribute some of the issues on Thursday to the wet conditions, but Allen wasn't sharp the past couple of weeks either.
With a tough stretch of games coming up, Allen must find a way to get this under control. If not, they could start dropping games they should win.
Special teams are often overlooked, but they are vital to a franchise's success. The Bills were reminded of that during this outing. In the terrible weather, they had solid performances from their special teams units, which included seeing Tyler Bass drill a 54-yard field. That was a win for the Bills, while the Chiefs had to watch Harrison Butker miss a 46-yarder in the fourth quarter.
Following the miss, Buffalo had to punt it away, but Tommy Doman Jr. was able to flip the field. The rookie punted the ball 57 yards and the Bills forced Josh Downs out of bounds at the seven yard line. Kansas City then had a three-and-out, but Matt Araiza had an ugly 38-yarder that gave Buffalo the ball near midfield. The Bills still couldn't capitalize, but Doman delivered with another solid punt. This time, he kicked it 46 yards and the Chiefs had to start from their own 11 with just 26 seconds to play.
Once again, special teams came up huge as Joe Andreessen tipped the final punt from Matt Araiza, and Greg Dortch ran the punt back 17 yards to the Kansas City 39. That allowed Bass to drill a 57-yarder , giving the Bills a 13-10 win.
This might not have impacted the game itself, but The Goo Goo Dolls were done dirty. While Wu-Tang Clan and Miranda Lambert got to perform in front of massive audiences, The Goo Goo Dolls were on air for about 30 seconds.
Instead of showing their halftime show, NBC aired a discussion between Mike Tirico and Mike Tomlin about Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers. The band signed on expecting a national audience and didn't get that, which is about as bad as outing a guy for having an "ice cream sandwich assistant."

title: Bills-Chiefs Halftime Show Takes Surprise Turn After NBC Programming Change
full_text:
One of the best parts of the Thanksgiving Day games is often the halftime shows. There have been some iconic performances throughout the years and a well-known band is set to perform at halftime of the Buffalo Bills matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs tonight.
The Goo Goo Dolls , who are from Buffalo, will be on the field to entertain the crowd at New Highmark Stadium. Unfortunately, fans who are watching the action on NBC won't be able to see the show.
In a surprise move, NBC decided to pass on showing the halftime concert. Instead, they're going to air a discussion between Mike Tirico and Mike Tomlin, who will be talking about the situation going on with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
pic.twitter.com/X7nKcug3KK
This is a massive letdown for fans who wanted to see the local band take the field, especially since there will be plenty of other opportunities for NBC to play the discussion between Tirico and Tomlin.
While the halftime show is preferable for Bills fans, there's no denying that the situation in Pittsburgh is interesting. Future Hall of Fame quarterback Aaron Rodgers was benched by head coach Mike McCarthy following a loss to the Philadelphia Eagles. McCarthy decided to turn to Mason Rudolph, a decision that did not sit well with Rodgers.
The veteran quarterback appeared on The Pat McAfee Show Wednesday and went scorched earth on McCarthy and the Steelers. Rodgers accused the coach of falling asleep during meetings, missing meetings, and struggling to do his job. He exposed a lot about what went on behind the scenes, even telling everyone that McCarthy had an assistant who got him ice cream sandwiches.
Rodgers and McCarthy are no strangers to one another, having spent 13 years together with the Green Bay Packers. They even won a Super Bowl during that span and while they had some issues near the end of that run, it seemed as though both were excited to work together again this year.
McCarthy does have some support, including from Art Rooney II . The Steelers also decided to move on from Rodgers, which could end up being the end of his storied career
Tomlin, who spent 19 seasons as a head coach in Pittsburgh should offer a unique perspective, but he still wasn't there with McCarthy.
