title: Expert Predictions For Detroit Lions Matchup With Chicago Bears
full_text:
The Detroit Lions will look to secure their seventh straight win when they take on the Chicago Bears Thursday afternoon.
The Lions are coming off a 31-21 defeat of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 11. Meanwhile, Chicago prevailed against the New Orleans Saints last week, 21-13.
Without further ado, here are the predictions from the Detroit Lions On SI staff for the Lions' Week 12 matchup with Chicago.
The Lions and Bears are meeting in what is the biggest Thanksgiving in recent memory for the franchise. The team that wins this game will step into the driver's seat for the NFC North with six games remaining and could put themselves in position to contend for the No. 1 seed.
As a result, I'm predicting that Dan Campbell will try to bring the fight to the Bears and be ultra-aggressive. With how explosive the Bears' offense can be, I expect Campbell to press the issue and go for it on multiple fourth-downs. This could turn into a shootout, but I think the Lions' ability to run the ball and manage the clock will be the difference-maker. After years of struggles on Thanksgiving, the Lions get over the hump and defeat the Bears in a barnburner.
If the Lions are going to notch their seventh straight victory Thursday, they're going to have to absolutely earn it.
They're set to face one of their stiffest tests of the season, going up against Ben Johnson and the Chicago Bears.
Heading into the Week 12 affair, the Bears own both a top-10 offense and a top-10 defense. And just like the Lions, they can absolutely pound the rock.
So, I believe this clash between NFC North rivals will come down to who wins the battle in the trenches. While it won't be easy, I believe that Detroit will open up just enough holes for Jahmyr Gibbs to run through, enabling Dan Campbell's squad to secure the Thanksgiving Day victory.
The Lions now face their toughest test of the 2026 season.
Ben Johnson will have the Bears offense ready to take advantage of certain weaknesses in the Lions’ secondary.
While both teams will look to establish the run, Detroit’s offense will execute more consistently.
Caleb Williams is turning the football over too much and Kelvin Sheppard’s defense will capitalize.
This game could become very high scoring, which favors Detroit.
Thursday is a major test for the Lions, going up against Ben Johnson and the red-hot Chicago Bears. Additionally, this is the Lions’ third game in 11 days, including an overseas flight to Munich, Germany.
The Lions have the opportunity to prove that the defensive improvement is more than just a lack of competition. In recent weeks, the Lions have seen their defense shut down the passing game, but their best competition in those contests was against an already injured Baker Mayfield.
The Bears have a knack for explosive plays, but also do not grade out well in play action. With Jahmyr Gibbs as the bellcow back in Detroit, that is a mismatch offensive coordinator Drew Petzing can exploit.
That said, with the recent injuries to Aidan Hutchinson, Jack Campbell and now underrated pass-rushing defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard, I see the Lions unable to come out on top on Thanksgiving.

title: Lions Week 12 Depth Chart Against Bears
full_text:
The Lions’ defense will receive its biggest test in a while when it takes the field Thursday against Ben Johnson and the Chicago Bears.
The Bears enter the Thanksgiving Day tilt with the No. 8 offense in the NFL, averaging 26.2 points per game.
It furthers the significance of the return of D.J. Reed to the Lions’ starting lineup.
Reed, the No. 1 cornerback for defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard's unit, has missed the last three games with a hip ailment. He'll provide a big boost to Detroit's secondary, curtailing the efforts of Chicago signal-caller Caleb Williams through the air.
Here's an updated look at the Lions' depth chart ahead of their Week 12 clash with the Bears.
Starter: Jared Goff. Backup: Joshua Dobbs.
Goff will make his 80th consecutive start when he takes the field Thursday against the Bears. He continues to be the straw that stirs the drink for the Lions, with 20 touchdowns and just four interceptions to his name thus far in 2026. Drew Petzing & Co. will be relying on him to play a clean game in the holiday clash.
Starter: Jahmyr Gibbs. Backup: Sione Vaki. Reserves: Jacob Saylors. Inactive: Isiah Pacheco (Injured reserve).
Gibbs took over in the second half again last week against the Buccaneers. The do-it-all back finished the Week 11 contest with 98 yards and two touchdowns on 23 carries.
Expect the Lions to ride him early and often once again Thursday vs. the Bears.
Starters: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa. Backups: Tay Martin, DeAndre Carter. Inactive: Kendrick Law (Injured reserve), Tom Kennedy (Injured reserve).
The Lions got a big game from Williams vs. Tampa Bay, with “Jamo” recording a game-high 93 yards and a score. Meanwhile, St. Brown amassed just 37 yards on five catches. I expect an uptick in production from the All-Pro receiver vs. the Bears.
Starter: Sam LaPorta. Backup: Brock Wright. Reserves: Tyler Conklin.
Starters: Penei Sewell (left), Blake Miller (right). Backup: Larry Borom. Inactive: Gio Manu (Non-Football Injury).
Sewell continues to be the very best tackle in all of football. He's logged 94.0 overall PFF grade through the season's first 11 weeks, including a 94.8 run-blocking mark (first among all OTs).
Starters: Christian Mahogany (left), Tate Ratledge (right). Backup: Miles Frazier. Inactive: Ben Bartch (Injured reserve).
Mahogany and Ratledge have been solid all season for Detroit. But, they certainly will face a stiff challenge Thursday against Bears interior defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons. Simmons is coming off a three-sack performance against the Saints in Week 11.
Starter: Juice Scruggs. Backup: Ratledge Reserve: Seth McLaughlin. Inactive: Cade Mays (Injured reserve).
Scruggs continues to log valuable reps in place of Mays, who has been placed on injured reserve for a second time this season. Scruggs, who owns an overall grade of 75.4 from Pro Football Focus, has been a godsend for Detroit, and has become arguably the best acquisition of GM Brad Holmes of the past offseason.
Starters: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams. Backups: Levi Onwuzurike. Reserve: Anthony Lucas (practice squad elevation), Mekhi Wingo. Inactive: Skyler Gill-Howard (Injured reserve)
Gill-Howard was placed on injured reserve after suffering a knee injury a week ago against the Buccaneers. It came on a goal-line play in which he was being used as an extra blocker. It's an unfortunate end to a solid rookie campaign for the sixth-round pick.
In his place, the Lions have called up defensive end Anthony Lucas from the practice squad. It marks the second time he's been elevated, as he also logged 12 defensive snaps against the Miami Dolphins in Week 9.
Starters: DJ Wonnum (Questionable; back), Derrick Moore. Backups: Tyler Lacy, Ahmed Hassanein. Reserves: Eric O'Neill, Tyrus Wheat. Inactive: Aidan Hutchinson (Injured reserve), Payton Turner (Injured reserve).
Wonnum is questionable for Detroit's holiday clash with Chicago with a back ailment. If he can't go, it makes it even more pivotal that Moore delivers a strong performance. Just last week against Tampa Bay, he generated five total pressures, including a sack of Buccaneers QB Baker Mayfield.
Starters: Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez. Backups: Trevor Nowaske, K.J. Britt, Owen Pappoe. Reserve: Joe Bachie, Amen Ogbongbemiga. Inactive: Jack Campbell (Injured reserve), Jimmy Rolder (Injured reserve), Damone Clark (Injured reserve), Devin White (Injured reserve).
Detroit's linebackers continue to step up in the absence of Jack Campbell. In the team's win over Tampa Bay last week, Rodriguez and Britt notably delivered strong efforts. The Lions certainly will need more of the same against Williams & Co. Thursday.
Starters: Roger McCreary, D.J. Reed. Backups: Rock Ya-Sin, Nick Whiteside Reserve: Khalil Dorsey. Inactive: Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (shoulder)
The cornerbacks room receives a big boost with D.J. Reed being active, after missing the last three weeks with a hip injury. The Lions No. 1 corner was on a heater prior to the ailment, receiving some of his very best coverage grades of the season from Pro Football Focus.
Reed and the Lions’ cornerbacks will have their hands full against Bears leading receiver Luther Burden III. Burden enters the Thanksgiving Day affair with 51 catches, 654 yards and four touchdowns on the season.
Starters: Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph. Backups: Chuck Clark (Questionable; hamstring), Andre Cisco Reserves: Christian Izien, Keith Abney. Inactive: Avonte Maddox (Injured reserve), Thomas Harper (Injured reserve).
Joseph did not have a hugely productive day in his season debut a week ago against the Bucs. However, he did stay on the field for the entirety of the game, a huge positive for Dan Campbell's squad.
Clark, who possessed the green dot for Sheppard's defense against Tampa Bay, is questionable this week with a hamstring injury. If he can't go against the Bears, it'd be a significant loss for the back-end of the defense.
Kicker: Jake Bates. Punter: Jack Fox. Long-snapper: Hogan Hatten. Kick returners: DeAndre Carter, Jacob Saylors Punt returner: Carter.
Bates missed one-of-two field-goal attempts against the Bucs last week. It came on a 53-yard attempt on Detroit's first offensive possession of the game.
The Lions definitely would like to see him go perfect Thursday, in what will likely be a close game against the divisional rival Bears.

title: Matt LaFleur Failed Packers in Loss to Sean McVay’s Rams
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Christian Watson was on the type of heater that had become typical of his season.
At the 2-minute warning of the Green Bay Packers’ game at the Rams on Wednesday, Watson had caught all four targets for 65 yards, including a 32-yard catch that set up the team’s first score and a touchdown that pulled it within 13-10 midway through the second quarter.
Everything changed at the 2-minute mark, though. On fourth-and-1, Jordan Love floated one to the sideline to Watson, who was obliterated by Rams safety Kamren Kinchens. Watson suffered a concussion, Kinchens was ejected …
And the game was over for the Packers.
The Packers went from a 13-13 halftime tie to losing 26-13. They gained only 55 yards in the second half, with Love throwing for 44.
“Oh, yeah, you need your best players out there,” coach Matt LaFleur said after the game. “When they’re not out there, it certainly hurts your chances. He’s a guy that’s tough to replace – the combination of speed and size, his ability to move around our offense and put him in different spots. I think he’s playing at a really high level right now.”
LaFleur’s answer sounds like excuse-making, though that probably wasn’t his intention.
Regardless, it’s a coach’s job to come up with answers and LaFleur failed miserably.
Is it hard to replace a premier receiver like Watson? Of course it is. He’s third in the league with 981 receiving yards and probably would have blown past 1,000 yards on Wednesday.
But look at what his good friend, Rams coach Sean McVay, overcame in leading his team to a fifth consecutive win.
What’s harder than replacing one premier receiver? How about replacing two.
Puka Nacua, who led the NFL in receptions and yards last season, is on injured reserve following knee surgery. Davante Adams, who led the NFL in touchdown receptions last season, is on injured reserve with a hamstring injury. He might not be an elite receiver with his 34th birthday approaching but had two huge games this season.
The Rams beat the Packers with Konata Mumpfield, a seventh-round pick last year, as the team’s leading receiver.
At least the Packers had Matthew Golden, a first-round pick last year and breakout star this year. However, instead of picking up the slack and carrying the passing game on his back, he caught 1-of-5 targets. He was given two opportunities during the second half. One pass was intercepted and another pass was ruled incomplete after initially being deemed an interception.
The Rams wound up blowing out the Packers in the second half. They went three-and-out-punt, two plays and an interception, three-and-out punt and seven plays and an interception. Their 19 minutes, 20 seconds of time of possession for the game was the fourth-lowest for any team this season, which played a role in the defense’s demise.
McVay is one of the best coaches in the league. He’s one of those coaches who can beat your team with his players and then beat his team with your players. No Nacua and Adams? No problem for McVay’s Rams. No Watson? Impossible-to-overcome problem for LaFleur’s Packers.
Obviously, all teams aren’t created equally from a talent perspective. With the dynamic backfield duo of Blake Corum and Kyren Williams, McVay has a powerhouse running game, and he leaned on it to run over the Packers during the second half. The Packers have no running game whatsoever.
But, again, credit to McVay, who probably would rather throw the ball over the yard but understands the reality and is willing to adjust.
It wasn’t just the receivers. The Rams opened the game without their starting center and left guard. On the first play of the fourth quarter, their starting right tackle was injured. On the second play of the fourth quarter, their starting left guard was injured.
With four backup linemen on the field, the Rams rushed for 122 yards in the fourth quarter.
The Packers couldn’t run for 122 yards in a game if they lined up with nine linemen on the field.
Green Bay is on pace for the worst rushing attack in NFL history. The left tackle was a first-round pick. The left guard – or the player who is supposed to be the left guard – was given a huge contract in free agency. The center was given a big contract in free agency. The right tackle was a second-round pick. Three veterans were added early in the season.
It’s possible that LaFleur was handed terrible personnel on the offensive line.
Then again, it’s possible – maybe even likely – that LaFleur’s offensive line coach, Luke Butkus, has done a terrible job in developing those players. It’s possible that the team’s never-ending quest for finding players capable of playing multiple positions means they don’t have blockers capable of playing a single position.
By injuries or by choice, the Packers have churned through seven starting line combinations.
It’s also possible the one thing that’s wrong with the running game is having a head coach and play-caller who won’t call running plays, even though running the ball has been a big part of his history with the team.
Against the Vikings, who have the best blitz packages in the game, the Packers ran the ball 16 times. Against the Rams, who have the best collection of pass rushers in the game, the Packers ran the ball 14 times.
How does that make any sense?
Against the Rams, the Packers handed off the ball six times for 37 yards in the second quarter. Savion Williams had a 13-yard run and MarShawn Lloyd had a 10-yard run. Only four running plays were called in the second half of a game that didn’t hit a two-score margin until there was 6:13 left in regulation.
Sean Rhyan had some thoughts on how to change the #Packers offense. @fox11news pic.twitter.com/kMsK0Fp6Yf
“When your first two runs are negative runs, it’s hard but it’s our first two runs,” center Sean Rhyan said. “You’ve got to let us be able to get through it and set our pads and figure out how they’re playing it instead of, shit, negative-6 rushing yards and just throwing it up. It’s hard, especially when they know what they’re trying to do.”
Good teams are capable of winning games in multiple ways. The Packers, at least on offense, are capable of winning games only if Love plays like an MVP.
That’s on LaFleur. It’s on his game plans, his play-calling and the men he hired for key roles on the coaching staff.
Eleven games into the season, it is what it is. Running games are built on the practice field in August, not do-or-die games in December and January.
The Packers’ flickering playoff hopes will rest on Love and his receivers. They can’t run the football because they haven’t run the football and won’t run the football. Everybody knows that, which is why they’re running out of time and their season is in danger of running into the abyss of elimination.
The Packers were turned into turkeys by the Rams last night in yet another big-game loss. That and more bad holiday puns in this week's Overreactions. ⬇️ https://t.co/0OWYrffCTQ

title: Snaps, Studs, Duds: Micah Parsons Wasn’t Only Big Change for Packers vs. Rams
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers’ blowout loss at the hands of the Los Angeles Rams on Wednesday night marked the 164th game of the season. The Packers possessed the ball for 19 minutes and 20 seconds, the fourth-worst mark for any team.
Here’s our weekly analysis of the Packers’ snap counts, with a big change at one position group and perhaps another big change coming next week. Plus, what did the return of Micah Parsons mean?
The Packers played only 46 snaps on offense.
Quarterback: Jordan Love went the distance. He helped the Packers forge a tie with a strong first half but was part of the team-wide debacle in the second half. More on that later.
Running backs: With Josh Jacobs inactive, Kaleb Johnson was the main man with 24 snaps. Chris Brooks was next with 19 and MarShawn Lloyd settled for scraps with three.
Johnson’s first three carries lost 8 yards. He didn’t have a prayer on any of those, with tight ends blowing blocks on the first two carries and nobody blocking on the third. He finished the night with eight carries for 13 yards. His worst play, though, was a false start in the fourth quarter. It doomed the drive, with the Rams turning Green Bay’s three-and-out punt into a field goal to make it a two-score game.
With the potential of Jacobs returning to the lineup next week, Johnson might be back in the doghouse.
“We got what we wanted on the pass and we have a false start,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “It’s unacceptable. We can’t put you in the game if you’re going to go out there and create negative plays. We can’t do it. It’s just tough to win games when you’re beating yourself.”
Receivers: Matthew Golden played a unit-high 38 snaps but was unable to carry the passing game with Christian Watson exiting after 26 snaps with a concussion. Without Watson for the second half, Savion Williams played 35 snaps, Bo Melton played 17 and J. Michael Sturdivant played eight.
Watson caught 4-of-4 targets for 65 yards. The rest of the receivers caught a combined 4-of-12 targets for 62 yards, including just 1-of-5 for Golden.
Tight ends: Tucker Kraft played all but one snap in another forgettable performance. The Packers paid Kraft top dollar and aren’t getting anything resembling a return on investment. He caught three passes for 24 yards with one fumble.
While the Rams bullied the Packers with two- and three-tight-end sets, Mark Redman played eight snaps and Jonnu Smith played six.
Offensive line: Kevin Zeitler made his long-awaited first start but suffered an injured ankle when Savion Williams clipped him on one of the team’s few successful running plays. So, Zeitler played 24 snaps and Aaron Banks played the final 22.
The rest of the line – including center Sean Rhyan in his return to the lineup – played every snap. PFF charged Rhyan, Belton and Banks with a team-high three pressures apiece. Banks provided some thunder as a run blocker, including a pancake on a nice run by MarShawn Lloyd.
The Packers played 78 snaps on defense.
Edges: What would the return of Micah Parsons mean for what had been a four-man rotation? As usual, Lukas Van Ness led the unit with 49 snaps. It was balanced otherwise, with Barryn Sorrell playing 31, followed by Brenton Cox with 30, Parsons with 28 and Dani Dennis-Sutton with 27. So, Parsons’ debut didn’t cost anyone a big share of the playing time.
The Packers had 12 pressures, according to Next Gen Stats. Parsons had four, Cox had two, Sorrell had one and Van Ness and Dennis-Sutton had zero.
As usual, Sorrell’s snaps were supplemented by a large role on special teams (16 snaps). Dennis-Sutton has become a bigger factor in the kicking game with 19 snaps.
Defensive tackles: Chris McClellan saw a huge jump in playing time. Same with Anthony Campbell.
Usually, Karl Brooks leads the unit in snaps and everyone else falls behind in a balanced rotation. Against the Rams, the rookie McClellan played 52 snaps. Brooks and Campbell were next with 43, followed by Jordon Riley with 35. Devonte Wyatt, who was shaken up at one point, played a unit-low 30 snaps and was guilty of the Packers’ 10th roughing-the-passer penalty of the season.
McClellan took advantage with eight tackles, including one TFL. His average tackle limited the gain to 1.9 yards. Wyatt and Campbell had the only pressures (one apiece).
Linebackers: With Zaire Franklin out for a fourth consecutive week following an injured shin, Isaiah McDuffie played every snap and Ty’Ron Hopper played all but one. They each had nine tackles, though McDuffie missed a team-high three. Hopper produced the team’s only takeaway with an interception, though the offense wasted it. More on that in a moment.
Kristian Welch and Nick Niemann didn’t play on defense but they did lead the team with 22 snaps on special teams.
Cornerbacks: Brandon Cisse and Keisean Nixon played every snap. With the Rams using so many run-heavy personnel packages, nickel Javon Bullard played only 24 snaps. Kamal Hadden got in for one snap.
According to Next Gen, Nixon allowed 6-of-7 passing for 52 yards. Cisse allowed only one catch but was flagged for pass interference to set up the Rams with their opening field goal.
Safeties: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams played every snap. Williams had eight tackles on defense and a big one on special teams. McKinney’s role was playing the last line of defense on breakaway runs.
LB Ty’Ron Hopper: Hopper recorded his third interception of the season. That’s the most by a Packers linebacker since Clay Matthews had three in 2011. Only Tampa Bay’s Alex Anzalone has more this season with four. Hopper also has seven passes defensed. Among off-the-ball linebackers, Hopper is tied for first in the league with Minnesota’s Blake Cashman.
Edge Micah Parsons: In his long-awaited return to the lineup, Parsons had one sack and four pressures.
QB Jordan Love: Love was 12-of-18 passing for 154 yards with one touchdown in the first half, when Green Bay rallied for a 13-13 tie. However, he was 5-of-11 for 44 yards with zero touchdowns and two interceptions in the second half, when the Packers were outscored 13-0 and weren’t close to being competitive on offense.
“Especially right now, you know what we’re doing,” Love said. “We’re leaning on the passing game and when the passing game isn’t working and I’m not at my best, as a whole, we’re not going to be able to stay on the field and keep drives going. That’s what happened.”
TE Tucker Kraft: You practice how you play. Every day, the Packers run a ball-security drill in front of reporters. No player puts in less effort than Kraft. So, it should come as no surprise that he had a costly fumble.
The run defense: There’s no sense in pointing out one player or the other. Green Bay’s run defense was embarrassed. The Rams rushed for 241 yards, with almost 200 yards in the second half. There have been six games this season in which a team allowed 240-plus rushing yards. The Packers have been a part of two of those; they gave up 242 against Atlanta.
Teams that have allowed 200-plus rushing yards this season are 1-21.
So, I was thinking, if I do a Packers playoff update, you'd all get back to me with the famous Jim Mora line about "Playoffs?!" And that, incredibly, was the perfect way to start this story. Come for the Mora, stay for the latest projections. ⬇️ https://t.co/HVUmQyKgPc

title: It’s Over: Three Overreactions After Packers Were Turned Into Turkeys by Rams
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers had to beat the Los Angeles Rams. The NFC playoff standings demanded it. Moreover, they had to show they were capable of beating a premier team.
Instead, the Packers were mashed like potatoes on Thanksgiving Eve. They got the stuffing kicked out of them in the second half of a 26-13 loss. Not even grabbing the wishbone can save the Packers, which is reason to cry in the cranberries.
Here are our three big takeaways after the Packers looked like made-up contenders during the NFL’s made-up holiday.
The Packers had their chance to show the world they are contenders on Wednesday night. However, following a familiar pattern, they showed they weren’t ready for primetime.
In the Week 1 matchup at the Vikings, the Packers were pulverized in the second half and lost by 17. Riding a three-game winning streak into a Week 7 showdown at Detroit, the Packers went 5-of-15 on third down and 1-of-4 in the red zone, missed two field goals and lost by three.
Still, Green Bay was 6-3 when it got its big rematch against the Vikings. The Packers were at home. They would be better prepared for Brian Flores’ blitzes. The Vikings played without a couple of their top offensive weapons and their star linebacker. Instead of turning the tables, the Packers lost by 20.
That all set up what essentially was a last-stand game against the Rams, with the winner taking a huge step toward the playoffs and the loser taking a huge step toward irrelevancy. The Packers, essentially, were handed a 10th home game. Micah Parsons made his debut. The Rams lined up without their two elite receivers and two starters on the offensive line.
And the Packers lost by 13. It might as well have been 31. They were not the least bit competitive in the second half.
The Packers have played five games against teams with winning records. They are 1-4, with the lone win coming against the Bears, who played without Caleb Williams.
General manager Brian Gutekunst and coach Matt LaFleur were handed contract extensions. Some top players were given contract extensions. Instead, it’s the same old Packers.
Parsons was acquired in a blockbuster trade to help get the Packers back to the Super Bowl. Half of his contract is about to go down the drain. It’s an organizational failure. The general manager didn’t do a good job building the roster. The coach hasn’t done a good enough job utilizing the roster. And too many big-money players – the quarterback was among them on Wednesday night – haven’t played to their paychecks.
Micah Parsons made his long-awaited debut. In his first game in 346 days, nobody quite knew what to expect other than his presence would help everyone around him hit another level.
Parsons wasn’t at Superman-level dominance but he was really good. He had one sack and four pressures in his debut. The problem is nobody else hit another level.
Lukas Van Ness? Three assisted tackles and two pressures. Devonte Wyatt? Zero pressures. The Packers had only one sack (by Parsons) and three quarterback hits (two by Parsons, one by Isaiah McDuffie).
Maybe everyone was so excited to see Parsons rush the passer that they forgot to stop the run. The Rams embarrassed the Packers with a soul-crushing 241 rushing yards. It was the fourth-worst performance of the Matt LaFleur era.
“We talk about all the time, the game honors toughness. I think we’re playing tougher,” Rams coach Sean McVay said.
The Packers, obviously, aren’t tough enough, which led to this killer line by Parsons.
“We need to figure out who’s going to be a dog or not,” he told reporters after the game. “Like that’s just the reality of it. To me, to be honest and this is around the league, if someone can line up 50 times and run down your mouth and you don’t have an answer for it … that’s accountability. That’s just how I really feel about it.
“I wasn’t able to get on the field because of it, because they didn’t want to waste my plays on first and second down. I think the whole thing is just bad and we’ve got to figure out who’s willing to play with us or who’s playing against us at this point because every quarter, every minute, every down matters and we’ve got to figure out who’s in this for the long haul and who’s in it for the ride.”
Meanwhile, on the other side of the ball, Jordan Love for the second consecutive week wasn’t up to the task. He has to be Superman because of an unreliable running game and offensive line. But these are the games that define great quarterbacks and Love wasn’t close to good enough.
Forget about playing like Superman. Or even Clark Kent. It was more like Jimmy Olson. He threw two interceptions and was fortunate it wasn’t four. Not for a moment during the second half did he play like a quarterback capable of winning the game.
Rams coach Sean McVay is a difference-maker.
Did the Packers have some injury issues, especially after losing Christian Watson to a concussion late in the first half? Of course. But the Rams lined up without Puka Nacua, Davante Adams and two starting linemen. Two more linemen went down during the game. And yet the Rams dominated most of the game.
“It was awesome,” McVay said. “You guys have heard me say it, and it's really been tested and on display. It's the greatest team sport that there is. There is a long way to go, so don't misunderstand me, but our group is just starting to build skills with mental, physical toughness, resilience, guys being able to step up.
“You never know when your opportunity is going to present itself, and that was on display defensively, offensively, and in the kicking game. I love this team, love the staff. I'm excited about what they've done and I'm excited about continuing to push the envelope and see how we can grow from here.”
That’s an unbelievable quote because of the state of the Packers with their 6-5 record.
Where was the mental toughness to turn the game around in the second half?
Where was the physical toughness with the Rams rushing for almost 200 yards in the second half?
Where was the resilience as the game got away from them in the second half?
In what phase did the Packers hold their own on offense, defense or the kicking game?
Packers coach Matt LaFleur can’t push the envelope when trying to prevent the envelope from going up in flames.
Team president and CEO Ed Policy saw the Packers lose their final five games of last season and decided to give contract extensions to LaFleur and general manager Brian Gutekunst. With a 6-5 record, a team built to win a Super Bowl seems to be headed for a cliff.
This is the time of year when teams should be making their move to the playoffs and beyond. The Packers, instead, just got clobbered by the Vikings and Rams. The offense ranks a woeful 20th in scoring, including just 15.2 points in five losses, due in large part to a poorly constructed and poorly coached line. The defense, in the words of Javon Bullard, got its “ass” kicked for a second consecutive game by a depleted offense.
The Packers are in deep trouble. Significant changes are needed for an organization headed in the wrong direction.

title: Packers Report Card: Bad Grades And Looking for Dogs After Loss to Rams
full_text:
The grades are in, and the Green Bay Packers’ season is starting to circle the drain. No, they are not simply going to give up, but perhaps Micah Parsons said it best before his debut on Wednesday.
Parsons said that every game was the “difference between the playoffs and Cancun.”
Well, through one game since that statement was made, the Packers are much closer to Cancun. Their defense was beaten bloody by Blake Corum and the Rams’ run game. Their offense could not find any semblance of a rhythm in the second half. As a result, a 13-13 tie at halftime turned into a 26-13 loss that conjured memories of Jim Mora’s infamous “Playoffs?!” rant .
“We need to figure out who’s going to be a dog or not. Like that’s just the reality of it,” Parsons said after the game. “To me, to be honest and this is around the league, if someone can line up 50 times and run down your mouth and you don’t have an answer for it … that’s accountability.”
Let’s jump into the grades, and they’re not going to be pretty.
It was a tough night for Jordan Love and the offense. At this point, the excuses wear pretty thin. The Rams’ Sean McVay and Matthew Stafford were able to cobble together enough offense with receivers that would not dream of starting in Green Bay.
Yes, they lost Christian Watson during the game, and that’s a big blow. That’s also part of the design of Green Bay’s offense. What happens when less is less instead of more, as was the narrative coming into the season?
Love finished 17-of-29 for 198 yards with one touchdown pass and two interceptions. He was only sacked once. With only 44 passing yards in the second half, he played poorly, even if he was largely let down by those around him. Any conversation about the MVP effectively died on Wednesday night.
“Not good enough. Definitely not,” Love said. “We’ll see when we look at it but just not good, especially the second half. Yeah, nowhere where my play needs to be and, obviously, it starts with me. I’ve got to be a lot better.”
Green Bay’s top receiver tandem of Watson and Matthew Golden caught five passes for 104 yards, but 65 of those yards came on Watson’s four catches. Golden caught 1-of-5 targets. Tucker Kraft remains disappointing and fumbled early in the game to set up a Rams field goal.
Green Bay’s quarterback has been asked to carry the whole franchise this season. As it turns out, asking one man to be Superman is a bad strategy, because eventually Superman becomes Clark Kent.
In what was the most predictable outcome ever, the Packers’ run game found no traction against the Rams’ stingy run defense.
They ran the ball 14 carries for 52 yards. Kaleb Johnson got the start. With no blocking whatsoever, his first three carries resulted in a loss of 8 yards. They didn’t have the ball nearly enough thanks to some of their issues on defense with stopping the run, but the Packers’ run game is bad. It’s not getting better, with their 65.9 rushing yards per game on track to be the worst in NFL history .
Now, they’re getting to the point where their passing game is starting to wilt, and they don’t have any other answers when that happens.
The final numbers from Matthew Stafford weren’t gaudy, but they didn’t have to be. Stafford was 16-of-23 for 140 yards and one interception by Ty’Ron Hopper.
Keisean Nixon has had better days against much better receivers. PFF charged him with 5-of-6 passing for 46 yards. Brandon Cisse was flagged for interference on the opening possession. Aside from Hopper’s interception, there were no passes defensed.
Micah Parsons had one sack and four of the team’s 11 pressures in his return to the lineup. He was active whenever the Rams did drop back to pass. Those moments were few and far between because the Rams may have been able to move the ball without ever attempting a forward pass.
The interception could have changed the game in Green Bay’s favor, but Jordan Love and Matthew Golden were not on the same page a couple plays later, resulting in an interception that made Hopper’s big play a relative footnote.
The numbers weren’t gaudy for a long time. The Packers were holding Blake Corum and Kyren Williams in check and forcing Matthew Stafford to make plays in obvious passing situations.
Then the second half came. Corum and the Rams’ offensive line, which featured mostly backup players, started to lean on Green Bay’s defense. Carries that went for 2 yards in the first half started going for 4 yards, carries that were gaining 4 yards started going for 6, and so on.
It culminated with a 35-yard-burst from Corum to set up Brandon McManus’ field goal to give the Rams a 10-point lead.
The final numbers were 32 carries for 184 yards for Corum. Kyren Williams had 12 carries for 46 yards. The Rams piled up 241 rushing yards as a team. The Rams entered the game without their three most-explosive weapons in the passing game. Everyone knew the Rams were going to run the ball, but they ran for 195 yards in the second half, anyway.
The most telling number is the time of possession battle. The Rams held the ball for 40:40 compared to the Packers’ 19:20.
“Some things just need to stay in-house, and I plan on directly checking that as a unit when we get back from this break,” edge Micah Parsons said. “But we all saw that game and we saw where we got exploited at. It starts with us. It starts with up front. I think I’m at that point where we say it’s not pointing fingers at things, but when runs open up like the Red Sea, we got to look at ourselves in the mirror regardless of how that is. We have to do a better job collectively up front.”
This was a win by total knockout from the Rams.
The Rams have a kickoff specialist who essentially killed any chance of the Packers being able to mount anything resembling an explosive return.
Joshua Karty specializes for the Rams in dirty kicks. For some reason, the Packers do not employ that despite drafting a kicker. This is making a mountain out of a molehill. The Packers have much bigger problems, but it’s worth observing that Trey Smack has not attempted a dirty kick this season.
Outside of that observation, special teams gave up one explosive punt return, but the kicker made all of his kicks. Maybe that is something that will help the Packers as their season enters December.
The Packers’ coaching staff was beaten up by Sean McVay and the Rams.
Matt LaFleur did not have any answers as his personnel dwindled with the loss of Christian Watson. That excuse falls on deaf ears when McVay is working with journeymen receivers. The Rams held the ball for two-thirds of the game.
But this is about the bigger picture.
The Packers do not win games like the one they played on Wednesday night. If there is a game in which they play an NFC team on equal or greater footing, the Packers are likely going to lose.
That’s been true for each of the last three years for LaFleur’s Packers. That’s why they’re 6-5 after back-to-back blowout losses. All five of their losses are against NFC opponents, and their most recent loss against the Rams provided a devastating punch to their playoff hopes.
Then again, perhaps the Packers should have expected that with the mountain of evidence that was in front of them last January. Despite that, they signed up for more of it. They’re reaping the fruits of their labor.

title: Playoffs?!? Packers’ Woeful Loss to Rams Came With Perfectly Imperfect Timing
full_text:
During the second half of the Green Bay Packers’ loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Wednesday night, Green Bay’s defense got run over and its offense got thrown into the ditch.
In what was a must-win game for both teams, the Packers were trounced 26-13.
In terms of the Packers’ playoff hopes, their miserable performance had impeccable timing.
On Nov. 25, 2001 – exactly 25 years ago – the Jim Mora-coached Colts lost 40-21 at home against the 49ers. It was their third consecutive loss and sent their record to 4-6. Mora was asked about the team’s playoff hopes following what he called a “disgraceful” performance.
“Playoffs? Don’t talk about – playoffs?! You kidding me? Playoffs?! I just hope we can win a game!”
There were no epic rants from coach Matt LaFleur after the game. Just a tip of the cap to the Rams and the acknowledgement that the Packers didn’t take care of the football or stop the run.
“That’s a recipe for disaster,” he said.
Not just for a game but an entire season.
The Packers opened the night with a 6-4 record, ahead of the Rams and Seahawks by tiebreakers and clinging to the final spot in the NFC playoff chase. Now, the Packers are 6-5 and essentially two games behind the Rams with six games to play.
Just how deep of a hole are the Packers staring at?
“To be real, you know that answer,” edge Micah Parsons said after his debut game . “This hole is massive. This hole is massive. We took a big swing and we missed ginormously. The only way to get out is we probably have to win out. That’s just the reality of this situation. I think the people know that. We know that. From player to coach, we have to play better. It’s not just the players. It’s coaches, the whole thing, we have to all be better. I definitely look at that.”
Playoffs? Are you kidding me? The Packers are in ninth place in the NFC, though they’d move up to eighth if Seattle loses to San Francisco on Sunday. Along with the head-to-head tiebreaker against the Rams, Green Bay’s 4-5 record in conference games is becoming increasingly problematic.
Here’s what the computers say about Green Bay’s playoff chances.
According to The Athletic’s Playoff Predictor had a 64 percent chance of qualifying for the playoffs before hosting Minnesota. Now, with back-to-back losses, that’s down to 25 percent.
At ESPN , the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs two weeks ago. Now, that’s tumbled all the way to 19 percent.
At NFL.com , the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs before the Minnesota game. Now, it’s 23 percent.
At Playoff Status , the Packers had a 66 percent chance of reaching the playoffs a couple weeks ago and would have been at 63 percent with a win over the Rams. Instead, their chances have been cut to 31 percent.
Using Stick to the Model ’s Playoff Machine, the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs before the back-to-back blowout losses. Now, they have a 16 percent chance. If Green Bay can somehow win five of its final six games, it would have an 82 percent chance of reaching the postseason.
But, to quote Mora, the Packers just have to win a game.
“Yeah, it’s extremely disappointing,” LaFleur said. “And like I told the team, it’s always 1-0, but we’re in a one-game season from here on out. We’ve dug ourself a hole, and we’ve got to put in the work to put yourself in position to even win a football game. And it all starts in practice.”
What gives LaFleur the belief the team can grab a shovel and dig itself out of the hole instead of simply dropping it on its collective toes?
“Because we’re going to take it one day at a time,” LaFleur said. “I know for a fact this group cares. They care a lot, and they’ve been willing to work. Unfortunately, like you just mentioned, we’ve put ourselves behind the 8-ball.”
The Packers’ six remaining opponents have a combined .550 winning percentage. That’s the ninth-toughest remaining slate of games. Never mind the NFC North teams. Everyone in the division seems out of reach. Focusing on the Rams and Seahawks, here is how it shapes up.
Rams (7-4): home against Chiefs, at 49ers, home against Cowboys, at Seahawks and Buccaneers, home against Seahawks. Those six teams have a combined .607 winning percentage, second-toughest in the league.
Seahawks (6-4): at 49ers on Sunday, home against Cowboys and Giants, at Eagles, home against Rams, at Panthers, home against Rams. Those seven teams have a combined .582 winning percentage, fourth-toughest in the league.
Packers (6-5): at Saints, home against Bills and Dolphins, at Bears, home against Texans and Lions. After the New Orleans game, four of their final five games are at Lambeau.
“You never know how the schedule is going to go and who they may lose to and who we may win against,” nickel Javon Bullard said. “Really, you just got to take it one game at a time. Shit, if we win out, you never know where the chips are going to fall.”
The Packers finished the night with 244 yards and three turnovers. The Rams had 241 rushing yards, 374 total yards and a 2-to-1 edge in time of possession.
“We knew we needed to come in and win this game,” receiver Matthew Golden said. “We knew it was a must win. It hurts we lost, but now like every game matters from here on out. We’ve got to take it one game at a time, and we’ve got to go out there and dominate.”

title: Here’s Where Packers’ Micah Parsons Vows to Be Better After Loss to Rams
full_text:
Appropriately given what it took to make his season debut on Thanksgiving Eve, Green Bay Packers star Micah Parsons was thankful to be back on the field during Wednesday night’s loss to the Rams.
“Personally, I’m just happy I had a game where I walked off the field and I can take that as gratitude,” he said after the 26-13 loss. “I’m thankful that I was able to play again and be with my friends and my brothers as teammates. But as the competitor, I’m just highly, highly disappointed with how we performed collectively.”
The game was tied 13-13 at halftime, the Packers going toe to toe with the preseason Super Bowl favorites. The second half, though, the Packers were thoroughly dominated in every phase. They gave up 241 rushing yards.
“We just have to be better,” Parsons said. “We talk about championships and so many more things. That wasn’t a championship attitude, competitiveness, drive. That second half is just inexcusable. I would say that’s my whole take on that.”
Playing in his first game since suffering a torn ACL at Denver on Dec. 14, Parsons started and played the first three snaps. Would Parsons be Peak Parsons or Rusty Parsons?
Rams coach Sean McVay wasn’t about to find out.
On early runs, the ball went away from Parsons. On passes, the ball was out of Matthew Stafford’s hand in the blink of an eye.
That was the right plan of attack. With the game tied at 13, the Rams got the ball with 1:50 left in the half. So, a 2-minute opportunity for the reigning NFL MVP and a reason for McVay to be aggressive. On first down, Stafford dropped back to pass but was buried by Parsons, who blew past standout left tackle Alaric Jackson in the blink of an eye.
sheeeeeeeesh pic.twitter.com/GoF3dq0YrB
That was enough. McVay ran the ball on second down, threw a screen on third down and was happy to get to halftime with a tie.
On nine passing-game snaps in the first half, four of the passes were screens. On the other five, Parsons had one sack, one hit and one hurry. It was a remarkable performance after a 346-day layoff.
The Rams found the ultimate recipe in the second half. They just ran the ball. Again and again. And again. Los Angeles ran the ball 35 times for 195 yards in the second half alone. You have to earn the right to rush the passer, and the defense didn’t put Parsons in position to make any impact plays as the game got away from them in the second half.
So, Parsons ended the game exactly how he ended the first half: One sack, one tackle (the sack) and two quarterback hits.
“The first game was OK,” Parsons said. “It was OK. It just really sucks how the game played out. I take accountability. I obviously didn’t have our room prepared enough for what we were about to face. We knew it would be a run and screen dominant game because of who they were missing. We just didn’t play good enough as a front and I hold myself accountable in that process where we just have to be better. We can’t let teams dictate the game like that.”
Parsons played 27 snaps – 15 against the pass and 12 against the run. He finished with four pressures – nobody else had more than one and the team finished with 10.
There would be no finger-pointing, Parsons said, but the problem was obvious.
“When runs open up like the Red Sea, we got to look at ourselves in the mirror regardless of how that is. We have to do a better job collectively up front,” Parsons said.
He added: "We need to figure out who’s going to be a dog or not."
Parsons said he needs to be a better, more serious leader.
“You like to play, you like to have fun with your teammates, you like to be all joyful and smiling all the time,” he said. “But reality, everyone just can’t flip that switch. That’s where a teammate had told me I could do better in that, and I swear I’m going to be better going forward. I like to play with the guys, shoot hoops before the walkthrough and do all these things that we do as team-bonding but, at this point, we just need to focus on all the small things and all the details (and) how we cannot get exploited like that.
“That’s somewhere where I’m really looking at myself in the mirror and how can I get my unit better because I go as they go and they go as I go. It’s a collective thing. I’m proud to be a part of this unit and I just want us to play better in these last games, that’s all I want. I came a really long way to look negatively on the outcome of this season, so I just really want to enjoy it with the guys that’s here.”
As for the knee, there were no issues physically or mentally. Parsons played without a brace and got after the quarterback when there were opportunities.
Because of the Rams’ game plan on offense, Green Bay’s horrendous run defense and the lack of help provided by the Jordan Love-led offense, there just weren’t many opportunities for Parsons to do what he does best.
“I push it in practice,” he said. “I was about as dominant as I’ve been before in practice versus the game. I’m just sorry I couldn’t really show you guys really how good it can get because we just didn’t do a good enough job on first and second down. It’s something we need to fix and, hopefully, we can see it next game.
“But I’m not worried about the knee. I’ve prepared and prepared and prepared to get to this point and I think when you prepare like that, you don’t worry about things. You just stay into the process.”

title: Packers Winners and Losers: Problems Start at the Top Against Rams
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers were in a must-win game on their Thanksgiving Eve matchup with the Los Angeles Rams. Both teams entered the game with 6-4 records. A win would have given the Packers a one-game lead in the standings as well as the all-important tiebreaker in the race for the final playoff spot.
The teams were deadlocked at 13 apiece at halftime in Micah Parsons’ return to the field.
The second half saw Blake Corum and the Rams’ run game grind the Packers’ defense into a bloody pulp. The offense couldn’t muster anything without Christian Watson on the field, as they mustered just two first downs in the second half before Jordan Love threw a back-breaking interception. As a result, the Packers are 6-5 and face an uphill climb to make the postseason.
That reflects poorly on the top two men in the organization, and they lead off our list of winners and losers.
If Jordan Love was going to be in the MVP conversation, that ended with consecutive bad games. Love struggled against Minnesota, but so did the entire offense.
Against the Rams, Love had a chance at redemption. He looked rattled by the pressure from the Rams’ defense even though pass protection held up for the most part.
On the pass that got Christian Watson injured, Kam Kinchens was ejected. Love threw a pass that led Watson into that hit.
Later in the game, it may have been a miscommunication, but Love threw a terrible interception after Ty’Ron Hopper snatched back momentum for the Packers.
If that one wasn’t his fault, his second interception of the game was. He nearly threw another one earlier in the game to Trent McDuffie that he was fortunate hit the turf before McDuffie could corral it.
Love and his team are 6-5. They have not been above the seventh seed in his three seasons as a starting quarterback. Now, the Packers have just a 14 percent chance of making the playoffs, according to the playoff odds shared on the Netflix broadcast.
The Packers are regressing. Wins and losses are not a quarterback stat, but it is what quarterbacks are ultimately judged by. The Packers have not been good enough, and that has included Love in some of the biggest games.
The storylines surrounding Matt LaFleur have been discussed a bunch since the 2025 season ended in disaster in Chicago.
LaFleur was ultimately given a vote of confidence from team president and CEO Ed Policy with a contract extension despite finishing last season with a five-game losing streak. However, his teams look pretty similar to the last three that came before them.
They are capable of great moments, mind-numbing inconsistency and shrinking in the biggest games of the year.
The last two games are a perfect example. LaFleur’s offense was only able to muster 10 points against Brian Flores and the Vikings. Without Christian Watson, LaFleur’s offense turtled against the Rams’ defense.
The Packers are 6-5 this season. All five of their losses are to NFC opponents that are in the playoff hunt. What gives anyone any confidence that the Packers would be able to bounce back and win any big games against a playoff team that is at reasonably full strength?
That’s where the Packers are at this point. They signed up for more of what they saw a season ago. Would the Packers eat LaFleur’s contract extension at the end of a non-playoff season the way 2026 is trending to be?
If losing to the franchise’s biggest rival in the postseason in embarrassing fashion was not enough, that feels unlikely.
This was dangerously close to that four-letter S-word that no football player wants to be referred to. The two most basic principles in the NFL are running the football and stopping the run. The Packers ran for 55 yards. That was not much of a surprise. The Packers cannot run on anybody.
Stopping the run? The Packers had been solid in that department this year, but their run defense betrayed them against Los Angeles. The Rams, who were missing their top three offensive weapons and two starting linemen, piled up 241 yards on the ground, with Blake Corum popping them for 184 yards on 32 carries.
The first drive of the second half was a tone-setter for the rest of the game. The Rams took the ball tied at 13 apiece. They held the ball for 8:02 of game clock. The Packers did not get the ball back until there was 6:58 remaining. The time of possession numbers as a result were 40:40 to 19:20 in favor of the Rams.
Wednesday's game was the equivalent of the Packers knowing what is coming but still being unable to stop it. There's nothing more demoralizing for a defense than to be physically dominated in the way the Packers were. To add insult to injury, the Packers were facing a team without two starting offensive linemen, and they had two more hobbled during the game as well.
The final score does not tell the whole story for how badly the Rams bullied the Packers, who were far too soft in a huge game.
Tucker Kraft’s disappointing season continues. The first half saw him fumble and have a costly drop.
Kraft was the last of four major contract extensions given out by the Packers this season, and he’s in contention with defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt as the least impactful of the bunch.
Wyatt’s lack of impact can be masked thanks to some of the other players on the roster. Kraft’s can’t. He’s the only tight end on the roster capable of making an impact.
He’s not just not making plays in the passing game, he’s making catastrophic mistakes. Maybe the fumble was a great play by linebacker Nate Landman, but it’s a play that cannot happen from an offensive captain. The drop is a play that cannot happen when the Packers are swimming upstream against a vicious Rams’ front.
When Christian Watson left the lineup, the Packers needed Kraft to emerge
The Rams were missing their top two receivers on Wednesday, but with the way that Matthew Stafford abused Keisean Nixon, you may never have known it.
On the Rams’ touchdown drive in the third quarter, Nixon was beaten for two third-down conversions, including a third-and-11.
The man who beat him was not Davante Adams or Puka Nacua, it was Konata Mumpfield. Nothing against Mumpfield as a player, but that’s not a player who can beat you in an obvious passing situation.
Nixon has been good this season, but Wednesday’s homecoming was not his best performance.
With Christian Watson on the sideline for the second half due to a concussion, the Packers’ passing game was down to just two members of their less-is-more passing game.
Jayden Reed is out for the season after a neck injury. Watson leaving the game late in the first half meant that the passing game was left to Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft.
Kraft is in the midst of arguably his worst season as a pro. Golden appeared to have some sort of miscommunication on an interception by Jordan Love in the third quarter.
Savion Williams, J. Michael Sturdivant and Bo Melton didn’t make enough plays, and the Packers were unable to find any rhythm on offense in the second half.
It’s been a long road, but it did not take long for Micah Parsons to reintroduce himself to the world. On the field for nine passing plays in the first half, he had a sack in which he showed the all-world speed and explosiveness that made him one of the best players in the sport.
Considering the state of some of the other Packers on the roster and their questionable returns from serious injuries like the one Parsons had, his return was a sight for sore eyes.
The Packers are thrilled to have their best player back, and he showed why on Wednesday night.
With the Packers trailing 20-13 with 4:34 left in the third quarter, the Rams’ offensive line was starting to lean on Green Bay’s defense.
Any points from the Rams would have been a devastating punch handed outby their offense. Matthew Stafford dialed up a play-action pass, but the throw did not find its intended target.
Ty’Ron Hopper, who has played well in the absence of Zaire Franklin, made another big play, picking off Matthew Stafford and giving the Packers a second…

title: Rams Beat Packers, Run Them Almost Out of Playoff Race
full_text:
Micah Parsons is in. The Green Bay Packers are out.
Or almost out in terms of the playoff race.
The Los Angeles Rams overpowered the Packers 26-13 on Wednesday night at SoFi Stadium. While Parsons made his long-awaited season debut and was impactful at times, the Packers were run over by Blake Corum during the second half and doomed by an impotent, sloppy offense.
It might wind up being a killer loss for Green Bay. The Packers, Rams and Seahawks entered Week 12 with 6-4 records. The Rams are 7-4 with a one-game lead in the standings but in reality a two-game lead with the head-to-head tiebreaker. The Seahawks will visit the NFC-leading 49ers on Sunday.
The Packers entered the game with a 40 percent chance of reaching, according to The Athletic’s playoff simulator. With a win, that would have increased to 61 percent. Instead, with a loss, it’s down to 25 percent.
A horrendous interception by Jordan Love with 3:39 to go ended the game – and maybe Green Bay’s postseason dreams. From there, Corum continued to turn the Packers into turkeys. His 9-yard run at the 2-minute warning gave the Rams 242 rushing yards, with 184 by Corum. The Packers had only 240 yards of total offense.
After a strong first half, Love was just 17-of-29 for 198 yards with two interceptions. Matthew Golden couldn’t carry the passing attack, catching 1-of-5 targets. Green Bay was 2-of-8 on third down.
With the score tied at 13 at halftime, the Rams embarked on a 15-play, 68-yard scoring drive to open the second half. Blake Corum carried the ball nine times on the drive, including a leg-churning, 1-yard touchdown run. The Rams converted four times on third down, including Matthew Stafford’s 20-yard completion on third-and-8 to Konata Mumpfield against Keisean Nixon during one of the rare occasions Micah Parsons was kept at bay on a true dropback pass.
The Packers needed an answer but, with Christian Watson out with a concussion, they went three-and-out. They were fortunate to have punted as Jordan Love’s third-down pass was thrown right to Quentin Lake.
The Packers had their chance to turn the game around when linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper got in the passing lane between Matthew Stafford and Tyler Higbee for an interception and return to the Rams’ 43. However, one play later, Love went deep to Matthew Golden but they weren’t on the same page, leading to safety Jaylen McCollough catching the easiest of his five career interceptions.
It was a killer mistake. The third quarter ended with the Rams on the move. During those 15 minutes, they ran 23 plays for 101 yards while the Packers ran five plays for 10 yards. Corum had 15 carries for 59 yards.
One of those carries came on a third-and-1 conversion. It was third-and-6 but the Packers were flagged for having 12 men on the field; the officials didn’t give Matt LaFleur the timeout. Then, on second-and-9 with Parsons on the field to rush the passer, Corum exploded up the middle for 12.
The defense escaped with a big third-down stop, so Love and the offense started at their 11 with 12:35 left in regulation. A 6-yard run by Kaleb Johnson was a promising start; a false start by Johnson was a setback. Love was almost intercepted on second-and-9 and Tucker Kraft couldn’t move the chain on a third-down screen.
With Corum storming up the middle for a gain of 35, the Rams extended their lead to 23-13 with 6:13 remaining in the game. Considering the Packers had zero first downs to that point of the second half and Christian Watson was out with a concussion, they faced long, long odds against Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and the Rams’ juggernaut defense.
Those odds fell to basically zero when Love threw his second interception. It was Green Bay’s third turnover – the third time in four games they hit that dubious mark. One more field goal turned out to be the whipped cream on the pumpkin pie for the Rams.
The Packers got the ball to start the game but went three-and-out. The first play of the game was a completion to Christian Watson, but he limped off the field. Back-to-back incomplete passes led to a three-and-out.
With the Rams’ offense on the field, Micah Parsons got the start. He played the first three snaps but the Rams didn’t run anything his direction – a theme throughout the first half. A 39-yard penalty on Brandon Cisse – a bit of a ticky-tack flag – put the ball in scoring position, and Brandon McManus booted a 43-yard field goal.
The Packers approached midfield on the next drive, even though Kaleb Johnson lost 6 yards on two no-prayer carries. However, Tucker Kraft got the ball punched out by linebacker Nate Landman and nickel Quentin Lake recovered, giving the Rams the ball at their 43.
A roughing-the-passer penalty on Devonte Wyatt – the 10th this season by the Packers – gave the Rams 15 yards. The defense stiffened, though. Parsons’ pressure on Matthew Stafford produced a wayward pass and helped force McManus to kick a 41-yard field goal.
Green Bay answered with a 54-yard field goal by Trey Smack. Johnson lost 2 yards on the first play, but Watson had a 32-yard catch-and-run-and-hurdle on the next play. The drive died, though, when Kraft couldn’t hang onto a pass over the middle after he was hit by safety Kamren Kinchens.
The first quarter ended with Parsons having played nine snaps and getting the one pressure.
The Rams blew right through Green Bay’s defense to start the second quarter. After Stafford found Kyren Williams on third-and-4 just before he was hit by Parsons, Stafford connected with receiver Konata Mumpfield for 24 and tight end Tyler Higbee for 14 more. One play later, Williams strolled through an enormous hole for a 7-yard touchdown to make it 13-3. Karl Brooks, Anthony Campbell and Isaiah McDuffie were blocked with ease.
The Packers hadn’t given up three consecutive scoring drives to start a game all season. So, they were in an early trouble spot considering the power of the Rams’ pass rush and needing an answer.
And what an answer. First, it was a flea-flicker from Jordan Love to Savion Williams and back to Love, who ripped a bullet to a toe-dragging Christian Watson for 21. Then, Love ripped one to Matthew Golden, who cut back inside for a catch-and-run gain of 39 to the Rams’ 20. Finally, on third-and-goal at the 6, Love faced immediate pressure from Byron Young but stepped up and hit Watson for a touchdown to cut the margin to 13-10.
The Packers forced a three-and-out on the next drive, with the Rams throwing a give-up screen on third-and-11 rather than deal with Micah Parsons.
The Packers tied the game 13-13 with 1:50 left in the half to cap a wild drive.
First, on third-and-1, Savion Williams ran for 13 on a well-blocked run up the middle; he wasn’t touched by a defender until he was about 5 yards downfield. Kevin Zeitler, who finally made his first start at right guard, suffered an injured left ankle when Williams sprinted past him. Aaron Banks, a career-long left guard, entered at right guard and pancaked Braden Fiske on MarShawn Lloyd’s 10-yard run.
On fourth-and-1 – actually, they needed about 5 feet – Love floated one up to Watson. Watson was obliterated by Kamren Kinchens at the sideline and couldn’t hang onto the ball. Kinchens was flagged for unnecessary roughness and kicked out of the game but Matthew Golden was flagged for offense pass interference, so it was the most painful of offsetting penalties.
Watson was down for a few minutes before walking to the locker room. Down one of his top playmakers, coach Matt LaFleur reconsidered his fourth-down decision and sent on kicker Trey Smack, who kicked a 48-yard field goal to tie the game at 13 with 1:50 left in the half.
On first down, Parsons roared past left tackle Alaric Jackson for a sack. The crowd roared and Parsons exhorted them to crank up the decibels. The Rams waved the white flag of surrender, and the teams went into break with a tie score.
Love was 12-of-18 for 154 yards in the first half.

title: Showdown Against Rams Marks Debuts for Two Potential Packers Saviors
full_text:
Almost two months after he was signed, guard Kevin Zeitler will make his long-awaited debut in the starting lineup for the Green Bay Packers against the Los Angeles Rams on Wednesday night at SoFi Stadium.
Zeitler was part of Green Bay’s No. 1 line during warmups. The starting line consisted of Jordan Morgan at left guard, Laken Tomlinson at left guard, Sean Rhyan at center, Zeitler at right guard and Anthony Belton at right tackle.
Rhyan is back in the lineup after missing the last three games. Zeitler will be making the 214th start of his career and his first since Jan. 4 while with the Titans.
The challenge could hardly be any tougher. The Rams probably have the best defensive line in the NFL. In their base defense, Myles Garrett and Byron Young are the edges and Aaron Donald, Kobie Turner and Braden Fiske.
“It’s a pretty legendary group over there,” Zeitler said this week.
Donald, an eight-time All-Pro, came out of retirement to chase a Super Bowl ring.
“A couple of times definitely over the years, [and it’s] absolutely stress-inducing every single time,” Zeitler said of Donald. “The guy’s a monster – always has been, always will be as long as he’s out on that field. It will take every single thing we’ve got as a team and as individuals to get it done.”
The Packers need their line to play its best game of the season against the Rams’ potent front. This will be their seventh starting combination of the year. Zeitler is the fourth player to start at right guard this year.
Green Bay gave up eight sacks last week. It enters Week 12 ranked last in the league in rushing, as well.
“The only thing we can do is do it out on the field,” Zeitler said. “It wasn’t pretty last week. I don’t think anyone can say otherwise. I think everyone’s acknowledged it in our room. We’ve got to turn it around. The only thing that matters is things changing on the field. We can talk all we want, but nothing matters until it changes and gets done.”
“It just has to happen. It’s as simple as that,” Zeitler said. “We work hard. We’re prepped well here. For whatever reason, things have not been going our way. Whatever that line is we have to cross, we have to get it crossed and get it done.”
☝️ pic.twitter.com/ldmpMYscA0
Micah Parsons, as expected, is active.
After 49 weeks away from the game, what will his emotions be like before the game?
“I would say I’m always pretty nervous before a game,” he said on Monday. “I’ll just be ready for the first snap. I’m just trying to stay right here with it. Not even look forward to that moment. Just enjoy every process, even leading up to the start of the snap. I’ll probably have some emotions after the game, but from what I hear from family, I’m not really big on emotions.”
Parsons went through three weeks of practice to put the finishing touches on his comeback. He went through pregame warmups without a brace on his knee.
His goal for the next seven games has nothing to do with individual stats and accolades.
“I would say I have no targets,” he said. “The only thing I’m targeting in a sense of mindset is to win every week to try to up lift this season, change this season around, and do exactly what the Packers brought me here to do. That’s it. That’s my only target and that’s to make a run for the playoffs and make guys around me better. That’s it.
“I think talking to a friend of mine who went through the ACL process, we were talking about it like, we push and we ignore so many other things that’s wrong with this because we’re always chasing the outcome and we just keep chasing the outcomes, whether it’s the All-Pros or the Pro Bowls and when you end up injured none of that stuff actually matters anymore. Everyone’s like, ‘Oh, well, when will he be back?’ And we chase these things for so long that those outcomes become dust and people don’t really care about that. It’s about what you can do next or can you do it again? So, I have no targets and outcomes.”
Well, there is one target. The Packers brought him to Green Bay to help win a Super Bowl. Parsons, whose record streak of five consecutive seasons of 12-plus sacks to open his career almost certainly will be snapped, wants to make that a reality.
“I think I’ve achieved everything that I’ve wanted in my career except for the big one and I think that’s kind of like my own mindset,” he continued. “Through the Saban documentary, I learned just stay in the process of every day. Own my process my today, so I owned it today. I got another process tomorrow and God willing, I’ll have another process Wednesday night and that’ll be the start of this new journey.”
The inactives for today's Week 12 game against the Rams
Two starters, running back Josh Jacobs and linebacker Zaire Franklin, are inactive.
Both players practiced all week and were questionable. Coach Matt LaFleur didn’t think Jacobs would play, and that was the case. Franklin, meanwhile, returned to practice this week but will miss a fourth consecutive game.
Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper will start against the Rams’ potent running game.
“I feel like they did great,” Franklin said. “It’s always a blessing to be surrounded by a lot of talent. I did my best to continue to support the guys in any way that I could, whether that’s energy on the sideline or notes in the meetings or helping coach up on the sideline. But there’s only so much you can do when you’re not on the field. So, just looking forward to being who I’m supposed to be on the field.”
In what's essentially a must-win game, here are three reasons why the Packers will earn a critical victory over the Rams tonight. (Opposite side of this story coming shortly.) ⬇️ https://t.co/t25ekTvQDE

title: Steelers Bench and Release Aaron Rodgers; Should Packers Sign Him?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Thanksgiving Eve was supposed to be about the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams.
Instead, the men who led the Packers to their last Super Bowl win, Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers, stole the turkey and pumpkin pie.
And the ice cream sandwiches. And then took a snore-filled snooze.
The Steelers on Tuesday night announced that they had benched Rodgers – Rodgers allegedly learned the news from teammate Pat Freiermuth. Rodgers, naturally, went on The Pat McAfee Show to go scorched earth on McCarthy, accusing him of napping in team meetings and skipping walk-throughs.
The Steelers, predictably, Rodgers released shortly thereafter.
It’s possible Rodgers’ NFL career is over. He had said this would be his final season, anyway, and now he’s out of a job. The bad teams have no need to bring in Rodgers as a starting quarterback. The good teams might not want to upset the apple cart by bringing in Rodgers as a backup quarterback.
However, what about the team for which he won four NFL MVPs?
The Packers are 6-4 entering Wednesday night’s game at the Rams. A win over Los Angeles would be a key step – and necessary step – toward returning the playoffs for a fourth consecutive year since the Packers traded Rodgers to the Jets in 2023.
The Packers are a good team with a really good quarterback. Jordan Love has been the rising tide that lifts all boats. He’s led a team with a horrendous offensive line, no running game and an abundance of dropped passes and penalties into position to reach the playoffs.
But there is no margin for error. If Love were to be knocked out for two quarters of a game or for two games, the Packers would face an almost insurmountable challenge to win. And given their backs-against-the-wall spot in the playoff race, their postseason hopes could be knocked out if Love were to be knocked out of a game.
The Packers enjoyed two years of sensational backup play with Malik Willis. With Willis signing to become the starting quarterback with the Dolphins this past offseason, the Packers pivoted to 37-year-old Tyrod Taylor. Taylor has had a long and successful career, but his best days are, clearly, behind him. His value to the roster is in his experience, wisdom and know-how.
Taylor is probably good enough to keep the Packers in the game against lesser opponents but he’s probably not good enough to go out and win a game against a quality opponent – and there’s a bunch of those on Green Bay’s remaining schedule.
Rodgers will turn 43 next week. He, obviously, isn’t the player who won Super Bowl MVP in 2010 and NFL MVPs in 2011, 2014, 2020 and 2021. He’s not the player who ranks fourth in NFL history in passer rating.
But he’s not bad – and would be an upgrade over Taylor. He had three consecutive games of three touchdown passes for the Steelers earlier this season. He’s immobile and no longer a magician in the pocket. But he can still sling the football and can win any play before the ball is snapped.
If Love were to miss a game or two, who would give the Packers the better chance of winning a game and keeping their season alive? Taylor or Rodgers.
Yes, there is baggage. That is obvious. Rodgers threw McCarthy under the bus in Green Bay and, predictably, did it again during their reunion season in Pittsburgh.
One high-ranking executive told Packers On SI that he wouldn’t touch Rodgers with a “1,000-foot pole.”
But if you’re general manager Brian Gutekunst and the goal is to build the best top-to-bottom roster to weather whatever challenge comes your way, then adding Rodgers should at least be a conversation.
The conversation would have to start internally with coach Matt LaFleur. LaFleur and Rodgers butted heads during their four seasons together, but they also reached incredible heights. From a team perspective, there were trips to the NFC Championship Game in 2019 and 2020 and the No. 1 seed in 2021. From a personal perspective, Rodgers won MVP in 2020 and 2021.
The conversation, obviously, would have to include Love. By all accounts, including their own, they enjoyed a strong relationship during their three seasons together. When the Packers traded Rodgers, Rodgers understood that Love’s time had arrived. What would Love think about sharing a quarterback room with Rodgers again?
And then there would have to be a long and brutally honest conversation with Rodgers.
What would Rodgers think about a full-circle ending to his career? From 2015 through 2017, Rodgers was the backup to Brett Favre. Now, he’d be the backup to Love for the final handful of games of his final season.
What would Rodgers think about being the clear and obvious backup quarterback? There would be no scenario in which Rodgers would compete for the starting job or push for playing time. He’d be the football equivalent of a fire extinguisher, with the glass broken only in case of emergency.
Would Rodgers be a distraction? Not if handled correctly by all parties. Other than talking to reporters upon joining the Packers, he would not make himself available to media. He would not go on the air with McAfee. He wouldn’t say a word. He’d be as anonymous as the backup long snapper during training camp.
Yes, he’d be a hot topic for a few days but, so long as Rodgers embraced the role of being one of 53 players on the roster – nothing more, nothing less – the story would quickly die down.
Rodgers remains a good quarterback. Not a great quarterback but he’s a good one. He could help the Packers if disaster struck on gameday. He could help Love behind the scenes because of his experience in 267 career starts and in LaFleur’s offense.
Love has taken a beating at times this season behind Green Bay’s undermanned and/or underprepared offensive line. Maybe Love can survive all 17-plus games and play every meaningful snap. He’s also one blown block away from the sideline.
While there’s a narrative that Rodgers is a selfish, uncoachable, back-stabber, he loved his time in Green Bay and holds the team in high regard. Chances are, he’d be a model citizen.
“The falls there are just awesome, when the weather gets that cool little nip,” he said before the Packers-Steelers preseason game. “I loved the night games at Lambeau, especially the Sunday nights, Monday nights and occasional Thursday nights. Just so much fun. There’s nothing like that crowd. Been other places, but there’s nothing like that fan base and the way they travel and the crowds at home.
“Players around the league they talk about how special it is to play at Lambeau, and sometimes you might miss that or forget about that when you’re playing because it becomes so normal to have such an amazing crowd and they’re tailgating and they’re loud and they rarely sell their tickets to other teams’ fans.
“There’s a lot of great things about Wisconsin. I grew up there, really, and became a little more mature as an adult over the years there and had a great time and still have a lot of close friends there, a lot of fond memories.”
Or, as Rodgers said in his good-bye to Green Bay after the trade “This is not the end for us. I will see you again Green Bay, you’ll always have my heart.”
Rodgers spent 18 glorious seasons with the Packers. If everyone is in the right spot mentally – and that is a big if, obviously – he could finish his career where it started.
