title: Texans' Azeez Al-Shaair Update Raises Doubts About Season Return
full_text:
The Houston Texans revealed some rough news last week when they placed Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair on injured reserve with a groin injury.
Al-Shaair had been dealing with a lingering groin injury for a majority of this season . The Pro Bowl linebacker ultimately missed games in Weeks 4 and 10 with the injury before the decision was made to place him on injured reserve before their Thursday night game against the Indianapolis Colts.
The injured reserve placement takes Al-Shaair out of the mix for at least four games. In this case from Weeks 11 to 14 of the Texans' season. But if he's healthy enough to give it a go after that  absence, there's a chance that Houston could activate Al-Shaair from injured reserve for a late-season return.
However, based on some recent news from Texans general manager Nick Caserio, it's looking a little less likely that Al-Shaair will be able to return to Houston's lineup before the end of the year.
According to an interview with Caserio from 95.7 The Fan , Al-Shaair's timeline for a return is "up-in-the-air" right now, and seems to be trending towards close to the end of the regular season, if at all.
"I think his timeline is fairly extensive here," Caserio said of Al-Shaair. "He's going to be out here for a while. What the actual timeline looks like, it's probably going to be close here–– like, whether or not he would make it back for the regular season."
"I think that's up-in-the-air right now. So, probably TBD there."
While the door does technically remain open for Al-Shaair to make his return to the Texans' lineup at some point this season, things don't exactly seem to be trending in the most positive direction. And if anything, might be pointing towards a season-ending injury for the Pro Bowl linebacker.
For one, Al-Shaair's injury is one he had to undergo surgery for. It's been a nagging injury that's costed him games and high-level performance this season, and already projects to be a multiple-week absence.
On top of that, the Texans have run thin on injured reserve activations this season. NFL teams are given eight activations to utilize in a given season, with two extra coming in the postseason to those who make it. Houston has already used seven of those eight activations.
So the Texans have one activation to use over the next seven games. The chances of Al-Shaair being able to return in time for an end-of-season return, combined with Houston holding out their last injured reserve activation for him, are slim.
Perhaps a return in the postseason could be a bit more likely for Al-Shaair, depending on how his recovery goes over the next several weeks. But on the surface, it seems like a regular season return is trending towards less likely.
And if that's the case for Al-Shaair, the responsibility only grows larger for the remaining healthy pieces in the Texans' linebacker room.
Right now, Henry To'oTo'o has filled in as the Texans' top linebacker and green-dot signal caller without Al-Shaair, while a combination of Jake Hansen and Wade Woodaz have been the second linebacker to fill into the middle of the field.
As of last week's win over the Colts in which the Texans' defense allowed three points , things might be trending in the right direction for this unit without Al-Shaair. But things will only continue to get tougher to hold things together the deeper we get into the regular season.

title: Texans Have 3 Keys to Beating Ravens, Starting With Derrick Henry
full_text:
The Houston Texans are eyeing the potential of logging back-to-back wins on the schedule this weekend, as they'll be hosting the Baltimore Ravens for a Week 12 matchup that means a whole lot to each team's hopes of a late run to the postseason.
For the Ravens, they'll be trying to escape their current seven-game losing streak and keep any shot of a postseason appearance alive with a win in Houston. They'll still be without Lamar Jackson, but with Jacoby Brissett now getting more comfortable, alongside the threat of Derrick Henry, they won't be the easiest task to stop.
As for the Texans, they'll be fresh off a win over the Indianapolis Colts, eyeing their fifth win of the season, which would put them one game back of a .500 record. A victory here could also put Houston just one game out of the seventh seed in the AFC, making this week extra important to capitalize on.
With that in mind, let's take a deeper look at three of the biggest keys to victory for the Texans against the Ravens, thus putting them a little bit closer in reach of their postseason aspirations.
Derrick Henry hasn't had near the same success in the Ravens' offense ever since Lamar Jackson has missed time. He hasn't seen over 20 carries or 100 rushing yards since Week 5. Henry has also averaged 3.7 yards per carry over that stretch; far below his career average of 4.8.
There's no question as to why the Ravens are stuck in a seven-game losing streak. Their offense isn't the same unit as it was at the beginning of the season, and Henry's lackluster production comes as a big part of that.
But Henry is more than capable of turning things up on a moment’s notice, and the Texans have to ensure that they don't fall victim to an explosive Henry performance that keeps the Ravens within reach of an upset victory.
We've seen multiple times this season in which the Texans' high-end rushing defense winds up underwhelming for some lackluster performances. Week 7 against the New York Giants is a perfect example , and that led to a crushing overtime loss.
If Houston lets Henry run over their defense like Cam Skattebo and Co. did, the road to a convincing victory becomes a whole lot harder. So this is the biggest key the Texans have to focus on.
The Texans could be without Danielle Hunter for a third straight game this weekend. He still hasn't practiced with the hamstring injury he suffered before Week 10's game against the Cleveland Browns.
If that's the case, his absence would leave this defensive line shorthanded once again––and while this defensive front is both talented and deep, it's certainly much better with Hunter as a part of the equation, considering he finished last season with 15 total sacks.
But the Texans still might not have to worry if they're without Hunter's. That's because Will Anderson has been performing at a Defensive Player of the Year level with or without Hunter in the lineup, and he'll be chasing to build off the momentum of one of his best days of the year against the Colts.
Last week, Anderson had a sack, nine pressures, a season-high 37.5% pressure rate, and recorded his first-ever safety against the Colts en route to allowing three total points to their offense. Anderson is on fire right now and will be a one-man wrecking crew for the Ravens to account for in the trenches.
If Anderson keeps playing at such a rate against the Ravens, it'll be a tough task for Baltimore to stop. But this week's task will be a little bit more challenging than what Indianapolis presented with a couple of backup tackles.
Anderson's expected matchup, Ravens tackle Roger Rosengarden, has allowed pressure on 10.8% of his pass blocks this season, the ninth highest rate among right tackles.
The Texans saw one glaring weakness from their game plan actually turn around in their favor against the Colts last week: penalties. Houston incurred just four penalties for 23 yards against Indianapolis.
It's the second time this season that the Texas have incurred four or fewer penalties in a single game, as well as the second game in which they've given up 25 or fewer yards due to penalties.
Compared to the issues Houston has faced in the penalty category throughout the first half of this season , this is an incredible trend to build on. The Texans have averaged over seven flags a game throughout their 11 games this season, and it has been something DeMeco Ryans and Houston's staff have been trying desperately to improve upon.
Against the Colts, the Texans managed to do just that. And if Houston can continue to stay disciplined this weekend, they'll have the perfect opportunity to take advantage of Baltimore's own penalty problems.
The Ravens rank seventh in the NFL for average penalties per game, and have the lowest average net penalties of any team in the league (-2.36).

title: Texans Expected to Make Big O-Line Shakeup, and It's the Right Call
full_text:
The Houston Texans have been rolling with the same five-man offensive line for the majority of the regular season.
That unit has consisted of Aireontae Ersery and Trent Brown at left and right tackle, Keylan Rutledge and Ed Ingram at left and right guard, and Evan Brown at center.
It's been a group that's had its ups and downs throughout the first half of the season; showing some positive strides from the last two years, but also showing room for improvement.
However, during the Texans' latest game— and win— over the Indianapolis Colts last Thursday , their offensive line performed at some of their best of the season so far.
The showing also came with a different five-man front from what Houston has been running for a majority of the season: Braden Smith, Houston's $20 million free agent signing from earlier this year, became the starting right tackle over Trent Brown.
And that's a look that the Texans are reportedly going to stick with moving forward.
According to a report from KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson, Smith is expected to be the Texans' starting right tackle for this weekend's game against the Baltimore Ravens.
#Texans starting offensive line expected vs. #Ravens : LT Aireontae Ersery, LG Febechi Nwaiwu (if Keylan Rutledge stinger continues to sideline him) C Evan Brown, RG Ed Ingram, and, now, RT Braden Smith after grading out highly vs. #Colts pic.twitter.com/FuayhJ4mLB
If Smith does wind up getting the start against the Ravens, it'll be Smith's first start of the 2026 season.
During the Texans' last game against the Colts, head coach DeMeco Ryans explained that Smith was expected to rotate in with Brown as Houston's right tackle. But after Brown went down with a back injury, it was Smith who took control of the reps on the right side for the rest of the game.
Given that he stood out for some of the best production the Texans have seen at the position this season––playing 59 snaps to allow just two pressures, zero sacks, and zero penalties––the team wants to continue leaning into Smith.
And in reality, it's the right move for the Texans to take on. While it might not be ideal for an offensive line adjustment like this to be done in Week 12 of the season, Houston could reap the rewards in the long haul because of it.
For the extent that Trent Brown has started for the Texans this season, he's been a serviceable option on the right side. He's allowed three quarterback hits and three sacks in a little over 600 snaps on the year.
But Brown has also allowed 24 pressures on the year as well. His biggest issue? Penalties, as he's incurred nine on the year so far; good for just around one a game.
Overall, Brown has been a solid, but replaceable right tackle for the Texans this year––which is largely what he was as a starter closing out the 2025 season. And where there's room for improvement, Braden Smith has clearly stood out in his opportunities to be a potentially better option for Houston to roll with at the position.
He stayed out of penalty trouble against the Colts, was an extremely positive force in the run game en route to David Montgomery's 107-yard day on the ground , allowed just two pressures on Stroud, and performed just as well as the Texans could've hoped for when they invested in him this offseason.
And that's really the key: the Texans invested in Smith to be a starter on their offensive line earlier this year. The only reason he didn't begin the year there is because he was on injured reserve with a foot injury .
Now, Smith is back healthy, and he's playing like the upgrade at right tackle that he was advertised to be. So for as much as continuity on the offensive line helps, pivoting to a better fit in Smith seems like the best course of action for the Texans to go for the second half of the year.
Based on Wilson's report, the Texans seem to recognize that as well––putting Smith on track to get the start this weekend, and build upon his positive performance from last Thursday to cement further confidence that he can be Houston's guy at right tackle until further notice.

title: Texans Get Marvin Harrison Jr. Back, But WR Injury Woes Continue
full_text:
The Houston Texans were able to see one of their recently injured wide receivers take a step towards suiting up once again in Week 12 against the Baltimore Ravens.
That's because Marvin Harrison Jr.–– who has missed the last two games due to a lingering hamstring injury–– was finally able to practice in limited capacity during Houston's Wednesday practice session .
It's the first time that Harrison Jr. has participated with the team in any capacity since November 12th, when he presumably suffered the hamstring injury in practice.
That led to an absence against the Cleveland Browns and Indianapolis Colts, and thus, a shorthanded Texans wide receiver room. But with increased participation over the next two sessions, there's a good chance that Harrison Jr. will be good to go against Baltimore.
However, the Texans' wide receiver injuries still managed to linger into their Wednesday practice, despite Harrison Jr.'s individual status trending in the right direction.
That's because Kayshon Boutte was a DNP during practice with a hip injury he suffered during last week's game against the Colts.
Boutte's DNP is eye-catching. Not only because the wide receiver wound up missing practice, but also for the fact that it came even after the Texans' extended mini-bye that came as a result of their last game being played on Thursday.
And the injury for Boutte unfortunately comes fresh off of Boutte's strongest game in a while.
Against the Colts, Boutte hauled in both of his targets for two receptions and 40 yards, also bringing in a big-time touchdown grab in the second quarter for C.J. Stroud's second of three scores on the day.
It marked Boutte's second game of the season in which he's had 40 or more reception yards, and his third touchdown reception on the year as well.
Boutte still has two days to potentially practice, and thus see his status for Sunday against Baltimore to trend in the right direction. But if he's unable to participate on Thursday, there's an increasingly likely chance that Houston will be down yet another receiver due to injury.
Despite the Texans having what's been viewed as a deep receiving room at many times this season, they haven't had a ton of opportunities to show off this entire unit in its full capacity, simply due to ongoing injury issues at the position.
Jayden Higgins was viewed as an emerging WR2 in the Texans' passing attack, then tore his ACL before the first game . Jaylin Noel just caught fire through the first half of the season, then had a season-ending toe injury.
Nico Collins has missed a couple of games with a hamstring injury. Marvin Harrison Jr. has missed two appearances since his arrival, also with a hamstring injury. Tank Dell just got back in Week 7 from his own knee injury. Now, Kayshon Boutte is dealing with his hip issue. You get the point.
Thankfully, thanks to that extensive depth at the position, the Texans will have a healthy-enough unit to roll into Week 12's game against Baltimore and still have a potent arsenal for Stroud to work with.
Collins, Dell, potentially Harrison Jr., and Xavier Hutchinson will all be good to go, and each of those guys has shown their respective flashes of production over the course of this season.
Yet, another wide receiver injury–– this time to Boutte–– just goes to show how beaten up Houston has been at the position all season long.

title: 3 Things the Texans Should Be Thankful for This Thanksgiving
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a lot to be thankful for this holiday season.
For one, they don't have to play their Week 12 game until Sunday , unlike 10 of the other teams currently participating in games from Wednesday through Friday––giving the roster a bit more rest and time with their families before a pivotal matchup against the Baltimore Ravens.
But outside of those implications, there's even more for the Texans to have gratitude for.
While the first half of this season hasn't gone exactly how anyone in the building has intended, hope is still alive to turn things around in the second half of the year. And with momentum seemingly coming at the right time, there might be even more for this group to be thankful for by the time we hit New Year's.
But for now, as Thanksgiving approaches, as does the home stretch for the NFL season with just seven games to go, let's break down three key things the Texans should be most thankful for:
It's funny how things work. It was less than 12 months ago where many fans and national media members were questioning C.J. Stroud's ability to be the Texans' long-term guy under center after a less-than-ideal playoff loss.
But after the first 11 games of this season, Stroud has left no doubts about his ability to be an elite-level quarterback in the NFL, as he's performed as one of the best at his position throughout most of the year––to the point where it's not too outlandish to consider him a dark horse MVP candidate.
He probably won't end up winning it, simply due to the sluggish start the Texans had to this season that currently puts them on the outside looking in for the postseason, but Stroud's individual production can't be overlooked.
He's on pace to record over 4,500 passing yards and over 35 passing touchdowns, which should be a leap that the Texans are more than thankful for. They'll get their chance to show their gratitude in the form of a lucrative contract extension later this offseason.
The Texans' defense hasn't been as consistently elite as they proved to be throughout last season. Their run defense has been solid, but has had its moments. The secondary has been prone to giving up big plays. The linebacker unit has been battered with injuries all season long.
But throughout all of the chaos the Texans have had on their defense, one presence has remained just as dominant, if not even more so, from where he stood last year–– and that's current Defensive Player of the Year frontrunner Will Anderson Jr.
Anderson has been a wrecking ball on the Texans' defensive line that has stamped him atop the NFL leaderboards for sacks (11.5), total pressures (60), and pressure rate (19.3%).
He's stepped up in the time that Danielle Hunter has been out with a lingering hamstring injury, so much so that he came away with the AFC's Defensive Player of the Week after his Week 11 performance against the Indianapolis Colts.
Without Anderson, who knows where the Texans' defense would rank right now? Thankfully, Houston doesn't have to worry. And if he keeps up this pace, his efforts should be rewarded at the end of the season with some new hardware for his trophy case and a second-straight All-Pro nod.
Somehow, the Texans are still right within the hunt of clawing their way into the postseason despite falling to an 0-4 record to initially start the season.
And based on how some of the surrounding teams in the AFC are trending (i.e. the Pittsburgh Steelers, Baltimore Ravens), Houston should be feeling more and more optimistic about their chances of a fourth straight postseason appearance every passing week.
Houston wasn't supposed to be here. After the Texans had dropped their first four games––and even after losses in Weeks 7 and 10 in very winnable games––many had written off this team and their chances of a late postseason run.
But as we stand with seven weeks to go, they're only two games back from positioning themselves as the seventh seed. And their next two games are against a couple of AFC threats right within the hunt as well.
It would make for the most miraculous feat we've seen in DeMeco Ryans' tenure as the Texans' head coach; coming back from 0-4 to be the second team in NFL history to make the postseason. But if Houston can keep the hot hand for the next few games, a playoff bid is very much possible.

title: Texans Injury Report: 5 Players Miss Practice Ahead of Ravens Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans have released their first injury report of the week rolling into their Week 12 matchup against the Baltimore Ravens .
And on the status for some players, things seem to be trending in the right direction. In the case of five others, they wound up not practicing on Wednesday, and thus makes their status a bit more cloudy as it relates to this weekend's action.
Let's break down the latest on the injury front from the Texans' practice a few days away from the Ravens traveling to Reliant Stadium:
TE Brevin Jordan (finger/foot) WR Kayshon Boutte (hip) DE Danielle Hunter (hamstring) OL Keylan Rutledge (neck/shoulder) DT Sheldon Rankins (ankle)
WR Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring) LB Jake Hummel (abdomen/groin) DE Logan Hall (hip/shoulder)
CB Kamari Lassiter (wrist) RB Woody Marks (concussion) S Reed Blankenship (hand) LB Jake Hansen (elbow) OT Blake Fisher (thumb) OT Trent Brown (wrist)
Let's break down some of the good news first: two of the Texans' bigger names on the offensive end that missed last week's game against the Colts managed to practice on Wednesday: that's running back Woody Marks (concussion) and wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring)
With two more days of practice to go for each, there's a good chance that both guys will be able to suit up against the Ravens considering everything continues to move in the right direction.
DeMeco Ryans noted that the team was "hopeful" Marks would make his return earlier this week, and signs appear to be pointing in that direction. Marks will pair up next to David Montgomery within the Texans' backfield, who came off a game where he posted his season-high in rushing yards with 107.
As for those that the Texans are at risk of being without on Sunday, though, there's a couple of names on each side of the ball to watch out for.
Most notably, defensive end Danielle Hunter still isn't practicing yet after suffering his hamstring injury before Week 10's game against the Cleveland Browns .
Houston will likely have to see Hunter practice once ahead of this coming weekend to have optimism around his playing status against Baltimore, but the team could be taking a rather cautious approach around one of their older, more impactful veterans on the defense.
Another older veteran on the Texans defense— defensive end Sheldon Rankins— also didn't practice on Wednesday.
Being without Hunter is enough of a challenge for Houston to overcome, but losing their top defensive tackle in Rankins could make things even tougher, if he is inevitably ruled out for this weekend. He's got two more days to practice and change the feelings around his status.
Offensively, the Texans had some concerns worth noting as well: wide receiver Kayshon Boutte is still dealing with the effects from his hip injury sustained on Thursday Night Football, and could put his status to play this weekend in doubt.
If Boutte is out, the Texans' wide receiver room will continue to look thin, as it has been since moving past the bye; relying on only Nico Collins, Tank Dell, Xavier Hutchinson, and Marvin Harrison Jr., if he continues to trend in the right direction.
Keylan Rutledge is also still dealing with some of the effects of his injury suffered last week against the Colts, which turned out to be his second stinger of the year in the second half.
If Rutledge is set to miss any time moving forward, expect the Texans to roll with Febechi Nwaiwu as their fill-in at left guard. However, still with two more days of practice to go, there's still room for his and everyone else's status to improve between now and game day.

title: Texans, C.J. Stroud Among Biggest Winners of Steelers-Rodgers Drama
full_text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers made an eye-catching, and really, a stunning change to their offense heading into Week 12 of the NFL season.
After having Aaron Rodgers under center as their starting quarterback for the last 26 consecutive games, the Steelers have decided to bench the future Hall of Famer for Mason Rudolph for their upcoming game vs. the Denver Broncos, leaving Rodgers as an inactive on their gameday roster.
pic.twitter.com/F2qo4OawcY
The change in the Steelers' quarterback room is one that was largely unpredictable.
Rodgers was all but locked into his spot as Pittsburgh's QB1, despite their lackluster passing production across the first half of the season, and after their latest 16-19 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, he might've finally played his last game in the NFL with no signs that Pittsburgh plans on turning to him moving forward.
However, as the Steelers have made a big change under center, there's a chance that the Texans and C.J. Stroud now come out of this decision as some of the biggest winners of all––and that's for more reasons than one.
One of the most important fallouts from this decision that connects with the Texans is the fact that Houston will be playing this same Steelers team in a little over a week come Week 13's Sunday Night Football matchup; a game that could have significant consequences for playoff seeding in the AFC.
The Texans have a history of taking care of Rodgers and the Steelers' offense as of their most recent matchup in the Wild Card Round of last postseason, where Houston claimed a dominant 30-6 victory on the road at Acrisure Stadium.
But for their matchup against the Steelers looming this season, they'll now be faced with the task of seeing Mason Rudolph, which could be a simpler–– or perhaps even tougher battle for the Texans to take on–– depending on how Rudolph looks as Pittsburgh's QB1 on Friday against Denver.
On top of the implications now in play for the Texans' Week 13 game, the AFC Wild Card race now has a bunch of backup-level quarterbacks competing alongside Houston that now tend to make their road to the postseason suddenly a bit more palatable.
Of the six teams that are reasonably within the hunt to make some noise in the postseason, only two of those teams have yet to make a significant change at the quarterback position: that's the Texans, who have C.J. Stroud playing at an MVP-level , and the Cleveland Browns with Deshaun Watson.
Current starting QBs of the six AFC teams I believe will fight for the last two playoff spots … • Browns: Deshaun Watson • Steelers: Mason Rudolph • Patriots: Tommy DeVito • Texans: CJ Stroud • Raiders: Fernando Mendoza • Ravens: Jacoby Brissett Advantage: Houston.
Having the edge at quarterback can be a much-welcomed lift for any NFL team on a given week, but that's especially so for those looking to make a run into the playoffs.
The top five teams sitting clearly above the Texans in the AFC standings each have an above-average to elite option at quarterback: the Buffalo Bills and Josh Allen, the Denver Broncos and Bo Nix, the Jacksonville Jaguars and Trevor Lawrence, the Cincinnati Bengals and Joe Burrow, and the Kansas City Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes.
The Texans and Stroud aren't far away from becoming that sixth or seventh team in the standings. With a few victories in a row over the next few weeks against winnable matchups like the Ravens and Steelers, along with the Philadelphia Eagles and Tennessee Titans, it might be just enough to give Houston the necessary lift in the Wild Card race .
And if that late-season run does come to form again for the Texans, that only helps Stroud and his case of cashing in an even bigger check once it comes time to negotiate a new contract extension later this offseason.
But making such a run happen all starts with the Texans taking care of business against the Ravens, then doing so once again against the Steelers the following week, which would then lift Houston to .500 for the first time this season.
With Pittsburgh's latest decision to turn away from a Hall of Fame quarterback like Rodgers until further notice, those chances of the Texans making that climb happen begin to look a whole lot better.

title: Predicting Texans' Final 7 Games as Playoff Hopes Remain Alive
full_text:
The Houston Texans are creeping closer and closer to being within range of a playoff spot in the AFC , as they sit at 4-6 with just seven games to go on the schedule, but ride into those upcoming matchups with some positive momentum on their side.
So how could those upcoming games for the Texans pan out? They've got three matchups at home and four on the road, and each of them are looking critical for their chances of clawing their way up the AFC ladder for a top-seven seed.
With that in mind, let's take a look at all seven matchups that are on the horizon for the Texans, predict how each could go, and see how their record pans out at the end.
The Ravens are on a six-game losing streak, are still without Lamar Jackson, and are taking the road against a Texans team with some momentum building up in their favor.
While the Ravens did play the Carolina Panthers close this past weekend, Houston's scoring attack combined with their improving defense should overwhelm them enough for the Texans to win back-to-back home games for the first time since 2025.
Prediction: Texans Win, 31-13
The Texans get a chance to face the Steelers in a primetime setting for the second time this calendar year on Sunday Night Football. And while Pittsburgh's defense could cause some distress for C.J. Stroud, it's hard to imagine their offense making much of a dent on the other end.
That's especially so after the Steelers just announced they were benching Aaron Rodgers in Week 12 for Mason Rudolph. This is a game the Texans have to take advantage of, and should, which would finally take them to .500 for the first time this year–– so long as they take care of Baltimore.
Prediction: Texans Win, 28-10
This is a sneaky game for the Texans that could quickly become a challenging one by the time we get to Week 14.
Washington is currently on a two-game win streak that could quickly turn to four with wins over the Arizona Cardinals and Tennessee Titans, and could lead to Jayden Daniels and Co. being a bit of a freight train to stop, especially on their home field.
However, the Texans would be a pretty tough force to stop at this point as well. They'd be on a three-game win streak, and if their defense is catching fire, Jayden Daniels and the Commanders’ offensive line might be overwhelmed enough for Houston to keep things rolling for a much-needed Week 14 win.
Prediction: Texans Win, 23-21
This is undoubtedly the toughest game left on the Texans' schedule; a rematch against a divisional opponent in which they already beat once this season. But it's even harder to beat a team twice in a season––and for a Super Bowl contender like Jacksonville, they could be best equipped to stop Houston on a hypothetical win streak.
Perhaps the Texans gut out a last-minute victory in their second game of the season against Jacksonville, as they did around this time last year. However, I've got Jacksonville and their improved roster from Week 6's meeting splitting their season series vs. Houston, and paving the way to an inevitable AFC South victory.
Prediction: Texans Lose, 17-16
This needs to be a game the Texans come out with a win in. The Eagles have sunken to the bottom of the NFC North, will likely be starting Joe Milton, and might just be gunning towards better draft positioning at this point in the year, rather than playing spoiler to Houston's playoff hopes.
The Eagles do lead the all-time series against the Texans 6-0. So maybe claiming a win here will be easier said than done. But their offense appears to have no chance of overcoming what could be a dangerous Houston defense at this point in the year, and could lead to a resounding road victory.
Prediction: Texans Win, 21-6
This is another challenge for the Texans that might be a bit too tough to overcome: a road test against a fiery offense in another playoff threat, the Packers, who could have their defense rolling for their best production of the season with Micah Parsons back in the lineup.
Maybe the Texans will be able to defy historical precedent in this game once again. Green Bay is 5-1 all-time against Houston. But it seems like it would have to take some real C.J. Stroud heroics or a star-studded Will Anderson to take down the Packers here. I'll have them coming up just short by less than a touchdown.
Prediction: Texans Lose, 23-17
This is the perfect moment for a cathartic win over a division rival they've already bested once this season. While the Titans will certainly be playing for pride in their final game of the year, Houston will be searching for any life that might be left for a playoff appearance and end the regular season off with a home victory.
The Texans have already dominated the Titans for a 20-plus point victory in October, and the same could be in store once Week 18 rolls around.
Prediction: Texans Win, 33-6
If each of these seven projections pans out, the Texans end up at 9-8. Not exactly eliminated from the postseason picture, but they'd certainly need some help in order to find their way to a seventh seed in the AFC.
The Texans would likely need the Steelers and the New England Patriots to lose three or four of their next seven games. Considering each of them has a backup-level quarterback set to start down the stretch, seeing such an outcome is far from impossible.
However, for the Texans to find the easiest route to the postseason, it relies on their ability to stack up as many wins as possible through their next seven games.
By the looks of it, a vast majority of those matchups appear to be winnable, but a loss in just one or two of those games makes the road quickly become a whole lot tougher.

title: What Woody Marks' Return Means for Texans Run Game vs. Ravens
full_text:
The Houston Texans' run game is set to get a bit of a facelift in their upcoming matchup against the Baltimore Ravens.
According to an update from Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans, the team is "hopeful" that Marks will return to the lineup in Week 12 after missing Thursday night's game against the Indianapolis Colts.
Marks has been in concussion protocol since the Texans' Week 10 game against the Cleveland Browns, in which he left and didn't return in the middle of the third quarter. Once Sunday against the Ravens arrives, Marks will be two weeks removed from that injury and should be good to go for his return to the field.
But for the Texans' run game, it'll be the first time that both Marks and Montgomery will be working in tandem with one another for the first time since Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans.
What can we expect from Houston on the ground as they'll be back to 100%? And will the backfield split be any different than what we last saw from when each of Marks and Montgomery were healthy at the start of the season?
Now, since the first four weeks of the season when the Texans had a collective 0-4 record, their run game has looked a lot better in the moments that Woody Marks or David Montgomery has led the operation by themselves.
However, we can look back to those first four weeks at the Texans were fully healthy in the backfield to get a better picture of what to expect for their running back split when both of their top guys are healthy.
From Weeks 1 through 4, Montgomery was on the field for an average of 54% of the Texans' offensive snaps and saw 47 total carries. Marks was out there for around 45% of the snaps and came away with 28 total carries.
So Montgomery, when both guys are healthy, is typically leading the way over Marks by a slight margin in snaps, but also takes a bulk of the Texans' carries in the backfield, while Marks operates as a pass-blocker and a more potent weapon in the receiving game.
However, based on how Montgomery operated in the Texans' last game against the Colts, maybe there's a route to him seeing a bit more than that 55% snap share.
There's a case that Montgomery should get a bigger workload in the Texans' offense moving forward because of how solid he looked against the Colts . And that outcome certainly remains a possibility if Montgomery continues to carry his efficiency into the next game against the Ravens.
However, at least initially, the Texans feel more likely to roll with their previous setup in the backfield at a 55-45 split and roll with the hot hand on a weekly basis, rather than simply lean on Montgomery more right off the bat.
Marks has been a solid weapon in the Texans' offense when he's been given the opportunities. He's a quick, home run hitter on the ground, can work well as a pass-catcher, and is an underrated pass-blocker that is deserving of seeing the ball in his hands to make plays on a weekly basis.
Houston has entrusted him with over 15 touches a game in every week that Montgomery has been sidelined, and it's hard to imagine he's totally taken out of the game plan moving forward now that the position looks a little bit healthier.
The one back in the Texans' offense who feels most likely to be taken out of the game plan is their now-third-string runner, Emari Demercado , who has taken around 25% of the offensive snaps to Marks and Montgomery when the other has been sidelined, but now feels due to see that number reach closer to zero.
Demercado has been a serviceable backup when the Texans have had him on the field this season, but he was only meant to be a plug-and-play veteran who stepped up due to injury.
Now that Houston is healthy in the backfield, Demercado reverts back to their RB3, and only sees looks on the offense if either of Marks or Montgomery is forced out for more time. There's a chance he could find some snaps on special teams so he's not a complete non-factor on the Texans' roster, though.

title: Predicting Anthony Richardson’s First Start Back for Colts
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are turning back to Anthony Richardson Sr. at quarterback , giving him his first start since 2024 . Nearly two years after his last start, the former fourth overall pick has an opportunity to prove he's developed into the player the Colts had envisioned he'd become.
Richardson has thrown just six passes over the last two seasons. His return comes at an important time for a Colts team that has lost five of its last six games and desperately needs a spark offensively.
There are plenty of questions surrounding what Richardson will look like in his first meaningful action in nearly two years. However, his combination of arm strength and athleticism gives Indianapolis a different dimension that hasn't been available for much of the season.
The biggest question surrounding Richardson is how quickly he can get comfortable again. While he has remained with the organization and continued developing behind the scenes, there's a considerable difference between preparing as a backup and operating an NFL offense on Sundays.
Richardson's accuracy and decision-making have been inconsistent throughout his career. In 2024, he completed just 47.7% of his passes while throwing eight touchdowns and 12 interceptions. Those issues won't necessarily disappear because he's had additional time to develop, and the extended layoff makes it difficult to expect a polished performance right away.
However, Richardson has indicated that his understanding of the offense has improved. He's specifically pointed to the importance of taking the easier completions, improving his footwork and staying on schedule rather than constantly looking for the explosive play, which is particularly relevant given he'll be working in an offense that is currently missing a consistent threat down the field. Simply making the routine throws and protecting the football would represent a positive step.
Where Richardson can immediately make a difference is with his legs. His rushing ability gives Indianapolis a weapon that opposing defenses have to account for on every snap. With Jonathan Taylor already established as one of the league's most dangerous running backs, the combination could create some difficult decisions for New York's defense.
In their last start alongside one another, Richardson rushed for 70 yards and a touchdown while Taylor exploded for 218 yards and three touchdowns against the Tennessee Titans. Richardson's ability to threaten defenses as a runner helped create opportunities for Taylor, who took advantage of them throughout the afternoon.
That same dynamic could be particularly important against the Giants. Indianapolis has struggled to consistently generate offense this season, and Richardson's presence could help create more explosive plays in the running game. Defenses won't be able to focus exclusively on Taylor when Richardson is capable of keeping the football himself.
Shane Steichen will have an important role in making sure Richardson isn't asked to do too much. Expect Indianapolis to incorporate some designed quarterback runs, play-action opportunities and easy throws early to help him establish a rhythm. The Colts should also look to get Taylor involved early rather than putting the entire offense on Richardson's shoulders.
Ultimately, a successful return doesn't necessarily require a spectacular statistical performance. If Richardson can give the Colts a more dynamic rushing attack, make enough plays through the air and limit costly mistakes, Indianapolis should see an improved version of their offense.
It's difficult to know exactly what to expect from Richardson after such an extended absence. There will likely be some errors, particularly as he gets reacclimated to the speed of the game and works through his progressions.
Still, Richardson's athleticism should give Indianapolis some opportunities to create explosive plays. I expect the Colts to lean on Taylor and the running game while allowing Richardson to use his legs to keep New York's defense off balance.
My prediction: 15-of-27 (55.5%) for 185 passing yards, one passing TD, one INT, eight carries, 45 rushing yards and one rushing TD.
Understanding how Richardson has played in the past, I'd expect an outing that's far from perfect, but one where he contributes both through the air and on the ground. It might not be a particularly efficient afternoon passing the football, but Richardson's ability to create plays with his legs should help make up for some of the expected rust. If he can produce that type of performance while taking care of the football, the Colts would have plenty of reason to feel encouraged about what he could bring to the offense moving forward, result of the game aside.

title: 3 Keys to Victory for Colts in Week 12 Showdown vs. Giants
full_text:
The New York Giants just beat the same Jacksonville Jaguars team that steamrolled the Indianapolis Colts 42-7 less than a month ago.
Indianapolis (3-8) has lost six of its last seven games, ranks dead last in total offensive EPA and just released its starting quarterback. Meanwhile, the Giants (6-3-1) are coming off an impressive 23-18 victory over Jacksonville.
But can Anthony Richardson Sr. provide the spark this team so desperately needs?
Making his first start since 2024, Richardson might have to turn into Superman on Sunday for Indianapolis to have a chance.
Here are three keys to a Colts victory in Week 12.
In 11 games during the 2024 season, Richardson amassed 499 rushing yards and six touchdowns while averaging 5.8 yards per carry.
That version of Richardson is exactly what this offense needs.
Jonathan Taylor is averaging just 4.0 yards per carry this season, and having a quarterback alongside him who's equally capable of doing damage on the ground should open up some much-needed rushing lanes.
I want to see Shane Steichen lean heavily into designed quarterback runs and read-option concepts, forcing defenders to account for both AR and JT.
This is a well-coached, defensively disciplined Giants team under John Harbaugh that held Jacksonville to just 77 rushing yards last week.
If Richardson can't get going with his legs, it's going to be a long afternoon.
Give J.J. McCarthy credit for finding ways to win, but we've seen just how ugly things can get with him under center.
Even in Sunday's victory over Jacksonville, McCarthy completed just 18 of his 38 passing attempts for 173 yards and a touchdown, finishing with a 69.3 passer rating.
The Colts need to make him uncomfortable early and often.
Granted, generating consistent pressure has been an issue for Indianapolis all season, and trading away DeForest Buckner certainly didn't help.
Adetomiwa Adebawore, who leads the Colts with five sacks, and guys like Laiatu Latu need to have themselves a day.
Force McCarthy to be the guy who has to win this football game for New York.
After putting together a Pro Bowl rookie campaign with 817 receiving yards, Tyler Warren has managed just 298 yards through nine games this season.
Over the last two games, Warren has totaled three receptions for 23 yards.
Warren is by far the most reliable receiving option Richardson has at his disposal. Giving Richardson easy completions over the middle and allowing Warren to do what he does best — impose his physicality on defenders after the catch — should be a point of emphasis for Steichen.
Indianapolis doesn't need Richardson to suddenly become an elite pocket passer, but it does need Warren to make life easier for him.
The odds are stacked against Indianapolis on Sunday, but if Richardson can get this offense moving again and the defense can expose McCarthy's inconsistencies, we might have ourselves a football game.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 3 Things the Colts Should Prioritize in Their General Manager Search
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are in need of a new general manager.
Indianapolis' new hire will inherit an organization at a crossroads. After years of consistent mediocrity under Chris Ballard, the franchise has an opportunity to start fresh in its football operations department and turn an average team into a perennial contender in the AFC. Getting that hire right will be crucial to determining whether the Colts can accomplish that feat.
Indianapolis Colts' principal owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon 's search should be about more than finding someone with an impressive résumé or experience in a successful front office. Indianapolis needs to identify an executive who understands how to build a winning roster, recognizes where the organization has fallen short and is unafraid to take a different approach.
There are several qualities that should separate the right candidate from the rest of the field. From experience and leadership to roster-building philosophy and the authority to shape the organization, Indianapolis needs to be deliberate about what it wants from its next general manager . Here are three areas the Colts should prioritize.
The Colts should begin their search by identifying executives who have played meaningful roles in building successful organizations.
Previously holding the general manager title shouldn't be as important as their body of work. In fact, doing so would limit the talent pool significantly. Some of the most qualified candidates are assistant general managers, directors of player personnel or other front-office executives who have helped shape winning rosters without being the face of the project.
The Buffalo Bills, San Francisco 49ers and Detroit Lions stand out as three organizations Indianapolis should examine closely. All three have established themselves as consistent playoff contenders in recent years, with front offices that have demonstrated an ability to identify talent and build competitive rosters, and do so sustainably. The Colts should look beyond the people at the top and evaluate which executives have played meaningful roles in those organizations' success.
Simply working for a successful franchise doesn't automatically make someone a strong general manager candidate, so the Colts will have to understand each candidates responsibilities, the outcomes they were most in charge of producing and how consistently they did so. A candidate who has consistently demonstrated an ability to contribute to a winning culture should carry considerable weight in the search.
Just as important is finding someone with a well-rounded background. Player evaluation and scouting are essential, but the general manager's job extends far beyond identifying prospects and free agents. Roster construction, contract negotiations, salary-cap management and the ability to oversee an entire football operation are all part of the responsibility. Indianapolis needs someone who can balance those demands rather than excel in one area while relying entirely on others to handle the rest.
The Colts' own experience under Chris Ballard provides a clear example of why that balance matters. Ballard built a reputation as a strong talent evaluator, particularly through the draft, but his shortcomings in other areas ultimately limited the organization's ability to improve. His approach to free agency was often too conservative. In the trade market, he tended to be too aggressive. Additionally, despite always having some of the most cap space available of any team in the league, Ballard always failed to maximize his resources.
Finding talented players through the draft is important, but it cannot be the only avenue through which a team builds its roster. The Colts need a general manager who can identify talent and maximize every resource at his disposal.
The next person in charge should also be a collaborative but decisive leader. Building a successful organization requires input from a variety of departments, and the person in charge needs to be willing to listen to those around them. At the same time, they must be comfortable making difficult decisions, holding people accountable and establishing a clear direction for the franchise.
Ultimately, the Colts should be looking for someone who has helped build a winner and is ready to lead an organization of their own. Previous experience in the GM chair would be a valuable qualification, but it shouldn't outweigh a candidate's actual track record, football knowledge and ability to lead.
The Colts need a general manager who understands that building a winning roster requires more than identifying talented players and waiting for the right opportunities to present themselves. The NFL is an increasingly competitive league, and teams must be able to adapt their approach to personnel decisions as the game continues to evolve. Indianapolis should prioritize an executive who embraces modern evaluation methods, understands the value of analytics and is willing to take calculated risks to improve the roster.
Analytics have to be a fundamental part of that process. The next general manager should understand how to combine film evaluation, scouting reports and advanced data to develop a more complete picture of a player's value. Analytics can help teams identify undervalued talent, evaluate positional value and make more informed decisions when weighing a player's projected production against the financial commitment required to acquire him. The goal should be to use every available resource to gain an advantage instead of leaning on more traditional metrics.
James Gladstone in Jacksonville is a great example of a general manager who leans into analytics and has seen rapid results. Since taking over the Jaguars in 2025, Gladstone has quickly turned the franchise into the best in the AFC South with a 20-7 record and a division title. The Colts would be wise to try a similar plan.
Just as important is finding someone who isn't afraid to be aggressive when opportunities arise. The Colts have often approached free agency with the mindset of waiting for the right value rather than actively pursuing players who could make an immediate impact. That philosophy can leave a team sitting on financial flexibility while other organizations address their biggest weaknesses. Indianapolis needs a general manager who is willing to spend when the right player becomes available, explore the trade market and use draft capital to pursue talent rather than hesitating.
That same mindset should carry over to the draft. Draft picks are valuable, but they are not guaranteed contributors, and the Colts shouldn't be afraid to move up the board or package selections to acquire a player they believe can change the trajectory of the franchise. There is a balance between making smart investments and being too cautious to take advantage of opportunities. The next general manager needs to understand that difference.
None of this is an argument for reckless spending or sacrificing the future for short-term gains; aggression must be calculated. Every signing, trade and draft-day move needs to be supported by a clear evaluation of the player's ability, financial value and fit within the roster.
Indianapolis cannot afford to be passive. The next GM should be willing to take measured risks, use every resource available to them and pursue talent through every avenue necessary to build a contender.
Beyond experience and philosophy, Indianapolis needs a general manager who understands the current state of the roster and has a clear plan for getting the franchise back into contention. The Colts have several areas that need attention, and their next hire must be capable of identifying which positions require immediate investment and which can be addressed over time. That vision should guide everything from free agency and the draft to the team's long-term financial commitments.
