title: 3 Things Colts Fans Should Be Thankful For This Thanksgiving
full_text:
One might assume that Indianapolis Colts fans have nothing to be thankful for this time around.
The Colts are in the midst of an organizational rebuild as they are currently 3-8 entering Week 12 and have fired, traded, and/or released numerous key contributors over the past month and a half. Not only is the season lost, but they also lack a first-round pick or franchise quarterback to lean on for optimism.
The Indianapolis Colts are a bad football team, and the near future may appear just as bleak, but there's reason to be hopeful.
So, grab some turkey and whatever else you fancy on this feastful day of togetherness, and follow along as I highlight some of the things Indianapolis Colts fans should be thankful for.
Yes, the Indianapolis Colts' 2026-27 season is all but lost, but some recent changes have given us all more reason to tune in on game days.
Before, the main reason for catching Colts games was to keep tabs on the intriguing young talent that remains following the organization's recent mass exodus of longtime contributors.
Now, following the release of starting quarterback Daniel Jones, Colts fans now get to watch Anthony Richardson lead the offense for what is likely his last hurrah donning the horseshoe.
Richardson secretly evolving into a reliable, steady hand at quarterback and thus turning the Colts' season around is highly unlikely, but at least his otherworldly athleticism will be on display.
Football fans from all over will at least be keeping tabs on Richardson's performance down the stretch. Yes, because they're also intrigued by what he's got after three and a half tumultuous years in Indianapolis, but also because he's appointment viewing - for better or for worse.
The Colts may still lose out with Anthony Richardson leading the charge, but at least his woes will be entertaining and insightful, whereas continuing to trot out Daniel Jones did nobody any favors .
The Indianapolis Colts have finally parted ways with general manager Chris Ballard after a decade of mediocrity .
That alone should give Colts fans hope for the future.
Indianapolis Colts' principal owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has spearheaded a much-needed rebuild by firing Ballard, trading away longtime franchise cornerstones in Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, and parting ways with a few other offensive starters.
Some of her decisions thus far have warranted criticism, but at least Irsay-Gordon is holding people accountable -- something this franchise has lacked for far too long.
For the first time in a long time, Chris Ballard is not calling the shots, ownership is seemingly focused on winning, and there appears to be light at the end of the tunnel.
The Indianapolis Colts' aforementioned core group of young, talented players is certainly worth being thankful for .
No, they don't have a franchise quarterback to build around, but at least Chris Ballard won't be around to add to his double-digit list of failed projects.
Instead, the Colts will provide a solid plate of sides to their next general manager, with his or her first order of business being to find the perfect entree.
Of course, this very method is what failed Ballard and Co. year after year, but this is the hand the next regime is being dealt.
After all, each NFL season often features at least one team that proves it's far ahead of schedule. You never know; this Colts core could right the ship much quicker than we could ever anticipate.
The Colts recently extended one of their most promising young players, defensive lineman Adetomiwa Adebawore. The fourth-year defender has blossomed into a legitimate star across the defensive front, logging a team-high five sacks on just 53.0% of snaps played.
DeForest Buckner's absence across the Colts' defensive line has allowed Adebawore to prove himself as the team's next star up front, and now Indianapolis appears to have netted a bargain to kick off their rebuild.
You would have liked to have seen edge defender Laiatu Latu emerge into a legitimate superstar at this point, after he was the first defender selected in the 2024 NFL Draft, but at least the next regime will have one more season of Latu to determine whether his development has earned him the opportunity to stick around for the long haul. Perhaps that sense of urgency will give him the motivation needed to unlock the next part of his game.
Furthermore, the Colts may be losing the trade, but Sauce Gardner's presence in Indianapolis' backfield will be a huge building block moving forward. Rookie linebacker C.J. Allen has also come into his own as of late and is proving to be the leader this revamped Colts defense needs.
And finally, not only do the Colts have a strong group of offensive linemen to walk away from their trade of Quenton Nelson, but they will also be ushering in a new era with proven stars at both running back and wide receiver.
Jonathan Taylor and Alec Pierce, who is currently rehabbing a calf injury, should remain strong building blocks for the new-look offense. Add in tight end Tyler Warren, who is notably having a down year after a promising rookie campaign, and the Colts' outlook on offense isn't nearly as bleak.
Not to mention, their failed coaching staff does possess some gems throughout, such as OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr., WR Coach Reggie Wayne, and STC Brian Mason. Therefore, the Colts have some proven in-house options to consider for their rebuild.
That is, of course, if they ultimately elect to part ways with head coach Shane Steichen following the season.
It's understandably doom and gloom as far as Indianapolis Colts football goes, but there's plenty to still be thankful for, and that begins and ends with what feels like hope for the first time in a long time.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Week 12 Injury Report: Alec Pierce Provides Encouraging Update, Caden Curry Out for Season
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts received mixed injury news Wednesday as they prepare for their Week 12 matchup against the New York Giants. While rookie defensive end Caden Curry will miss the remainder of the season with a wrist injury, wide receiver Alec Pierce provided an encouraging update on his recovery from a heel injury that has sidelined him for most of the year.
Pierce revealed Wednesday that he actually suffered a partially torn Achilles tendon during the Colts' Week 2 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs, clarifying that the injury was separate from the one he had offseason surgery for in March, offering some additional context about his extended absence.
The fifth-year receiver said he has made significant progress over the past several weeks and has returned to jogging on a treadmill while incorporating plyometric exercises into his rehabilitation. Pierce remains hopeful that he can return before the end of the season, although the Colts have emphasized that they will not rush him back before he is completely healthy.
Meanwhile, Curry's promising rookie campaign has officially come to an end. The Colts placed the sixth-round pick on injured reserve Tuesday after he suffered a ligament tear in his wrist during last Thursday's loss to the Houston Texans.
Curry required surgery to address the injury and will miss the remainder of the 2026 season. He finishes his rookie campaign with 26 tackles, one sack, one tackle for loss, two quarterback hits and two fumble recoveries across 11 appearances. He also established himself as a valuable contributor on special teams.
Indianapolis also received some encouraging developments on the practice field Wednesday, particularly in the secondary and along the offensive line.
Gardner and Raimann both returned to full participation after missing last week's game against Houston. Taylor-Britt also practiced fully as Indianapolis opened his 21-day window to return from injured reserve. If the Colts can get him back in time for Sunday, it'll be a much-needed boost to a secondary that's lacking any firepower outside of Justin Walley now that Gardner and Charvarius Ward are both dealing with their own injuries.
Jalen Travis, Seth McGowan, Ward, Drew Ogletree, Will Mallory and Jerry Tillery all remained sidelined, while Deion Burks was absent for personal reasons. In wake of both offensive tackles being unavailable last week, the Colts signed former Chiefs tackle Wanya Morris to their active roster, adding some insurance in the instance that both Travis and Raimann don't dress against the Giants, though Morris hasn't appeared in a game this season.

title: 3 Narratives To Follow With Anthony Richardson's Return as Starting Quarterback
full_text:
No doubt by now the quip has lost its luster, although maybe it's been a while since you last heard it.
It's traditionally followed by a list of highly drafted quarterbacks just getting their feet wet in the league, all older than the embattled Colts' signal caller who's already reached the final year of his rookie deal.
For a while the remark was flippantly used as a source of copium, eventually giving way to excuses often made on behalf of the youth.
Just not on behalf of franchise quarterbacks.
The Indianapolis chapter of Anthony Richardson's professional football career had a tidy ending. There was of course, the promising start, many injuries, a benching followed by a brief resurgence, a lost camp battle; even a midseason injury plot twist for good measure. 2026 was to be a footnote in the opening chapter, barely noticeable.
A footnote no longer, Richardson has a chance to rewrite the final pages of his eventful exposition.
Finally, the pen is back in his hands.
It wasn't just that Daniel Jones was the worst of 37 qualified quarterbacks in the NFL with at least 100 dropbacks this season ( -0.20 EPA on 392 dropbacks ); it was the manner in which he was doing it.
There was no confidence when his back foot landed at the top of his drop. He didn't trust himself to test tight windows, and the athleticism that once bailed him out of sticky situations hadn't returned to pre-injury levels.
Indubitably, thousands of Americans will witness their father-in-laws attempting scrambles reminiscent of Daniel Jones' current form in Turkey Bowls across the country this weekend.
Anthony Richardson's playstyle if anything, is the antithesis of that.
The ball may end up going to the same place Jones' did (the ground or other team), but it has an inordinate amount of smoke coming off of it when doing so.
No throw is off limits, and no window too tight. Even if the results are the same, the path getting their is akin to taking the scenic route.
The Colts have been on I-465 for eleven weeks.
I recently listed three free agent quarterbacks the Colts could look to sign in free agency, and many were frustrated with the exclusion of Anthony Richardson from that list.
In an ideal world, Richardson finishes the final six games strong and re-signs with Indianapolis on a cheap, one year deal. All hard feelings, or lack thereof, are swept under the rug, while Richardson stares in the face of the "bust" label with justified indignation.
Nobody needs the Colts analyst to tell them this isn't an ideal world.
Nevertheless, Richardson has been gifted a unique opportunity. A six game audition for thirty-two teams. An opportunity to shed the labels tossed his way as a twenty-two year old, fair or otherwise.
Time and time again those that practice in the art of revisionist history opine that the NFL has a quarterback development problem. You'll hear that young quarterbacks aren't allowed to fail anymore due to impatient franchises salivating to replace them.
Well Anthony Richardson has certainly failed before, and the Colts don't have anyone, or any draft pick to turn to.
The subsequent results have a chance to become the next case study in quarterback development.
Don't feel bad if you've been keeping one eye on the Colts and another on your weekend to-dos the last few weeks.
The Colts played themselves out of appointment television status. Not only were they playing poorly, but they were boring. Naturally, fandom apathy can occur in these situations.
It's time to bid lethargic Sundays ado in the Circle City.
The offense is going to change materially because it has to. Shane Steichen can reach back into his deep bag of QB counter runs out of funky formations and deep shot plays that now have more than a snowball's chance.
As I touched on earlier, Anthony Richardson's style of play is such that you're much more likely to sit up in your chair when he does anything on the field, for better or for worse.
It's possible Richardson's big arm unlocks something in Deion Burks or Anthony Gould, or more importantly, Tyler Warren. Maybe the threat of the quarterback run once again unlocks Jonathan Taylor, whose recent stagnation has led to further speculation about his future with the Colts.
But above it all, maybe it provides a flicker of inspiration to a team who desperately needs anything to grasp onto. A season with so much expectation immediately extinguished by an untenable roster crafted by a star-crossed general manager that'd been piloting the franchise to mediocrity for a decade.
The Indianapolis Colts are once again looking to Anthony Richardson as a reason for belief. In 2023, it was in anticipation of his ascension to franchise quarterback.
Three and a half years later, it's in hopes he leads them to competency, a level they've been a far cry from all season.

title: 3 Ways Anthony Richardson Will Unlock Colts Offense
full_text:
Now that Daniel Jones is no longer a member of the Indianapolis Colts , all eyes turn to Anthony Richardson Sr. to take over for the final six games of a lost 2026 season.
Colts fans begged, dare I say, pleaded, for the organization to bench Jones and see what Richardson could do for the rest of the year.
Now they'll get their wish.
It's impossible to predict how this six-game experiment will go, given Richardson's shaky past and arguably the worst offensive supporting cast in the league.
Regardless, Richardson will get a huge opportunity to somehow, some way, elevate this offense in a way Jones couldn't come close to.
Given his ridiculous traits, Richardson already gives Shane Steichen more to work with and make defenses think on a broader scale.
With this in mind, let's dive into three ways Richardson can finally get this offense to hit a stride.
Yes, Jones is mobile, but after the fractured fibula and Achilles tear last year, he was wildly underwhelming this year as a running threat.
Enter Richardson, who is one of the NFL's deadliest quarterbacks when he decides to take off with the football.
Obviously Richardson is incredibly fast, but one of the overlooked pieces of his game as a scrambler is how unbelievably physical he can be.
A play I'll never forget was in 2024 when Indianapolis faced the 3-7 New York Jets. Richardson was in the red zone and Steichen called a quarterback-designed run.
What ensued was one of the most brutal hits I've ever seen or heard, from a quarterback. Richardson destroyed Jets safety Jalen Mills to expand the lead in the second quarter.
WOW. Anthony Richardson with the truck-stick TD 💪 📺: #INDvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ 📱: https://t.co/waVpO909ge pic.twitter.com/ckY85OazuX
There are few quarterbacks in the NFL with the physical gifts Richardson possesses, and his X-Factor is his running ability.
That alone will force linebackers and coverage to be on high alert for when he tucks the pigskin and takes off, opening up other opportunities for the rest of the offense.
This must be stated immediately: Richardson doesn't have Alec Pierce like he did when he put up one of the most beautiful deep balls the NFL has ever witnessed in 2024's opener against the Houston Texans.
ANTHONY RICHARDSON 60-YARD DIME TO ALEC PIERCE. 📺: #HOUvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ 📱: https://t.co/waVpO909ge pic.twitter.com/p0xddm5Kl1
Now, Richardson will be working with a barren wide receiver corps with no true vertical weapon. While that is the case, Richardson's deep ball is still so potent that it can actually help with that problem.
Indy's wide receiver room consists of Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, Anthony Gould, Quez Watkins, and Deion Burks.
Out of that collection of pass-catchers, Dulin and Burks are the burners, while Treadwell can have his moments down the field.
Jones was never known for his ability to chuck the pill downfield, but Richardson has a Howitzer for a right arm.
Just his sheer power in his deep throws will give any receiver extra time to outrun the coverage. If any of these pass-catchers are going to win down the field, Richardson gives them the best chance to do so.
Jones was more docile as a running threat this year than at any point in his career. This allowed defenses to tee off on Jonathan Taylor since he was the only true threat in the backfield.
Now, that will no longer be the case with Richardson commanding things under center.
Richardson as the field general immediately makes this QB-RB combination one of the most electrifying.
Taylor's 2026 hasn't been awful, but certainly hasn't been up to his standards. Through 11 games, Taylor has amassed 760 rushing yards on 188 attempts for 4.0 yards per carry, the lowest of his career.
Yes, the eight rushing scores are nice, but in the grand scheme of things masks the overall struggles Taylor has had this year with little to no other threats to open up things for him.
The ground game is a must for this offense, and it's been suffocated for most of the season. That has the best chance to change in a big way now that Richardson is the starter.
Drake Wally is a Senior Writer for the Indianapolis Colts On SI. His works have also appeared on Bleacher Report, MSN, Yahoo, and SBNation. He also co-hosts the Horseshoe Huddle Podcast.

title: 4 Burning Questions the Colts Must Answer Down the Stretch
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have reached a point in their season where the focus is beginning to shift toward the future. While focusing on a push for a playoff spot isn't on the cards, there's still plenty that the Colts need to find out about their current squad before their rebuild officially gets rolling in the offseason.
Here are four burning questions for Indianapolis down the stretch.
The Colts are turning back to Anthony Richardson after finally ending the failed Daniel Jones experiment. Following Jones' struggles throughout the second half of the season, Indianapolis released its starting quarterback and handed the keys to Richardson, who will get another opportunity to establish himself as the franchise's long-term answer.
It is a significant opportunity for Richardson, who has not started a game since 2024. The former fourth-overall pick has experienced plenty of adversity throughout his NFL career, including bizarre injuries, inconsistent performances and losing his starting job multiple times. Now, he has an opportunity to change the narrative surrounding his future.
There are legitimate reasons to be skeptical. Richardson has completed just 50.6% of his career passes and has struggled to consistently demonstrate the accuracy and decision-making required to succeed as an NFL quarterback. However, his physical tools and rushing ability are undeniable, and give the Colts a dimension that has been largely missing from their offense.
The remaining schedule provides Richardson with an opportunity to show what he can do with an extended run as the starter. Can he improve his accuracy, protect the football and give the offense some much-needed life?
More importantly, can Richardson convince the Colts---or maybe another franchise---that he deserves another opportunity in 2027?
For much of the first half of the season, Jonathan Taylor was arguably the most important player on the Colts' roster. His production helped carry Indianapolis through its early-season success, establishing the running game as the foundation of an offense that was among the league's most productive.
That has changed considerably over the past several weeks.
Taylor has struggled to find consistent running room, failing to record 50 yards or more in three of his last four outings.
The recent struggles have been especially noticeable given how productive Taylor has been throughout his career. That said, trades, injuries and offensive line reshuffling has made it tougher on Taylor to be the bell-cow back he's been since joining the Colts in 2020.
With Indianapolis now turning to Richardson at quarterback, there is an opportunity for the running game to benefit from the additional threat of a mobile quarterback. Plus, rookie Seth McGowan's hamstring injury likely means in increase in snaps for Taylor.
He remains one of the best running backs in football, and the Colts need Taylor to look like it again. A strong finish would provide some encouragement heading into the offseason and give Indianapolis a much-needed offensive foundation.
Can Taylor rediscover the explosiveness that made him so dangerous earlier this year?
The Colts have invested significant resources into improving their defense, but the results have been inconsistent throughout the 2026 campaign. One player who needs to become a more consistent difference-maker down the stretch is defensive end Laiatu Latu.
After recording 8.5 sacks during his second NFL season, expectations were understandably high for Latu entering his third year. He appeared to be developing into the type of disruptive pass rusher Indianapolis envisioned when it selected him in the first round of the 2024 NFL Draft.
But that production has not carried over into this season.
Latu has recorded just three sacks through 10 appearances, a noticeable drop from his 2025 production. While sack totals do not tell the entire story, Indianapolis needs more consistent disruption from one of its most important defensive building blocks, especially a player they invested a top-15 draft pick in.
The Colts have struggled to generate pressure consistently, and Latu is one of the players who needs to take on more responsibility in that department. His ability to win one-on-one matchups, collapse the pocket and create opportunities for the rest of the defensive front will be particularly important as Indianapolis evaluates its personnel heading into next season.
There is still plenty of time for Latu to finish the year on a positive note. He has already demonstrated that he can be a disruptive pass rusher at this level, but the Colts need to see that disruption translate to production.
Perhaps no individual has more riding on the remainder of the season than Shane Steichen.
Indianapolis already made a significant organizational change when it fired general manager Chris Ballard in October. Steichen survived that decision, but his own job security remains a major question as the Colts continue to spiral toward another disappointing finish.
The head coach entered the 2026 campaign with considerable expectations after Indianapolis started last season 7-1 before completely collapsing down the stretch. Instead of building on that promising start, the Colts have experienced another season of inconsistency, and their recent performances have raised serious questions around his future with the team.
The offensive struggles have been particularly concerning. Indianapolis has scored just 10 points in its last two games combined. Steichen is the team's offensive play caller, and he has acknowledged his responsibility for the unit's shortcomings.
Of course, there are legitimate circumstances working against him. The Colts have dealt with significant injuries, traded away their best offensive assets and recently made a quarterback change. Evaluating Steichen's performance requires acknowledging the personnel challenges he has faced.
Still, the results have not been close to good enough. Indianapolis is 3-8, has lost seven of its last eight games and, trade deadline fire sale aside, has not delivered on the promise of being a playoff contender again.
The remaining games could provide Steichen with an opportunity to prove that he can still lead this organization in the right direction. If he can scrape together a couple wins despite an underwhelming and inexperienced roster, he could prove to be worthy of at least one more year. However, with a new general manager expected to eventually take over the roster-building process, there is no guarantee that Steichen will be part of the next chapter.

title: Breaking Down the Colts Final Six Games of 2026
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have six games left, and let's be real: there isn't much to look forward to.
At 3-8, the season is over. After firing Chris Ballard and trading away players like Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, Indianapolis is already looking toward another rebuild.
Now, it's about developing the young guys, figuring out who belongs in 2027 and seeing what Anthony Richardson Sr. has left to offer.
Richardson might make this offense fun again. He might also remind us why he lost the job, and with his injury history, I'm worried about him staying healthy.
Here's how I see the final six games playing out.
New York just beat the same Jaguars team that embarrassed Indianapolis 42-7, and with the way the Giants are playing, it's tough to envision a Colts victory.
New York's defense has to be licking its chops at the thought of facing Richardson, but with AR making his first start since 2024, maybe he gives this lifeless offense a spark.
A much-needed break for everyone involved with this franchise. Fans included.
Philadelphia is freefalling, too, although maybe not quite as badly as Indianapolis. Coming off a bye, perhaps Shane Steichen can finally have this team prepared.
And if Joe Milton III is still starting, I like the Colts' defense to make him uncomfortable.
Indianapolis should be foaming at the mouth to avenge its embarrassing loss to Tennessee earlier this season.
The Colts' defense has shown improvement, and I still believe they're better than this Titans team.
Good luck stopping Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
This could get downright ugly, especially if Indianapolis can't generate pressure against one of the league's most dangerous passing attacks.
Cleveland has already beaten Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Houston this season, and all three have given Indianapolis serious problems.
This feels like an ugly, low-scoring game, but I trust Deshaun Watson and the Browns more than this Colts offense.
Even if Jacksonville has its playoff positioning secured and rests starters, I'm not convinced Indianapolis can compete.
And if the Jaguars play their starters? We already saw what happened last time, and Jacksonville has had Indianapolis' number recently.
Divisional games can get weird, but don't bet on it.
At this point, wins aren't bringing a division title or playoff berth. What matters is seeing growth from guys like Justin Walley, CJ Allen, Seth McGowan and Adetomiwa Adebawore while figuring out whether Richardson belongs in anyone's plans beyond 2026.
Oh, and remember: the Jets own our 2027 first-rounder. The last thing we need is gifting them a top-five pick.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Rookie Report: CJ Allen, Seth McGowan Lead Indianapolis' 2026 Draft Class Through 12 Weeks
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts 2026 draft class has made their mark on the season, with a handful of rookies becoming more impactful as the year goes on. While some have exceeded expectations, others are still working to establish themselves as dependable contributors.
With 12 games in the books, let's take a look at Indianapolis' eight draft picks and evaluate their output as we head into the final stretch of games.
CJ Allen has been the best of the bunch, without a doubt.
The second-round choice had to navigate injuries at first, but once he got his chance, Allen has taken full advantage. The 21-year-old has taken over playcalling duties on defense and has been a production machine, achieving a level of play the Colts haven't seen in a rookie linebacker since Shaq Leonard.
Allen has recorded 50 tackles, five tackles for loss and two sacks this season. He has demonstrated an ability to make plays behind the line of scrimmage, adding a disruptive element to Indianapolis' linebacker room, and has contributed in pass defense as well.
Allen's development is one of the biggest positives from this draft class, and the Colts appear to have found a potential franchise cornerstone.
A.J. Haulcy has been one of the more heavily utilized members of Indianapolis' rookie class, starting at safety and receiving a substantial share of the defensive snaps. His role has given him plenty of opportunities to make an impact, and he has shown some encouraging flashes throughout his first professional season. However, his overall performance has been inconsistent.
Haulcy has accumulated 53 tackles, one interception and three passes defended. The tackle production demonstrates his involvement in the defense, while his interception provided a glimpse at what more he can offer.
However, there have been occasions when Haulcy's coverage and tackling have left something to be desired. For a rookie who has been trusted with a starting role for much of the season, consistency needs to become the next step.
Haulcy has the opportunity to develop into an important piece of the secondary, but Indianapolis needs more dependable play from him down the stretch.
Jalen Farmer's rookie season has been defined by an opportunity that arrived earlier than expected.
The fourth-round selection out of Kentucky began the year as a developmental offensive lineman, but the Quenton Nelson trade eventually pushed him into a starting role. His transition into the lineup hasn't been entirely smooth, although there have been encouraging signs as he adjusts to the speed and physicality of the NFL.
Farmer has accumulated approximately 237 offensive snaps this season, gaining valuable experience in the process. Pass protection has been a particular challenge, and he still has work to do before he can be considered a reliable long-term starter. However, his performance against Miami offered a glimpse of his potential, earning an 83.8 overall PFF grade for the game.
That was a significant improvement and demonstrated that he can hold his own against NFL competition. The Colts may not have a solidified starting left guard for the foreseeable future in Farmer, but if they continue to develop him, he has impact player upside.
Bryce Boettcher has quietly become a useful contributor for Indianapolis, taking advantage of opportunities created by injuries and changes within the linebacker room. The fourth-rounder hasn't received the same attention as Allen, but he has established a role for himself and demonstrated an ability to contribute when called upon. His involvement has increased throughout the season, particularly as the Colts have needed additional depth at linebacker.
Boettcher has recorded 50 tackles and one tackle for loss. His strongest contributions have come against the run, where he has shown an ability to diagnose plays and get involved near the line of scrimmage. He recorded 12 tackles against the Cowboys and followed that performance with seven against the Dolphins.
While he still has room to improve in coverage, Boettcher has given Indianapolis another capable option at linebacker. His development makes for an interesting offseason discussion when it comes to upgrading the position, but regardless, the Colts have a player they should be able to continue to count on.
George Gumbs Jr. has had a difficult time finding his footing in Indianapolis, spending much of his rookie season on the fringes of the defensive line rotation.
Gumbs entered the NFL as a developmental pass rusher, and his limited playing time has made it difficult for him to establish any meaningful momentum.
Gumbs has recorded just five tackles this season and has yet to register a sack. His lack of production must come with the context that he simply hasn't featured in the defensive line rotation much at all. The Colts have had several established veterans ahead of him, making it difficult for a rookie to break into the rotation.
Gumbs still has time to develop. Now may not be the time to jump to conclusions on his potential as a pass rusher.
Caden Curry has been one of the more pleasant surprises in Indianapolis' rookie class. The sixth-round selection out of Ohio State entered the season with relatively modest expectations, but he has gradually worked his way into the defensive line rotation.
Curry's playing time has fluctuated depending on the availability of other defensive ends, but he has demonstrated an ability to make plays when given opportunities.
Curry has recorded 26 tackles and one sack this season. His production isn't necessarily eye-popping, but it's encouraging for a sixth-round pick who wasn't expected to make an instant impact. Curry still has time to become a more consistent presence as a pass rusher, but his high effort and ability to take advantage of opportunities have made him a player worth betting on down the line.
Like Allen for the defense, Seth McGowan has been Indianapolis' biggest offensive rookie success story.
The seventh-round selection out of Kentucky has carved out a meaningful role behind Jonathan Taylor as the season has progressed. McGowan has provided the Colts with a dependable alternative in the backfield, allowing them to give Taylor occasional breaks without completely changing the identity of their rushing attack.
McGowan has rushed for 292 yards and two touchdowns on 58 carries, averaging an impressive 5.0 yards per attempt. He has also caught six passes for 10 yards. Unfortunately, head coach Shane Steichen shared Monday that McGowan will miss time with a hamstring injury suffered against Houston, so his impressive rookie campaign will be cut short prematurely.
Still, for a seventh-round pick, McGowan's impact illustrates the value the Colts found late in the draft.
Deion Burks has had a quiet rookie season, although his circumstances have created an opportunity for a larger role in the closing weeks.
Burks spent much of the first half of the season buried on the wide receiver depth chart, making it difficult for him to make his way into the offensive game plan. Much of his early involvement came on special teams, but changes to Indianapolis' receiving corps have created more opportunities for the rookie.
Burks has recorded six receptions for 60 yards and has added 21 rushing yards on three attempts. His production hasn't yet demonstrated that he can be a consistent contributor in the passing game, but there's time for him to change that this season.
The wide receiver position is one the Colts need to evaluate heavily in the remaining weeks, and Burks has an opportunity to show he should be a part of future plans. Even then, Indianapolis will need to see more out of their final draft choice if he's going to stick around in 2027.

title: Jaguars' Brian Thomas Jr. Trade Decision Is Already Paying Off After Parker Washington's Injury
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are facing a test of wide receiver depth, which perhaps is something they have already been preparing for.
The Jaguars are set to be without Parker Washington this week against the Tennessee Titans, and they might be without him for quite a bit depending on what "week-to-week" means for the franchise. As a result, the decision the Jaguars made a few weeks ago with Brian Thomas Jr. at the trade deadline has already paid off.
The Jaguars opted not to trade Thomas at the deadline for quite a few reasons. Jacksonville clearly did not feel like the offers they were getting for Thomas were close to how much the Jaguars valued fhe former first-round pick, but there was also very clearly the idea that the Jaguars believed Thomas would help them eventually.
Whether that help would come in his limited role, such as his two receiving touchdowns over the last four games, or as a key piece of offensive depth always remained to be seen. The hope was never that Thomas would only be needed when the Jaguars sustained an injury, of course, but that is where the Jaguars now find themselves after Washington's shoulder injury.
Scenarios like this are exactly why keeping Thomas could pay off for Jacksonville. That is not to say Thomas should be expected to see his role change all that much; he should still be expected to be primarily an outside receiver who plays in 11 personnel. But Washington has seen such a high volume of targets this season, that is only natural to assume Thomas could see more passes thrown his way than he has over the last few months.
Had the Jaguars traded Thomas, they would be in quite a bad spot at receiver. Jacksonville will already need Josh Cameron to step up with Washington out, but this need would have been amplified even more. If the Jaguars dealt Thomas before the injury, the Jaguars would’ve been forced to turn to the practice squad or 6th-round rookie receiver CJ Williams, who has only been active for one game. Williams will likely be active this week, but as the No. 4 receiver. That is a far, far cry from being the No. 3 receiver, though, especially as the Jaguars prepare for a playoff run.
Keeping Thomas on the roster has given the Jaguars the flexibility on offense and at wide receiver that they wouldn’t have had otherwise. That flexibility is clearly what the Jaguars are going to have to lean on while Washington is out considering the impact he has had on the offense.
"We got smart players, which has been a testament to the group, to their coaches, guys knowing different spots, guys understanding the big picture, the concepts and understanding. Obviously, there's a lot of detail that goes into each play, in which you can't expect them to know every little possible detail, but that's where coaching comes in," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Friday.
"This is where coaching is obviously really important to help the guys out. Put them in positions to be successful, give those guys the most opportunities that things that they know that they can go and operate at a high level. Simplicity is what we're going into this game anyways trying to do in a lot of ways. It's in alignment, unfortunately.”
The trade-off is what, not having a third- or fourth-round pick? It made sense at the time for the Jaguars to keep Thomas, and it makes even more sense now.

title: 3 Instant Observations on Parker Washington's Injury and What It Means for Jaguars
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will be without Parker Washington for a bit.
Washington popped up on the Jaguars' injury report Thursday with a shoulder injury, and Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Friday that Washington would miss Sunday's game against the Tennessee Titans and be considered week-to-week moving forward.
So, what does Washington's injury mean as the Jaguars gear up for a critical AFC South game against the Titans in Week 12? We break it down below.
#Jaguars star WR Parker Washington is week-to-week after aggravating an AC joint injury in practice. He’s out this week, coach Liam Coen confirmed. pic.twitter.com/j9phmchMNE
All things considered ... this could have been worse? It is hard to say there is any upside to the Jaguars being without Washington for likely at least a few weeks, including next week's big game against the Chicago Bears. But considering how dire such an injury could have been, it certainly feels like the Jaguars got out of this thing relatively okay? And there are a few reasons why I feel that way, going back to last year when Travis Hunter got injured in practice on Oct. 30.
When Hunter was injured, Coen never said the injury was week-to-week, and he also said Hunter would be placed on injured reserve, which he was that day. Coen never indicated Washington would even go on injured reserve, which suggests there are some differences here.
The Jaguars should be able to beat the Titans without Washington, too. If they can't, then the Jaguars have some bigger problems. Losing Washington will certainly impact the offense, but all early signs indicate that we should see Washington at some point again in 2026. The Jaguars have some precedent for dealing with serious injuries, and the entire way the Washington injury has been handled and discussed suggests the Jaguars did not exactly see a doomsday scenario with this particular injury. Only time will tell, of course, but those should be the early indications at least.
One of the few positives to the situation for the Jaguars is that they have an offense that can be built to sustain such an injury. The Jaguars have other talented pass catchers that they trust on their roster, whether at receiver with Jakobi Meyers, Brian Thomas Jr, and Josh Cameron, as well as tight ends like Brenton Strange, Nate Boerkircher, and Tanner Koziol. With that said, the Jaguars will likely need to change what the offense looks like to some extent with Washington out.
Washington’s ability to beat Man coverage from the slot is a big reason the Jaguars have thrived and 11 personnel in the passing game over 12 months. While Josh Cameron has logged some snaps at the slot this year, the most beneficial solution might be for the Jaguars to really lean into the 12/13 personnel formations. They could still use their receiver room at trust them to execute at a high clip, but injuries like this seem like the reason the Jaguars add to tight end and give themselves the option to do more than just line up in 11 personnel every play like they had to last season.
One natural question that people might have after Washington’s injury is rather that means we will start to see Travis Hunter more at the wide receiver position. Hunter was the Jaguars full-time slot receiver last season before his injury, which is the same spot that Washington has occupied since the Jaguars by week a year ago Hunter has had limited snaps at receiver this season, spending far more time at the cornerback position, but he would be a reasonable option to put back in the slot to help offset the loss of Washington. With that said, this doesn’t appear to be something that Jaguars will look at heavily in Week 12.
Washington’s injury happened so late in the week, with so much of the hay already in the barn in terms of preparation for the Titans. That means it would be tough to ask Hunter to go from starting cornerback to starting wide receiver with just a days worth of practice notice ahead of time. Hunter might still see more snaps on offense this week than he has in past weeks, especially considering his past role in the slot and his ball skills that rival Washington’s, but this does not seem like an overly likely solution for Week 12.

title: 5 Bold Predictions for Jaguars-Titans Rematch: Trevor Lawrence's Rushing Solution
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a big AFC South rematch in Week 12, hosting the Tennessee Titans in another key divisional game.
Jacksonville is looking to bounce back from last week's loss to the New York Giants, and the perfect way to do that is by defeating the Titans and avoiding their first losing streak of the season and just the second losing streak of the Liam Coen era.
So, how do we see this week's battle with the Titans playing out after Jacksonville's Week 10 win over them two weeks ago? We break it down below.
Trevor Lawrence needs a bounce back week perhaps more than any other individual player on the offense, but this is certainly a week that should give him the chance to do so. The Titans' defense has been lit up for weeks, with Lawrence himself having a huge game against a bad Robert Saleh defense two weeks ago. There is plenty of reason to think Lawrence can have success through the air this week, but I also think this is the week we see Lawrence finally use his legs.
Lawrence had a career-high nine rushing touchdowns a season ago, including five such touchdowns during the Jaguars' 9-1 second-half stretch. It was always unlikely Lawrence would produce on the ground in such the same way in back-to-back years, but he has zero rushing touchdowns through 10 games this season. I think we see Lawrence score on a designed run after the Jaguars have kept it out of the playbook for much of the season.
If there was a game in the post-Davon Hamilton stretch that reflected the impact of losing the star nose tackle, it was the Jaguars' Week 10 win over the Tennessee Titans. But the run defense looked much-improved last week with Jordan Davis in the lineup , and this is a game that could set up for the Jaguars to have a strong game in the trenches after Tony Pollard and the Titans' offense rushed for far too many yards two weeks ago.
The Jaguars lacked the space-eaters in Week 10 to really combat the Titans' rushing attack. Jacksonville wants to play with light boxes, and this came back to bite them in Week 10 as Pollard was able to pick up several chunk gains against such defensive fronts. Jordan Davis changes that math, though, and I think he sets the Jaguars up to have more success this time around.
The Bhayshul Tuten injuries over the last several weeks has certainly slowed down the Jaguars' rushing attack, and I feel like the Jaguars' response this week will be to lean on their power running game with Chris Rodriguez Jr. I am not so sure if I would go to say that the Jaguars would sit out Tuten this week against the Titans, but I do think it makes sense for the Jaguars to limit his workload this time.
To do so, the Jaguars would have to trust Rodriguez with carrying the load in the ground game. There has only been one game this year in which he has had more carries than Tuten, but it makes a ton of sense for that pattern to change this week against the Titans. The Jaguars don't need to run Tuten into the ground this week, and that should lead to Rodriguez getting more touches.
Travis Hunter is a special, special cornerback. So special that he has been able to generate a game-changing turnover every three games in his first real season as a full-time cornerback. The last one he had was two weeks ago against the Titans and Cam Ward, with Hunter picking Ward off with an electric play over the middle of the field. Hunter was not targeted all that much downfield last week, but Ward is the type of quarterback who would be willing to test him.
With Carnell Tate healthy this time, I think we see Ward throw at Hunter quite a bit Sunday. I believe Hunter will be able to turn at least one of those plays into another big turnover, further making his case to be an All-Pro option for the AFC at cornerback this season. Hunter has been one of the best cornerbacks in football this year, and that continues Sunday.
The Jaguars have had some so-so days in the red-zone in recent weeks. They had to settle for a few too many field goals against the Tennessee Titans the last time they played, failing to score touchdowns after getting to the Titans' 27, 30, 21, and 18-yard lines. The Jaguars' up-and-down nature in the red-zone cost them dearly against the New York Giants a week ago, and they need to start finding the answers down there as they get into their critical stretch.
I think the Jaguars will find more success this week against the Titans, scoring touchdowns on at least 75% of their red-zone trips. Jacksonville, I think, will lean more on the tight end room and running game to score in the red-zone this week than they were able to a week ago, leading to more scores in the confined space of the red-zone.

title: What Jaguars Can Expect from Nate Boerkircher, Other Rookies in the Impending Playoff Run
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are in the thick of a tight playoff race, and they are going to need all of the help they can get.
The Jaguars have seen their rookie draft class step into significant roles throughout the season, all the way through their Week 11 loss against the New York Giants. But with seven games left, it is time for the rookie class to make their greatest contributions yet.
So, how can the Jaguars start stepping up starting in Week 12 against the Titans and then all the way through the rest of the push for the playoffs? We break it down below.
The Jaguars have not made Nate Boerkircher much of a threat in the passing game in terms of volume, but he has been impacted when called upon with 10 catches for 156 yards and two touchdowns. He has been up-and-down in terms of his run blocking in recent weeks, which is where the Jaguars will have to see him make his biggest impact moving forward. The Jaguars' running game has tailed off over the last three weeks, largely due to Bhayshul Tuten's injuries, but they need role players like Boerkircher to improve, too.
There is likely not much Albert Regis can do for the Jaguars other than stay ready. He was a healthy scratch on Sunday as the Jaguars had both Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux in the lineup together, and that was even with Matt Dickerson being out with a neck injury. Regis will likely be a healthy inactive each game moving forward unless the Jaguars have to start dealing with injury issues up front.
Emmanuel Pregnon has been one of the iron men of the Jaguars' offensive line, starting every game and playing every snap -- something the Jaguars have not gotten at left tackle or center. Pregnon has had a few rookie errors pop up when it comes to penalties, and that is what the Jaguars will need him to focus on moving forward. The Jaguars' offense has been on fire when they have not gotten in their own way with self-inflicted mistakes, and it will take a group effort from players like Pregnon to ensure they curb that issue.
Jalen Huskey is likely in the same boat as Albert Regis. He got some playing time in Weeks 8 and 9 as the Jaguars dealt with safety injuries, but the addition of Jessie Bates III to the defense this past week made him a healthy scratch as the team's No. 5 safety. It seems unlikely Huskey will be active again any time soon, which means the most he can do to help the Jaguars right now is to be ready when his moment does come along.
Wesley Williams was a healthy scratch for the Jaguars during the first nine games of the season, but he was able to make his NFL debus against the New York Giants last week and record his first tackle for loss in the process. Williams' development has been a slow burn as a rookie, but the Jaguars are high on him and what he can provide from a depth perspective. The return of B.J. Green means he might have to bide is time, though.
Rookie tight end Tanner Koziol has seen his role increase since the bye week, other than in Week 11 against the Giants when the Jaguars seemed to play with more 11 personnel. Koziol is an important part of what the Jaguars do when they play with three tight ends due to his ability to split out and give the Jaguars a mismatch at the tight end position, which forces defenses to play the Jaguars a btit differently when he is on the field.
Josh Cameron can help the Jaguars in a lot of ways moving forward, whether as a pass-catcher, a downfield target, a run-blocker, and more. But the area I think the Jaguars may need him the most is on special teams. The return game has faded in recent weeks and the Jaguars have seemingly already pulled Parker Washington from punt return duty to save him from extra hits. The Jaguars need a returner to step up and provide a spark, and Cameron should be that returner.
Like Regis and Huskey, the best thing CJ Williams can do for the Jaguars right now is to simply keep preparing the same way he has been. The Jaguars love Williams in the building, but he has been inactive each week since Week 1 due to the Jaguars not facing any injury issues at wide receiver. If the Jaguars do face any injuries down the road, though, he will be the player who gets promoted.
Seventh-round defensive end Zach Durfee had an impressive training camp but also dealt with a few injuries during those weeks. As a result, he was placed on injured reserve with a designation to return at the end of camp, but he has not yet had his 21-day practice window opened like we have seen with others such as Patrick Mekar i and B.J. Green. This could be a redshirt season, similar to Jalen McLeod a year ago.
Seventh-round linebacker Parker Hughes was placed on injured reserve during training camp, which means he is not eligible to play this season. He will be back during the 2027 offseason program, so consider this a redshirt year for the athletic linebacker prospect.

title: 3 Things the Jaguars Must Do to Avoid Their First Losing Streak of 2026
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have only ever sustained one losing streak in the entire Liam Coen era, and they need to make sure a second does not begin this week.
The Jaguars are of course expected to be massive favorites over the Tennessee Titans this weekend, and for good reason. The Jaguars are 7-3 and just beat the Titans by 17 points in a 40-23 win in Nashville a few weeks ago.
But the Jaguars can not afford to overlook the Titans after last week's brutal road loss to the New York Giants. So, how can the Jaguars avoid their first losing streak of the 2026 season? We break it down below.
The biggest thing the Jaguars have to do to win this week is to protect Trevor Lawrence. Lawrence was beaten and battered against Abdul Carter and the New York Giants' defensive front last week, and the difference between Lawrence's level of play when he is protected compared to when he isn't shows that this could make all of the difference. If the Jaguars can give Lawrence clean pockets for four quarters, he should pick the Titans apart.
"Lawrence has averaged a career-high 8.5 yards per attempt from a clean pocket this season, the fifth-most among qualified quarterbacks. Lawrence has recorded an explosive play on 20.6% of clean-pocket dropbacks, a career-high and the third-highest rate in the NFL," NextGenStats said this week.
"The Titans have generated pressure on 22.2% of dropbacks since trading away Jeffery Simmons ahead of Week 8, the lowest rate in the NFL. Prior to Week 8, the Titans generated pressure on 35.0% of dropbacks, near the league average (35.9%). Since Week 8, when failing to generate pressure the Titans have allowed 10.4 yards per attempt (most) and an explosive play on 23.5% of dropbacks (3rd-highest)."
This one is obvious. The Jaguars are walking wounded right now, with injuries to the offensive line in particular becoming worrisome. The Jaguars were without starting center Robert Hainsey last week and saw left tackle Walker Little get injured last week against the New York Giants, and both were listed as limited in Wednesday's injury report to start the week off. The Jaguars could really use at least one of them getting healthy enough to play.
This does not even mention Bhayshul Tuten, who has been banged up for the last few weeks and has seen his special traits become a bit normal as a result. Tuten didn't practice on Wednesday, and the Jaguars really could take this week to rest him and get him ready for the home stretch, though that remains to be seen if it will be considered.
The Jaguars have seen Cam Little make four field goals in each of the last four games, which is an amazing feat for the young kicker. With that said, that streak does say quite a bit about the Jaguars' issues in the red-zone recently. The Jaguars have struggled to be efficient as they would like in the red-zone in recent weeks, including during their loss to the Giants when they went 1-for-6 at turning red-zone trips into touchdowns.
The defense did not fare that much better, allowing the Giants to go 2-of-3 despite not having a quarterback on their roster who doesn't throw a knuckleball. The Jaguars need to ramp up their urgency on both sides of the ball when it comes to the red-zone, and that starts this week against the Titans.

title: Parker Washington Lands on Jaguars Injury Report, Leaving Them Potentially Slim Options
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have been dealing with critical injuries for the last two months, and now another big name has been added to the injury report.
Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington was listed as a limited participant in Thursday's injury report as the Jaguars prepare for the Tennessee Titans in Week 12. Washington was not on the injury report previously, which suggests that his injury potentially occured during the team's Thanksgiving practice on Thursday.
It remains to be seen just how serious the injury is, and it will surely be discussed Friday by head coach Liam Coen as he gives his final press conference of the week. But it is no secret that an injury to Washington is the last thing the Jaguars could possibly afford ahead of their playoff push, especially considering running back Bhayshul Tuten is also dealing with his own injuries and missed his second practice in a row.
Tuten and Washington are the two best players on Jacksonville's offense not named Trevor Lawrence, and it is hard to see a scenario where the Jaguars could sustain success on offense without both of them healthy.
According to NextGenStats, Washington has totaled 23 receptions on 46 downfield targets (10+ air yards) for 483 yards and five touchdowns. Washington's 483 downfield receiving yards have nearly surpassed his entire total from last season (501) with seven regular-season games remaining. Washington has produced 17 receptions for 308 yards and three touchdowns in the intermediate area of the field (10-19 air yards), the ninth-most among wide receivers.
Washington has been absolutely critical to the Jaguars passing game this season, establishing himself as the offense's No. 1 receiver. He leads the team in every major receiving category, numbers that would look even better if he did not have multiple touchdowns negated this season.
If the Jaguars do not have Washington on Sunday, their options to replace him are slim. The Jaguars have other talented and productive pass-catchers in Jakobi Meyers and Brenton Strange, and Brian Thomas Jr. and rookie receiver Josh Cameron have each made some big plays at times this season. The Jaguars also have sixth-round rookie receiver CJ Williams on the active roster, though he has not appeared in a game since the Week 1 opener.
None of these players are true slot receivers like Washington, though. None of them have also built the connection with Lawrence that Washington has over the years. And the solution can not be simply let Travis Hunter play more on offense, either, because the Jaguars badly need him on defense every single week.
Time will tell if Washington's injury is one to be concnered about but, for now, the options to replace his role seem slim if it truly does come to that.

title: 3 Things the Jaguars Should Be Thankful For This Thanksgiving: AFC South Keeps Giving
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Happy Thanksgiving, everyone.
The Jacksonville Jaguars have plenty to be thankful this year, especially considering how many past Jaguars seasons were typically over and had the focus turned to the NFL Draft by the holidays. That is not the case with this Jaguars squad , though, as they sit at 7-3 and in a three-game lead in the AFC South entering Week 12.
So, what can the Jaguars be thankful for this go around? We break it down below, opting to not look at the immediate obious choices like Trevor Lawrence and Liam Coen.
For the Jaguars, the AFC South is the gift that keeps giving. The Jaguars still have the Houston Texans not all that far behind them in the race for the divisional title after Houston won in Week 11 and the Jaguars lost to the New York Giants. But the Texans are still sub-.500 and have plenty of issues in their own right, and the Jaguars have been the clearly better team over the last two seasons. They are not yet out of the Jaguars' hair, but the Jaguars have dealt with bigger problems before.
But then you get to the Indianapolis Colts and the Tennessee Titans and, well, things get a bit clearer. The Colts are so dysfunctional and nonsensical that they make the Urban Meyer year look almost tame. The Colts are in some kind of weird middle ground between tanking and trying to hold onto fleeting misconceptions that they still have the structure to be a winning team in a few years. Not trading any of Jonathan Taylor, Grover Stewart, and Daniel Jones makes them look like the most unserious team in the NFL, and their lack of a first round pick due to the Sauce Gardner trade only hammers this home more.
Sources: The #Colts opted not to trade QB Daniel Jones despite receiving interest, believing they had already paid too much in signing bonus money. But they continued stripping the rest of the roster. Now, shortly after, they release him and get nothing back. None of it made… https://t.co/Pwsih7pv41 pic.twitter.com/KBBtxWQRsC
Then there are the Titans, who very much look like a team that could have Robert Saleh be one-and-done. The Titans fought the Jaguars with some guts and effort a few weeks ago in Nashville, but moral victories in a 40-23 loss at home are still few and far between. The Saleh/Gus Bradley braintrust has predictably led to the Titans having one of the worst defenses in recent memory. If the Titans run it back with any of their main cast and crew of decision-makers, then there will be a team eliminated from the AFC South race before the season even begins. We will see how things play out between these two on Sunday.
The Jaguars have one of the NFL's best cornerbacks on their roster, and he has only played 17 games in the NFL. Travis Hunter has become everything the Jaguars needed him to become this year, with his development happening rapidly as the Jaguars switched him over to defense full-time and wide receiver part-time. It was clear this was always the best way to deploy Hunter, and he has shined in the role this season.
Travis Hunter is a burgeoning STAR pic.twitter.com/Tk5KfHpd6l
Few players are doing bigger things than Hunter on the defensive side of the ball. His three interceptions have all been huge plays for the Jaguars, but his down-to-down consistency in coverage and the run game has made him arguably the defense's best and most impactful player just 10 games into his full-time cornerback role. No other team in the NFL has a Travis Hunter, and that is worth celebrating.
The Jaguars have one of the best coordinator duos in the entire NFL in Anthony Campanile and Grant Udinski. Considering the Jaguars went over a decade without having a future head coach as a coordinator, it is a bit wild to know the Jaguars have two now. Campanile has turned the defense into a top-five unit over the last two seasons, while Udinski certainly looks like he is set to be one of the NFL's next top young offensive minds.

Udinski and Campanile are expected to be among the top HC candidates this offseason - and even hotter names than they were… pic.twitter.com/Lgu6TWwHdD
Enjoy Udinski and Campanile while they are in Jacksonville, folks. Chances are that they will not be in Duval that much longer.

title: Carnell Tate, Cam Ward and More: 3 Most Important Things Jaguars' Liam Coen Said About Titans Matchup
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are moving forward, which means turning their focus to the Tennessee Titans.
The Jaguars defeated the Titans 40-23 in Nashville just two weeks ago, and now the Jaguars will need to be at their best against their rivals once again to ensure they bounce back from last week's tough road loss.
So, what did Jaguars head coach Liam Coen say on Wednesday about the Titans matchup that stood out? We break it down below.
The Jaguars saw Cam Ward play a decent game the last time around; he threw one brutal interception to Travis Hunter but otherwise was able to make a few plays and here and stay on-track more often times than not, leading the Titans to several field goal drives as a result. Ward did not light up the Jaguars by any means, but he is probably playing his best stretch of football over the last month, and Coen has taken notice.
"Calm, cool, collective, composure part of the game. He's got a lot of confidence right now," Coen said.
The Jaguars are not a team that goes around underestimating their opponents, but Ward is a better quarterback than the one they just faced in Week 11 in New York. If the Jaguars do not take the Ward matchup with the same seriousness that they do every other week, he has the type of talent to make them and other defenses pay down the stretch.
"He's given the play makers opportunities on the perimeter, making plays with his legs, especially on some of the money downs, critical downs, fourth downs," Coen said. "He had a fourth-down scramble against us. He had another fourth-down scramble, fourth-and-eight the other day, where he creates and moves around and ends up finding a completion. I think you're seeing the guy just play better and better.”
The Jaguars did not see Carnell Tate the last time they played the Titans, and the top-5 pick out of Ohio State is set to face the Jaguars for the first time this Sunday. The Titans' passing game was clearly missing him in a big way the last time around considering some of the plays their wide receivers didn't make, which means his inclusion to Sunday's game will be a big storyline to watch when kickoff comes along.
“He just provides, I think, not just a possession receiver that's long and has a catch radius, but also a guy that can get down the field a little bit,.Had the slant obviously the other day that kind of a weird play where they go to touch him down, but he just so happened to just be getting up and then ends up taking the house. That's a smart play from a young player like that," Coen said.
"And before he had gotten hurt prior to our game, he was doing some really good things in the red zone and contested catches, slot fades, things like that. I had a lot of like for him coming out in the draft process. He's getting more and more confidence again as you can see it.”
Tate has caught 36 passes for 471 yards and two touchdowns in eight games as a rookie. Hardly numbers that would terrify a top-ranked defense like Jacksonville, but Tate is also set to likely see more and more volume with Wan'Dale Robinson out for the year. Travis Hunter's matchup with him will be one to watch.
A week after their toughest loss of the season , the Jaguars will have to pick themselves up and look past the wounds from Week 11. That process started earlier this week as the Jaguars began their preparation for the Titans, with Coen noting that the players' response on their off day on Tuesday said everything that was required.
“Yeah, again, we had 56 guys work out yesterday. It's pretty cool to see. You come off a tough loss, you don't play your best, and you get beat. I think it's a pretty easy message from the group and the whole message is, guys, so much football left," Coen said.
"We didn't get the result we wanted. We got to continue to stick to the process, but fine tune and detail the process in terms of the preparation, the way that we go attack the week. Obviously, we'll walk through today and get these guys' legs back a little bit, get them feeling better, go attack Thursday's practice the right way with pads on.”
The Jaguars are 5-1 under Coen after a loss since the start of 2025. They will have to prove they know how to bury a loss once again this week against the Titans, especially considered they are such big favorites entering the week. All indications are that the Jaguars got the wake up call they needed in New York, at least so far early in the week.

title: Jaguars-Titans Injury Report: Is a Rest Week Finally Coming for Bhayshul Tuten?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' injury reports are not getting any shorter as the year goes on, but this one could be an important one.
The Jaguars had nine different players listed as limited on Wednesday as they move past their Week 11 loss to the New York Giants and prepare for a home game against the Tennessee Titans. The Jaguars only had one player listed as a non-participant, and it is a big one: running back Bhayshul Tuten.
Tuten has been banged up for the last few weeks , and the Jaguars running game has taken a big hit in the process. He has still played in each of the last three games, rushing 48 times for 150 yards (3.12 yards per carry) and two touchdowns, which catching six passes for 45 yards. After the Jaguars rushing attack ranked No. 7 in rushing EPA/Play and No. 8 in success rate, but over they last three weeks they rank No. 20 and No. 24, respectively, during that span.
Could Tuten finally be getting the rest week he perhaps should have gotten in Weeks 9 and 10 against the Baltimore Ravens and Indianapolis Colts? That remains to be seen considering Tuten has played in each of the last three games despite missing several practices, but it would make sense for the Jaguars to put him on ice this week, with Jaguars head coach Liam Coen stating Wednesday that his recovery is a top priority.
"We got to get him healthy though. Like, we have to get him feeling better. That's priority number one right now," Coen said.
Tuten left Sunday's game against the Giants twice after being stepped on, and his foot/ankle injury has limited his explosiveness and ability to break tackles over the last few weeks. But the Jaguars have still leaned on Tuten in a big way, such as giving him 26 carries when they olayed the Titans two weeks ago.
“Obviously the speed, the ability to break tackles, the pass game part of it, I think. Just looking at the group and what he's able to provide," Coen said Wednesday when asked what Tuten has been able to provide while he has been banged-up. "The understanding of the scheme obviously is helpful, but it's really just you watch him in the development that he's had, the way that he's able to break tackles and still get, tough yards, the zero-yard runs that end up becoming a little bit more."
Tuten has not been himself since the last time the Jaguars were home at EverBank Stadium in Week 8. They need him badly to get back to 100%, and him missing practice Wednesday is the first potential sign that the Jaguars may give him the week off he might badly need. We will see what the rest of the week looks like, of course, but it is a start.
With that said, there was some good news for the Jaguars on the offensive line front. Left tackle Walker Little and center Robert Hainsey each were limited with knee injuries Wednesday, while veteran Patrick Mekari was limited in his first practice of the season.

title: Jaguars Open Patrick Mekari's Practice Window, and Here are 3 Ways He Can Help
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are set to get some important offensive line depth back on the field sooner rather than later.
The reinforcement is set to come in the form of Jaguars veteran offensive lineman Patrick Mekari, who had his 21-day practice window to return from injured reserve opened on Wednesday. Mekari can now be activated off injured reserve some time over the next three weeks, potentially giving the Jaguars a chance to boost their offensive line depth down the stretch of the 2026 season.
"Yeah, I think it's great to get Patrick going. Guy has put in so much work since training camp, arriving, and obviously having a tough, you know, early stretch of getting hurt right from the get go. And the guy is 305 pounds right now," Liam Coen said on Wednesday.
"He's the strongest he's been in a long time. He feels good. He's worked his tail off to get back and give himself a chance to go help this team win. So good to get another experienced veteran, smart football player in the fold, and be able to give us depth right now and competition, right? Constantly evaluating the competition of the group, and each week, each guy, you know, guys have to compete to continue to hold jobs and continue to play and be in those positions. So I think that is what Patrick's going to be able to provide for us."
So, how could Mekari help the Jaguars moving forward as they look to improve after 7-3? We break it down below.
If there is something the Jaguars' offensive line is lacking right now, it is offensive tackle depth. The Jaguars have been able to survive the Anton Harrison injury thanks to having Walker Little waiting in the wings as quality tackle depth, but the Jaguars sustained another potential blow to the tackle position last week with Little leaving Sunday's game against the Giants with a knee injury. There has yet to be an update about Little this week, and likely will not be one until the injury report comes out later this afternoon.
Mekari is clearly a guard-first, but he has taken snaps at both tackle spots throughout his career and would likely give the Jaguars a more pro-ready option at tackle than second-year lineman Wyatt Milum, as long as he is healthy. Both are better inside at guard, but Mekari seems to be more equipped to play tackle than Milum.
The Jaguars have had the same starting guards for the entire 2026 season, with Emmanuel Pregnon at left guard and Ezra Cleveland at right guard. With that said, it certainly helps to have a player come in who could push either player at guard down the stretch, in addition to any push they are already getting from Milum and Daniel Faalele. If there is one guard who could in particular use the push, it might be Cleveland.
Cleveland is coming off arguably his worst game of the season and he has been less consistent this year than the past. Jacksonville has clearly preferred Cleveland over Milum for back-to-back seasons, but the Jaguars signed Mekari to be a starter last season. Perhaps they still believe he can be that player and push Cleveland for a spot at guard.
The Jaguars are simply beat up along the offensive line. Anton Harrison is out for the year, Robert Hainsey missed last week with a knee injury, and Little is now dealing with a knee injury as well. The Jaguars can not really afford another singular offensive line injury as-is, and that was before the Jaguars opened up Mekari's window to return to practice.
Mekari has not been in pads for quite some time, so it will clearly take him time to get back into the swing of things. But he does at least boost the Jaguars' overall depth due to his ability to play all five offensive line spots, which is not something you see a team get very often during the final stages of the season.

title: The Worst Part of the Chiefs' Loss in Buffalo? The Predictability
full_text:
It's not shocking or particularly disorienting that the Kansas City Chiefs lost a regular season game against the Buffalo Bills. That's usually how it goes around this time of the year, then the Chiefs get their revenge in the postseason. That's the deal between these two AFC contenders. But Thursday's defeat was an incredibly frustrating one for the most predictable reasons.
The Harrison Butker conversation has been stalled out for more than half of the season . He's been the worst kicker in the NFL , nothing has changed, and I don't think there's anything left to add regarding his perpetual struggles. We've all seen it. Meanwhile, speaking of storylines I'd rather not think or write about any longer, the Chiefs signed Justin Tucker to the practice squad a month ago .
But the issues that cost the Chiefs in Buffalo weren't all Butker-based. Of course, that's an easy and generally fair takeaway when your team's kicker goes 1-for-2 and the other guy hits two fourth-quarter kicks from 54 and 57 yards out in a three-point loss, but the predictable failures went beyond Butker.
Even on a night when the Chiefs outplayed the Bills both offensively and defensively, Kansas City could not get an edge. Their average starting field position was their own 21-yard line , with four drives beginning inside the 12. The Bills' average starting field position was a full 20 yards better, starting in Kansas City territory four times. In a game with zero Chiefs turnovers, that's preposterous.
The Chiefs average starting field position was their own 21. Four of those were inside their own 12. The Bills average starting field position was their own 41. Their worst starting field position was their own 24 and four of them started on KC's side of the field.
Punter Matt Araiza averaged 41.5 yards per punt on his seven boots, including a 36-yard punt that didn't make it across midfield and a fumbled snap that preceded a 13-yard punt, minus a five-yard procedural penalty, for a net of eight yards.
Yes, the elements certainly played a factor, but Bills punter Tommy Doman Jr. averaged 45.8 yards per punt, with three of his five punts landing inside the 20, including some perfectly placed kicks and a pair of poorly evaluated return decisions by Josh Downs.
But even those issues aren't the ones that finally, truly ended the game.
With 14 seconds left, tied at 10, the Chiefs were set to punt from their own end zone. I said, out loud, "They're going to block this and win in regulation." Those words left my mouth. Did I believe them? Was that a real prediction or just the final bit of Thanksgiving pessimism escaping before an incoming disaster? That, I don't know. But I can't imagine that any Chiefs fans were tuned in at that moment and confidently telling themselves, "Well, at least this will be a clean operation and we'll try again in overtime."
THE PUNT IS TIPPED. KCvsBUF on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Pkpl8dQONB
The special teams penalties are another topic that has graduated beyond the need for further evaluation. Why have they so consistently plagued the unit in recent years? Andy Reid said after the game that he's still "comfortable with" the leadership on special teams , expressing continued confidence in special teams coordinator and assistant head coach Dave Toub.
Toub's units have had more than their fair share of struggles for several years , but I also don't care to make this an entirely Toub-based conversation either. Is it his fault that Butker has been in steep decline? Probably not, but it's not helpful to hear Toub declare that he's "not a kicking guy." Did Downs make individually bad decisions on Thursday, or was that how he was coached to field (or not field) those punts? That's hard to say, but it's been a long time since the Chiefs had a consistently good and trustworthy return game. Why do opposing kickers always seem to have great days against Kansas City? Another area where a special teams unit—for one reason or another—hasn't been able to make a positive impact.
This is Dave Toub. He coaches this. Every returned they've had under his employ has caught every punt possible. It's never been a good idea. It never works. But they do it every time. https://t.co/jIIZR0BMla
In football, wins and losses never come down to one player or one play. The game is too complex for that to ever be entirely true. But on a night when the Chiefs' defense held up extremely admirably and the KC offense outplayed Buffalo's unit, the Bills won in just one phase, and that was enough to take the win on Thanksgiving night.
