title: Chiefs Week 12 Winners and Losers in Loss to the Bills
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs lost an absolute heartbreaker to the Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving evening, and the consequences will likely be felt through the end of the 2026 season. It was another classic Chiefs-Bills matchup , but this one felt entirely different.
Brutal temperatures, wind, and precipitation turned a game between two high-flying offenses into a 13-10 rock fight, and Tyler Bass ended it with a 57-yard field goal with four seconds left. The Chiefs had chances, but poor execution and questionable circumstances cost them the game.
We'll likely see this matchup again in January, probably in Buffalo, but Week 12's conditions don't really indicate how the two teams match up. At the very least, the weather made it impossible for either team to show who they truly are, and it also hurts Kansas City that Kenneth Walker wasn't in this game.
Still, there are distinct reasons for the outcome, which has Kansas City sitting at 8-3 and behind the eight ball in both the AFC and AFC West standings. Here are the winners and losers from the Chiefs' latest regular-season loss to the Bills.
The weather played a big role in holding Josh Allen to 81 passing yards, but that does not mean defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo didn't call a great game. He was especially good in the fourth quarter.
With the game tied at 10, his unit sacked Allen twice on well-timed, well-executed third-down blitzes. Nick Bolton ended the first of those drives, and Mansoor Delane and Chris Roland-Wallace shared the next sack. The offense failed to capitalize on either stop, but Spagnuolo had his fastball when the team needed it most.
You would have liked to see the defense hold up better against the run. Only four runs went for more than 10 yards, two by Allen and two by James Cook, but Cook got the yards the Bills needed to stay ahead of the sticks all game long. He averaged just 3.7 yards per carry on 32 attempts for 117 yards, yet Buffalo converted 9-of-16 third downs because their running back put them in advantageous spots.
Even so, Kansas City outgained the Bills by 11 yards despite running 16 fewer plays and holding the ball for more than 13 fewer minutes. No matter how you slice it, the defense played spectacularly.
Limiting the Bills to 230 total yards was not the only impressive part. The Chiefs also intercepted Allen twice. That is one reason the loss is so frustrating. When you hold a former MVP to 10-for-21 with no touchdowns and two interceptions, you want to capitalize.
The first turnover kept Kansas City in the game when things looked grim. Down 7-0 midway through the second quarter, Buffalo was knocking at the Chiefs' 9-yard line when George Karlaftis tipped a pass into safety Alohi Gilman's hands. The Chiefs didn't score on it, but it prevented a 14-0 or 10-0-point deficit that would have been deadly on a night like this.
The second interception also came in the red zone, this time with the Chiefs leading 10-7. From the 14, Allen appeared to complete a pass to Khalil Shakir, who bobbled it into the hands of cornerback Nohl Williams. Kansas City again failed to capitalize, but the lead held for the time being.
It should be noted that Travis Kelce made two fairly major blunders late in the game. On the Chiefs' final offensive drive, Patrick Mahomes found him wide open on a third-and-10, but Kelce was slow to turn around, and the ball hit the turf. A completion would have sent the game to overtime.
On another fourth-quarter drive that ended in a missed field goal, he appeared to catch a 16-yard pass before it was called back for offensive pass interference after he extended his arms on Terrell Bernard.
That said, the Chiefs may never have found an offense without Kelce starting the engine. Kansas City opened with four straight punts and salvaged the first half with three points at the very end of the second quarter.
On that drive, Kelce caught passes for 10, 21, and 24 yards, and in more than 28 minutes of play, the Chiefs had just 51 yards up to that point. It felt as if Mahomes and Kelce proved to the rest of the team that it was possible to be effective in extreme weather. Kelce finished as the team's leading receiver with four catches for 71 yards.
If there was one reason the Chiefs lost this game, it would fall squarely on the special teams unit. In a three-point loss, Harrison Butker's woes returned. In the fourth quarter, he pushed a 46-yard field goal wide right for his eighth missed field goal of the season.
Buffalo's Tyler Bass made both a 54-yarder and a 57-yarder in the fourth quarter in the same conditions, making Butker’s miss all the more frustrating. Andy Reid said afterward that he would go back through everything and wouldn't make a decision on Butker right away, with Justin Tucker still on the practice squad.
The pitiful special teams play did not stop there with Dave Toub's unit. The weather clearly affected punter Matt Araiza all night. He averaged just 41.6 yards per punt, and three of his seven punts gave the Bills drives starting at the Kansas City 49, 47, and 39. One came after Araiza muffed the snap and the unit was flagged for illegal man downfield, netting just eight yards. His final punt was blocked and went a net 28 yards after Greg Dortch returned it 17 to the Kansas City 39, which set up Bass's game-winner with four seconds left
The return game was no better. Josh Downs fielded five Buffalo punts and struggled several times to judge whether to field them, which kept the Chiefs in poor field position. They started drives at their own 4, 9, and 11. Nate Carter also fumbled a kickoff, and Jaydn Ott was flagged for holding on the same play. The lone bright spot was Jalen Royals' 37-yard kickoff return to open the second half.
It has been a tumultuous season for the third-year left guard, and Week 12 was the latest chapter. The former BYU Cougar was flagged three times and, according to PFF, was the only Chiefs offensive lineman to allow multiple pressures. He was called for holding twice. One call was declined, and the Chiefs overcame the other thanks to Kelce on that first field goal drive.
The one that really hurt was a dead-ball personal foul after he swung at a Bills defender, although it was a questionable call. He did not actually land the swipe. That said, Kansas City had all the momentum after scoring 10 straight points, but instead of facing a third-and-3, the Chiefs faced a third-and-16 and punted.
The Bills tied it at 10 on the ensuing drive. In a game against a top contender where the smallest margins matter, Suamataia showed up poorly for the offense.
The Chiefs may have won the turnover battle, but they went 2-for-11 on third downs while Buffalo went 9-for-16. It is hard to win any game when you are not converting, and in this one it led to two red-zone field-goal attempts and seven punts. They had a couple of third-and-shorts on their first two drives, but the other nine were all third-and-medium or longer, and several were beyond third-and-20. They were behind the sticks all game, averaging 8.5 yards to go on third down.
That was the crux of the problem, and it had a whole lot to do with penalties. The Chiefs committed seven offensive penalties. The real killer came on the drive where Butker missed the 46-yarder. The Chiefs ran 11 plays over more than six minutes and came away with no points.
Tight end Noah Gray's 19-yard catch set up the Chiefs at the Bills' 17-yard line, but after an incompletion to Kelce, the Chiefs were flagged on three plays in a row: a late hold on Hunter Nourzad, a false start on Fred Johnson, and an ineligible man downfield on Creed Humphrey, which pushed them all the way back to the Buffalo 32.
Two failed third-down plays late in the game stand out. First, with the game tied at 10 and just under two minutes to go, Kansas City had the ball deep in its own territory, and Rashee Rice appeared to move the chains on a third-and-10. title: Chiefs Sound Off on Controversial Reversal of Rashee Rice Catch vs. Bills
full_text:
On a night that saw the Kansas City Chiefs hold the ball for 13:50 less than their opponent, convert on seven fewer third downs and commit five more penalties than them, none of those developments is the main talking point.
Instead, a different shortcoming is what many are reflecting on in the aftermath of a 13-10 heartbreaker to the Buffalo Bills. Given that the outing was close from start to finish, there's a lengthy list of plays that can be put under a microscope, but one rises above the rest.
With the game tied at 10 and less than two minutes remaining in the fourth quarter, Kansas City was backed up deep in its own territory but seemed to convert on a third-and-10 pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes to wide receiver Rashee Rice. Following a review, however, the perceived grab was reversed, prompting a punt.
Dear Football Fans, This is a Safe Space. Is this a catch by Rashee Rice or an incompletion? pic.twitter.com/T8yv5hXA4U
That sequence marked a critical moment in the prime-time tilt in favor of the home team. Was it the right call? Speaking to the media on Thursday night, head coach Andy Reid revealed whether he got an explanation and if it was satisfactory.
"Yeah, not one that I agreed with, but yeah," Reid said. "They said this came from New York, so it's not from these guys. Our guys called it a completion, the guys that were working the game. I'm not quite sure what they saw. I saw he had control of the ball, and then his elbow hit, and then the ball hit, but he had control. Normally, in those kind of situations, it's got to be clear and obvious. To me, that was not clear and obvious."
The rest after the punt is history, as Buffalo gave Kansas City the ball back with minimal time at its own 11-yard line. Reid dialed up a pair of passing plays in three shots — one was a fumbled snap, with the lone actual throw falling incomplete. The end-of-possession punt assisted the Bills in setting up a game-winning field goal by kicker Tyler Bass, putting an end to a frustrating night for the visitors.
No one knows what would've happened had Rice's attempt been kept a catch. With that said, it's one thing to be skeptical of the validity of the process being completed. It's another to take what was decided on the field and change it upon further review without, in Reid's words, clear and obvious evidence. How big of an impact did the overturning have?
Per advanced box score data from RBSDM , it was significant. Not only did the play come with -0.6 expected points added, but it also raised the Bills' win probability from 60.5% all the way up to 69.2%. The lowest that figure would get the rest of the way was 51.2% when the Kansas City defense sacked Buffalo quarterback Josh Allen third down to give the offense the aforementioned one last opening to make magic happen.
The pool report with NFL VP of Instant Replay Mark Butterworth on the overturned ruling of a catch by Rashee Rice. “As the receiver is going to the ground, he had the ball in his right hand and when he contacted the ground, his hand slid up the ball and we deemed that a loss of… pic.twitter.com/Cl094uWVk0
Taking the podium after Reid, Mahomes said he didn't get to "see a lot of reviews" inside Highmark Stadium, but he believed Rice's hand was under the football. Those in charge, taking a more detailed look from behind monitors, had a different opinion.
Don't get it twisted: Kansas City could've done several things better (or at least differently) to put itself in a better position to potentially secure a win. Cutting back on missed opportunities in the passing game, penalties in general or special teams mishaps would've perhaps altered the final score. But whether it's fair or not, one of the first places folks tend to look is officiating.
Reid made his stance surprisingly clear. Not so much for Mahomes. If one thing is obvious with Thanksgiving's clash of titans in the books, however, it's that the matchup didn't short anyone on drama.

title: Andy Reid Reflects on Chiefs’ Special Teams Miscues in Walk-Off Loss to Bills
full_text:
In tonight's Thanksgiving Day showdown , the Chiefs outgained the Bills in total yards, averaged more yards per play, and won the turnover battle by two, but were still unable to pull out a victory in Orchard Park. Tyler Bass walked Kansas City off with a 57-yard field goal to drop the Chiefs to 8-3 on the season.
The entire reason the Bills were given that opportunity in the first place, though, stemmed from a blocked punt off the foot of Matt Araiza. It was one of countless special teams blunders that Andy Reid's squad made over the course of this evening. Not only did Araiza shank several of his seven punts, but the Chiefs also left three points on the board with Harrison Butker's eighth missed field-goal attempt of the year in the fourth quarter. This certainly wasn't one of the finer showings for special teams coordinator Dave Toub's unit .
Following the loss, Coach Reid spoke to the media about the team's countless miscues. He emphasized that they simply cannot happen in close contests like these.
"The bottom line comes down to we can't go backwards in a game against a good football team, and we did that," Reid said after the game. "Two penalties set us back, and then a missed field goal. Those things can't happen in tight games."
On three of Araiza's seven punts, he booted them away from deep inside Kansas City territory and watched them land there, too. The Bills surprisingly didn't score any points on the first two; that changed when the Bills trotted Bass out with four seconds left on the game clock for the decisive game-winning kick. It was a fitting end to an otherwise frustrating night for Kansas City's special teams.
"We've got to do better. Field position is a big thing," Reid stated. "The positive was, our defense played its tails off... You can't have those things." It's been a seemingly never-ending cycle of shortcomings for the Chiefs' special teams , whether it's penalties on returns, missed field goals, or consistently losing the field position game. Despite these recurring errors, Reid reiterated multiple times that he is fully confident in Toub's leadership as the man in charge and that the group as a whole needs to perform better.
Now sporting an ugly 14-of-22 mark on field goals in 2026, it feels like it's only a matter of time before the Chiefs pull the plug on Butker. They have given him every possible chance to turn things around with the franchise, but Justin Tucker — who Toub described as "off the charts" during his tryout with the team last month — is currently on standby on the practice squad .
Harrison Butker has 8 missed field goals this season Nobody else has more pic.twitter.com/94Wg2yrZ01
Even having missed kicks in seven of the Chiefs' 11 games to this point, Reid is not ready to make a decision on Butker's future with the organization. "I'll go back and go through all of it again here, but I'm not going to make any decisions right this minute," Reid confirmed.
It was always going to be a game of margins under the challenging conditions in Buffalo today. Ultimately, the Chiefs failed to capitalize on many occasions and let special teams mistakes come back to haunt them. Even sitting at 8-3, Kansas City fans can't help but think that these issues will follow them into the postseason.

title: 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs' Heartbreaking Loss to Bills on Thanksgiving
full_text:
The football world figured it'd be in for an instant classic when the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills squared off on Thanksgiving. While the holiday outing was indeed as close as some predicted, it was anything but pretty for either side.
On a cold, windy and rainy night in Orchard Park, it wound up being a battle of which crew could avoid mistakes at critical times. Unfortunately for head coach Andy Reid and company, they were on the wrong side of that and ended up dropping this one by a final of 13-10 via a walk-off field goal.
With the defeat, the Chiefs fall to 8-3 on the year. Let's jump into 10 instant observations and takeaways from Week 12.
Kansas City knew that coming into the regular season without 2025 first-round pick Josh Simmons would be a challenge. Fielding a developing left tackle seemed to be the path either way with Kahlil Benson taking over for him, which constituted a pretty young left-side duo with Kingsley Suamataia at guard. In the opening half of play, that relative inexperience showed.
The first example of the foundation cracking some was Benson whiffing on a tackle-for-loss by edge rusher Bradley Chubb on a third-and-1. Suamataia couldn't cover for him, then went on to commit two holding penalties on a third-and-7 and a first-and-10. It was a start to forget for Benson, but Suamataia's mishaps persisted throughout the entire first two quarters.
Bradley Chubb with a big TFL to stop the drive. KCvsBUF on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/LdJvs5bVcQ
In our Week 12 game predictions story here for Chiefs On SI , I wrote that a ball-control type of game script would go in Kansas City's favor. That take couldn't have aged much worse in the first half.
The Chiefs held the ball for just 10:57 in quarters one and two, averaging 2.7 yards per play on drives one and two. Unless you're generating explosives on that side of the ball, only running six plays isn't going to get the job done in just about any circumstance. Kansas City was able to slowly get some things going by the time the half ended, although you couldn't have drummed up a much worse runway to kick the outing off.
Well in advance of Thanksgiving Day, it was revealed that the weather conditions in Orchard Park would be suboptimal at best. Temperatures were set to stay above freezing at kickoff, but plenty of rain and wind set up what many thought would be a lower-scoring affair than originally anticipated. That wound up being the case prior to the break, to say the least.
On the Chiefs' side, defensive end George Karlaftis allowed Buffalo field general Josh Allen to get out of his sack attempt and pick up a first down. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes and center Creed Humphrey failed a snap exchange, too. That's without even bringing up special teams — more on that momentarily.
The ball was slippery for both sides, to be completely fair, yet the Bills had a much easier time dealing with the conditions in their home stadium to start.
Given the rocket arm that Allen has and his ability to stretch the field vertically as well as any signal-caller, it sometimes comes off as a slight to bring up the rushing attack first when discussing the Bills. It's worth noting, though, that he and halfback James Cook make up perhaps the best ground duo in the sport. Even with a modest -0.5% pass rate over expected ( per nfelo ) entering Week 12, the group has established itself as a run-heavy one.
That trickled into the rainy moments of Thursday, with the Bills sticking to 24 rush attempts as opposed to 10 passes. Cook, in particular, was effective with 19 carries for 71 yards and a score while also picking up numerous key conversions. KC simply didn't have the ball long enough to make too many decisions, but a split of nine rushes to 15 passes wasn't great.
It wouldn't be a postgame column without a reflection on special teams at some point. Anyone who's been around for this recurring "10 instant observations" series knows where I stand on coordinator Dave Toub, so it'll always remain important to assess whether the output is aligning with the reputation and hype.
Before wide receiver Jalen Royals' 37-yard kickoff return to open the second half, that certainly wasn't reality for Kansas City.
Trade acquisition Josh Downs let an early punt go instead of returning it, only for it to be downed at the 4-yard line. The offense stalled on the ensuing possession, which ended in a Matt Araiza punt of just 37 yards. Later, running back Nate Carter fumbled a kickoff and fellow halfback Jaydn Ott got flagged for holding on the same play.
Add in an Araiza fumble, paired with an ineligible man infraction that resulted in a punt of eight net yards, and you get the picture of how many mistakes were made. Harrison Butker's missed field goal in the fourth and lackluster protection on Araiza's last punt were salt on the wound.
Before the season, just about everyone thought the Chiefs' defensive line would revolve around and go as tackle Chris Jones did. On the contrary, it's been Karlaftis who's emerged as the best player up front for Steve Spagnuolo's unit.
Karlaftis had 10 passes defended from Weeks 1-9; he managed to add to that total with a tip on a second-and-7 pass from Allen in the red zone. The ball was promptly picked off by safety Alohi Gilman, helping prevent what would've been a field goal and perhaps even a touchdown on the drive.
Much is made of Karlaftis' background as a water polo player, almost to the point of a running joke, but it's real. He's seemingly always finding ways to get his hands up at the right time and with correct placement, which once again came to his aid in Week 12.
Alohi Gilman picks off Josh Allen in the red zone! 👀 📺 SNF Thanksgiving Night on NBC & Peacock pic.twitter.com/OkYPG9jpEJ
One of the more interesting subplots of this matchup was slated to be how both sides fared on third down. Entering Thursday's play, for instance, Kansas City and Buffalo were 10th and ninth, respectively, in conversion rate on offense and ninth and seventh, respectively on defense.
Lump in that both clubs resided in the top four in EPA per play on late downs in general, via SumerSports , and something had to give. Through the first three quarters, it certainly did.
Possessing control of the football to begin the fourth, the Bills were already 8-for-12 on third down. The Chiefs, on the other hand, were 1-for-7. The 10-7 scoring advantage for the visitors highlighted just how strange of a game it was to that point.
There are many other things that made up the final result, but having your opponent outperform you by a 38% clip on third down (2-for-11 versus 9-for-16) will rarely mean you came away with a win.
Given the ball via kickoff in a game that was all knotted up at 10 apiece, the Chiefs merely needed to walk away with something besides time being elapsed. Despite running 11 plays, their only drive of double-digit plays to that point, they managed to lose 25 yards due to penalties and walk to the sideline with only the aforementioned missed field goal.
Tight end Travis Kelce's offensive pass interference was admittedly weak, albeit only to get bailed out by rookie wideout Cyrus Allen's impressive third-and-15 snag. Later in the series, fill-in guard Hunter Nourzad was called for a late hold, and recent signing Fred Johnson (who was also in the game for an injured lineman) committed a false start.
Humphrey was then called out for being an ineligible man downfield on a broken play. Kansas City undoubtedly faced some adversity on its drive that salted away 6:02 from the clock, yet a good chunk was self-inflicted.
Thanks to a joint sack by linebacker Nick Bolton and defensive back Chris Roland-Wallace, Kansas City was afforded yet another chance to take the lead down the stretch. The first two plays of the next drive were rather uninspiring, but wideout Rashee Rice was able to save the day with a tough grab on third-and-10 to move the chains.

title: Live Game Thread & Updates for Kansas City Chiefs vs. Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving
full_text:
For the second consecutive year, the Kansas City Chiefs will play on the road in a Thanksgiving Day showdown. After losing to the Cowboys in Dallas a season ago, they will head to Orchard Park to take on the Bills tonight. While KC has gotten the better of Buffalo in its recent playoff matchups, the Bills hold a 5-1 regular-season record over the Chiefs in the Patrick Mahomes era. Andy Reid's squad is looking to change that narrative in this highly anticipated affair. For those who want to track the action live, we'll be covering the game at Chiefs on SI with constant updates throughout the evening.
14:53: Bills win the toss and elect to receive the ball first. They will open the first drive of the night on their own 29-yard line. 11:51: Allen scrambles for a first down to move the chains and advance into Kansas City territory. All running plays so far for Buffalo in these rainy conditions. 10:56: The Chiefs force a stop on a third down target to Khalil Shakir, which results in a touchback punt. Patrick Mahomes and the offense will trot onto the field with hopes to put the first points of the night on the board. 8:54: Chiefs go three and out after a trio of Emmett Johnson runs get stuffed by the Buffalo defensive line. It could be a while before the offenses get going in this one. 7:18: Mansoor Delane plays DJ Moore perfectly in coverage, resulting in an incompletion on third down. Less than eight minutes into the game, there have already been three combined punts. The Bills downed this one inside the five, meaning Kansas City will start with terrible field position. 5:40: Matt Araiza shanks his punt after another three-and-out, which rolls out of bound in Kansas City territory. This is a game of field position, and the Bills have a prime opportunity to capitalize on this next drive. 2:50: George Karlaftis was inches away from a third-down sack that could have put Buffalo out of field-goal range. Instead, he evaded the pressure and found Shakir over the middle of the field for a first-down conversion. The Bills are now in the red zone for the first time tonight. 0:00: On fourth and short, the Bills ran it up the gut with James Cook III and squeezed out a first down. The Bills will snap the ball from the three yard line on first and goal when the second quarter begins.
14:32: A phantom false start call (which was completely wrong) almost gave the Chiefs' defense a break. Regardless, Cook ran it in the next play from six yards out to give Buffalo an early lead. Bills lead, 7-0. 12:17: While Kansas City finally picked up a first down on a pass to Travis Kelce, Mahomes was unable to connect with a wide-open Josh Downs on third down. Araiza fumbled the long snap for an atrocious 13-yard punt. Yet another drive where Buffalo starts inside the 50. 7:46: A huge, much-needed break for the defense. Alohi Gilman comes up with a clutch red zone interception in the end zone that he kneeled for a touchback. Just when it looked like the Bills would make this a two-score game, the Chiefs have been given some momentum before the half concludes. 5:38: You can fill out your bingo card with a bad snap from Creed Humphrey. Kansas City now faces a second-and-long situation, putting its field position at risk in a game where every yard matters. 4:32: The first-down miscue costs the Chiefs and sends Araiza out for the fourth time today. He finally got a solid one off, and the Bills will start at their own 24-yard line. 1:50: Buffalo is unable to convert on third down, and Tommy Doman Jr. shanks his own punt for 23 yards. It'll be a two-minute drill for Kansas City, and the hope is that they can at least put three points on the board before getting the ball back after the half. 1:08: Following a Kingsley Suamataia holding call, Mahomes finds Kelce on back-to-back throws, including a game-long 24-yard gain. The Chiefs are in business with a little over a minute to go. 0:25: It's decision time for Andy Reid on fourth-and-one from the Buffalo 31-yard line. He certainly can't be confident in Harrison Butker to drill it from 49 yards out in this weather, so it can be reasonably assumed that the offense stays on the field here. 0:17: Mahomes makes it to the line to gain on a fourth-down play-action scramble, but he used eight seconds of clock to do so. It's going to be tough for the Chiefs to find the end zone without a huge chunk play. 0:00: The Chiefs had one shot at trying to score a touchdown, but Mahomes had to sail it out the back of the end zone on first and goal since KC was out of timeouts. Butker drilled a 26-yard field goal as time nearly expired, cutting the deficit to four points going into the locker room. It certainly feels like the Chiefs should be trailing by more right now. Bills lead 7-3 at halftime.
14:50: An excellent kick return by Jalen Royals sets up the Chiefs at their own 45 to open the second half. Let's see if the offense can get any points out of this drive. 14:07: Johnson is finally starting to come alive on the ground. Back-to-back runs of over 10 yards have already put Kansas City in field-goal range. 11:28: A seven-play, 56-yard drive results in Kansas City's first touchdown of the evening. Who else but Johnson to punch it in, who carried the ball four times for 33 yards over the past few minutes. All of the life was sucked out of Highmark Stadium on that drive. Chiefs lead, 10-7. 10:58: The second time today where the Chiefs' defensive line had Josh Allen dead to rights and he escaped a sack. What would have been a three-and-out turns into a positive scramble and puts the Bills around midfield. 5:40: The Chiefs get a massive break on a dropped Khalil Shakir pass, which somehow ends up in the hands of Nohl Williams for an interception. The Bills had gotten to the 14-yard line and were likely going to tie the game at 10 at the very least. Instead, the Chiefs get their second red zone takeaway of the night and now can extend this lead to two possessions. 3:48: A questionable unnecessary roughness call on Kingsley Suamataia sets the Chiefs back and forces them to get conservative on third down. I for one wasn't particularly a fan of that flag, though it was Suamataia's third penalty of the night, which is flat-out unacceptable. Injury Report: Defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga just jogged off the field after a third-down conversion by the Bills. 0:00: At the end of the third quarter, the Chiefs still lead 10-7, but the Bills are driving and have picked up a pair of first downs (both via one-yard runs on third down). It'll be first-and-10 for Buffalo to open the final quarter from Kansas City's 45-yard line.
12:18: A holding call wipes away what would have been a first down on a designed QB run by Allen. The Bills now face third-and-16 in difficult field-goal range and likely need to pick up a few yards to consider sending Tyler Bass out for a kick. 11:58: Bass somehow splits a 54-yard try through the uprights to tie this one up. That penalty wipes away a 17-yard gain that would have put the Chiefs at Buffalo's 30-yard line. Mahomes needs to pick up 15 yards on the next two plays to keep this drive alive. 9:21: On third-and-15, Mahomes pulls off one of the most "Mahomey" throws he's made all year. Rolling to his right, he found rookie Cyrus Allen over the middle of the field for a jumping catch. Easily the play of the night for Kansas City so far. 6:55: Hunter Nourzad, filling in for Trey Smith at right guard, picks up a costly holding call on second down. To his right, Fred Johnson is manning the tackle spot for Joshua Ezeudu, who is getting his ankle worked on. 5:56: Harrison Butker's nightmare season continues. title: Chiefs vs. Bills: NFL Week 12 Preview, Score Predictions for Thanksgiving
full_text:
After a somewhat light start to the season on the schedule front, it's about to get real for the Kansas City Chiefs. Awaiting them on Thanksgiving Day is one of their perceived top threats in the conference, the Buffalo Bills.
In a classic tilt between all-world quarterbacks, dynamic head coaches and elite rushing attacks, many are calling for bushels of points on Thursday. On the other hand, an ugly weather report for the holiday may have different plans.
With kickoff on the horizon, which side will come out on top? The Kansas City Chiefs On SI crew makes its predictions for Week 12 of the regular season.
Joshua Brisco: This has been true for a large number of Chiefs-Bills matchups in the past, but this game truly feels like a coin-flip. The loss of Kenneth Walker matters, but the Bills have unanswered questions on both sides of the ball. Buffalo wins these regular-season showdowns, but it’s arguably more important for Kansas City this time through.
The Chiefs’ offensive tackles are cause for concern, but Patrick Mahomes has been playing tremendous football behind that same line for much of this season. James Cook is a weapon, but Steve Spagnuolo’s defense is typically stout against the run. Ultimately, this feels like a game that comes down to a late field goal or a fourth-quarter turnover.
I’m relatively confident that this game will live up to the hype, but I could easily see either team escaping with the narrow victory.
Jordan Foote: In my Week 12 preview, I echoed Brisco's sentiment and chalked this one up to a relative coin-flip as well. The Bills have plenty of holes on their roster and, in many ways, remind me of this Chiefs squad. Usually, having home-field advantage would be the deciding factor in a game like this, but Buffalo simply doesn't look like a club that's firing on all cylinders.
The Kansas City defense will surely be put to the test against the dynamic rushing duo of Allen and Cook. There also may not be a more lethal play extender than Allen in the dropback game when he's operating at peak capacity. Still, the Chiefs have a running game of their own with Johnson enjoying some success. A heavy ball-control style of outing goes to KC.
Expect a close one at the new Highmark Stadium. I'm not rolling with a combined 60-plus points, instead giving the visitors a one-score edge thanks to either a timely stop on defense or some Mahomes magic on the other side of the football.
Joshua Schulman: The Chiefs are looking to change their fortunes against the Bills in the regular season. Patrick Mahomes may own Josh Allen in the postseason, but he’s 1-5 against Buffalo in regular-season meetings.
With Kenneth Walker out for the third consecutive week, Emmett Johnson will take on a larger workload in his place. He’ll need to have a big day with cold temperatures and heavy rainfall expected in Buffalo.
While the Chiefs have bounced back in a huge way since their two-game losing skid, they haven’t faced much competition. Behind Buffalo’s defense improved defense and a rowdy home crowd, I think it’ll be tough for the Chiefs to pull this one off.
Tyler Brown: This is the kind of game that comes down to the last possession, and I think it ends up going Kansas City’s way despite Mahomes’ 1-5 record against Allen in the regular season. I think they match up that well. Allen is playing somewhat erratically, as shown by his nine touchdowns and nine interceptions over the past eight games.
The Bills’ defense has looked great against backup quarterbacks, but it allows more than 30 points a game against good-to-average offenses, and Kansas City is as good as any. Mahomes has been dealing for a month, and he should find openings against a vulnerable defensive backfield. With Emmett Johnson carrying the load, the rushing attack will keep the Bills guessing. Travis Kelce, Josh Downs, and Rashee Rice can do the rest.
It will not be easy to stop Allen, and you have to account for Cook as well. Allen always seems to find another gear against this team, and the Chiefs will have to keep him out of the red zone, where he is a touchdown vulture. But in a possible Thanksgiving shootout in the rain, I like the team that appears more balanced.
The Chiefs have only one win against a team with a winning record, so this could be fool’s gold, but the process behind their recent surge looks legitimate.

title: Five Things the Chiefs Should Be Thankful For This Thanksgiving
full_text:
While the Kansas City Chiefs are in their final hours of preparation before facing off with the Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving night , the holiday is a good time to reflect on some things that have gone well through the first 10 games of the season.
What's worth being thankful for in Chiefs Kingdom? There are some obvious blessings and some more surprising developments that all deserve a seat at the table.
In one of the quieter revelations of the Chiefs' season, rookie No. 6 overall pick Mansoor Delane and second-year third-rounder Nohl Williams have quickly developed into one of the league's best cornerback duos . While Delane has been managing an ongoing shoulder ailment, Williams has taken the second-most defensive snaps on the team in 2026.
With the exception of an understandably tough day against Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Delane has looked like every bit of a No. 1 NFL cornerback, and I'd argue that Delane still looked completely qualified against the Seahawks. Smith-Njigba got the best of the rookie, but the Delane wasn't lost against the reigning Offensive Player of the Year. Meanwhile, Williams has been consistently excellent on the other side of the field.
Anything stand out? https://t.co/tkIqLr6oHs pic.twitter.com/eg4H7W39Mx
Arguably the most thrilling part about the rise of this duo? Williams is under contract through the 2028 season, maxing out at a $2 million cap hit, while Delane's four-year, $42 million deal runs through 2029, with a fifth-year option for 2030.
Not only do the Chiefs have an excellent pair of starters right now, they have a young tandem that should continue to grow in years to come.
It was obvious that the Chiefs had to add a wide receiver before the NFL trade deadline , and Josh Downs appeared to be one of the only realistic options. While that wasn't an ideal place to begin negotiating, Downs' immediate impact has been impressive .
Not only has Downs been quick to pick up the playbook, he's brought an ease to the field in his first two games as a Chief.
With all of the necessary disclaimers about a small sample size and the quality of the Chiefs' opponents the last two weeks, I've been struck by how comfortable Downs looks in the Chiefs' offense, and even more excited by how quickly Patrick Mahomes decided to start going Downs' way.
Mahomes targeted Downs 10 times in two games for eight catches, 112 yards and a touchdown, and it never looked difficult or out-of-sync. Even as someone who was optimistic about what Downs could bring as a man-coverage-beater and a quarterback-friendly target, I thought it could be weeks before we saw the trickle-down effect of his addition to the receiver room. It took only a few reps before it became clear.
Now, the Chiefs can retool their receiving rotation , and the other pass-catchers should see less attention from opposing teams when Downs establishes himself as the biggest threat on a given play. There's still much more to prove in the weeks to come, but it would be hard to ask for anything more from Downs after such a short time in Kansas City.
Defensive end George Karlaftis has been a steadily improving player throughout his time in the NFL, but last season, while dealing with a thumb/hand injury ( a broken hand, according to D-line coach Joe Cullen ), Karlaftis appeared to plateau. With the injury behind him, Karlaftis has taken another step forward in 2026.
Karlaftis leads the team with eight sacks, 12 tackles for loss and 26 quarterback hits through 10 games, and many advanced stats support the box score .
NFL Pass Rusher Efficiency Week 1-11 Greg Rousseau is a machine #BillsMafia #Skol #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/bjfGvvbRVW
Will Karlaftis continue to evolve into one of the league's preeminent menaces off the edge? It's still too early to know that for sure. But if he can continue to be the player he's shown himself to be through the last few weeks, he'll be a foundational piece for years to come.
Most sacks since Week 8: 1. George Karlaftis - 7.0 2. Jeffery Simmons - 5.0* 2. Quinnen Williams - 5.0 *Joined Bears in Week 8 (had bye in Week 10)
Before Kenneth Walker suffered the groin injury that will hold him out for at least three games, including tonight's showdown in Buffalo, Walker would be the rightful holder of this No. 2 spot. Chiefs fans should still be enormously grateful for Walker's role on this team, of course—his early-season Offensive Player of the Year candidacy was completely legitimate, and the Chiefs will be better when Walker returns.
With that being said, rookie fifth-round pick Emmett Johnson has been extremely valuable to the Chiefs' offense, particularly in Walker's absence .
It's not just that Johnson has recorded back-to-back 100-yard rushing games in his two starts against the Atlanta Falcons and Arizona Cardinals. His 345 receiving yards are the third-most on the team, but that's not his best contribution either. The most valuable thing that Johnson has brought to the offense is normalcy, consistency and competence that allows the Chiefs to continue being an effective running team even without their superstar free agent addition.
When teams lose their only noteworthy running back (or when they enter a season without a back of that caliber), it becomes hard to respect the running game and easy to fall into an aggressively pass-happy offense, allowing defenses to assume one-dimensionality. Johnson has been better than just normal, consistent and competent, but that's what has allowed him to stay on the field, earning him more opportunities to make big plays while the threat of the run remains legitimate in Kansas City.
No need to overthink No. 1.
Mahomes has been phenominal so far this season, and he's playing at an MVP-caliber level after tearing his ACL and LCL in Week 15 of the 2025 season . It's easy to forget how uncertain Mahomes' future was after last year's season-ending injury because it was evident by the time training camp began that Mahomes would be starting in Week 1. Still, Mahomes' return shouldn't be taken for granted. Nor should his play.
There's been plenty of talk about the Chiefs' weaknesses at wide receiver before they made the trade to add Downs, but the most underrated part of Mahomes' season comes with how he's navigated a borderline-disastrous offensive tackle situation .
Pick your choice of offensive line pass protection grading metrics —often subjective, to be fair—and you'll find the Chiefs near the bottom of most of them. Meanwhile, Mahomes has been sacked only 13 times this year, tied for 28th-most in the league.
According to Warren Sharp , Mahomes has been sacked on just 10.4% of his pressures, the best rate in the league among Sharp's long list of qualifying quarterbacks.
Year after year, Mahomes maximizes his surroundings and overcomes the team's deficiencies so effectively that many people around the league forget that the Chiefs have any weaknesses at all. Mahomes improves Kansas City's ceiling and floor every season. Every Chiefs fan should be thankful for that.

title: Part 11: Chiefs-Bills Matchups Will Always Come Down to Mahomes and Allen
full_text:
The real football season officially starts now. After t hree straight games against middling opponents , the Kansas City Chiefs travel to face the Buffalo Bills in what both teams could bill as the biggest game of the season.
Both teams have played softer schedules up to this point, so we don't really know who they are. The Bills are 9-1, the Chiefs are 8-2, and the winner will hold the AFC's No. 1 seed at the end of the night. The forecast calls for 38 degrees and rain, and it doesn't get much more football on Thanksgiving than that.
The stakes are high, as usual, whenever these two teams and these two quarterbacks meet. Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen are tied 5-5 in head-to-head matchups, and each meeting feels like an “ESPN Classic."
History says Buffalo has the upper hand. The Bills are at home in their brand-new stadium, and Allen is 5-1 against Mahomes in the regular season. That has worked out fine for the Chiefs, though, since they are 4-0 against Allen in the playoffs.
Both teams made offseason changes that were just shy of sweeping. Buffalo fired longtime head coach Sean McDermott and replaced him with his former offensive coordinator, Joe Brady. The Chiefs shook up their offensive coaching staff and added running backs Kenneth Walker and Emmett Johnson , which completely changed the dynamic of that unit.
Sometimes the biggest matchup in a game is the most obvious one, and when these two quarterbacks meet, the conversation starts and ends with them. Let’s dig in.
Mahomes is going scorched earth right now, but it goes without saying that the Chiefs need to stick with what has made them the No. 1 offense in the NFL: establishing and dominating with their rushing attack. The Bills are top 10 in rushing yards allowed per game, but they are much closer to the middle of the pack in yards per carry. In the end, Emmett Johnson will be critical, but Week 12 is all about one guy.
The Bills are fifth in total offense and second in points per game, averaging more than 31, and Mahomes will have to keep up. If Kansas City is going to outpace Buffalo, it will need its two-time MVP to play like one. The timing is good, too, with Mahomes averaging more than 300 yards per game and a 13-0 touchdown-to-interception ratio over his last four contests.
He should find success at all three levels. According to PFF, all of the Bills' starting linebackers allow more than 73 percent of their targets to be caught. Safety Cole Bishop, who always seems to have his best game against Kansas City, allows a 101.9 passer rating when targeted. Slot cornerback Dee Alford is allowing 13.4 yards per catch, which suits Travis Kelce, Josh Downs , and Rashee Rice well.
On the outside, Davison Igbinosun is playing good football for a rookie but has eight penalties, among the league's worst. Christian Benford is getting picked on the most, leading the team with 312 yards and four touchdowns allowed, and Maxwell Hairston has also struggled at times.
It depends on how much Andy Reid wants to get into his bag for a regular-season game, but he could have a fun time drawing up a game plan against this defense. It ranked among the league's worst in most categories before a recent stretch against the Ravens, Vikings, Jets, and Dolphins, all of which were played with backup quarterbacks, aside from Geno Smith.
If you lump those games in with their game against the Chargers, they are allowing just 10.6 points per game. In the other five games, against above-average to good offenses, they have allowed 31.6 points per game, and it is safe to say the Chiefs belong in that category, if not at the top.
If Mahomes wants to stake a claim to his third MVP season, he'll need a big performance on the biggest stage against another MVP quarterback. With running back Kenneth Walker out again, Mahomes can use his weaponry, which is gelling by the week, to light up the scoreboard and move his team to 9-2.
Allen is in another MVP race this season, and while he is not having his best year through the air, Steve Spagnuolo summed him up on Monday: "It just seems like, when he plays the Kansas City Chiefs, he's on fire. He becomes Superman."
This season, Allen has 14 touchdowns and nine interceptions and is averaging just over 252 yards per game, but as usual, you also have to watch his legs. He averages more than 29 rushing yards per game, though that number is inflated by his 121 yards against the Rams.
With Spagnuolo flipping on that film this week, it's fair to wonder whether we'll see more of second-year linebacker Jeffrey Bassa, who has at times come in to spy the quarterback. The other key is keeping the Bills outside of the three-yard line. Allen has 11 rushing touchdowns this year, and all but one have come from inside that area.
Through the air, this will be a big test for slot corner Chris Roland-Wallace. Allen's favorite targets are slot receiver Khalil Shakir and tight end Dalton Kincaid. On the outside, Nohl Williams, Mansoor Delane, and Kristian Fulton will have to shut down D.J. Moore, who has long been a reliable security blanket for many quarterbacks. Third-year wide receiver Keon Coleman is also on pace for a career season.
Allen and the offense operate best when running back James Cook gets into rhythm, so the Chiefs' front seven will be critical in forcing the Bills into passing situations. Nick Bolton, Drue Tranquill, and the defensive line are having career years in that area, which should help put Allen in compromising spots.
The multi-time All-Pro quarterback has thrown the sixth-most interceptions this season and ranks fifth in turnover-worthy plays with 18, according to PFF. The Chiefs match up fairly well in this game, but in a regular-season game, you never know what you will get from Reid's club, and you can bet your bottom dollar that Allen will put his best foot forward.

title: Mike McDaniel has finally figured out how to effectively use Omarion Hampton
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are lost.
We recently wrote, too, that Omarion Hampton is the perfect example of everything wrong with the Chargers.
Here is Hampton, a pricey first-round pick made by a Chargers front office that decided to ignore other problem areas and grab a low-impact position. And here is Jim Harbaugh, an old-school, run-first coach, hiring the new-era Mike McDaniel, who has decided that Hampton should be part of a three-back rotation with the so-so likes of Kimani Vidal and Keaton Mitchell for reasons .
There are other problems, no doubt. The continued investment and reliance on Quentin Johnston is one. Don’t forget the Justin Herbert injury saga , either.
But the Hampton stuff? It’s only getting worse.
It was inevitable that reporters would eventually put McDaniel on the grill a bit about Hampton.
After all, Harbaugh had just said that “yeah, in hindsight, we should have done that sooner,” in regards to making Hampton the workhorse back. That, after 22 carries for 105 yards and a score in Week 10.
So, here is McDaniel, getting in a back-and-forth with The Athletic’s Noah Furtado about Hampton’s usage:
Mike McDaniel on why it took to this point in the season to use Omarion Hampton as traditional RB1: "That kind of confuses me. I've given him, I mean, he's played about 29 plays a game or something like that, I heard at the beginning of the week. But he consistently has been on…
Hampton (138) has outcarried Vidal (45) and Mitchell (49) this year. The point of contention, really, is that he was a first-round investment and the rotation hasn’t been all that effective. He’s averaging 4.1 yards per carry with four scores…why not let him really get in a rhythm instead of oddly yanking him from games?
There’s another big problem: Earlier in the year, McDaniel stressed that this sort of rotation was meant to hopefully keep all guys fresh deep into the season. The implication was a playoff push. The Chargers are 1-9. The keeping guys fresh thing falls pretty flat, or even flatter than it has in the past.
Really, we should commend McDaniel for trying to be open, at least. Coach-speak is boring. But the comments here seem to fly in the face of what Harbaugh said about Hampton’s usage, too.
Overall? It’s just noise at this point. Spending on a first-round running back was a luxury pick the Chargers couldn't afford to make and now they’re debating how to use him during a 1-9 season. How they should be using him is obvious, and McDaniel seems to know it, but the Chargers as a whole seem more preoccupied with controlling outward messaging than actually doing things the right way.

title: Chargers Roster Move Hints at More Bad Justin Herbert Injury News
full_text:
The Justin Herbert injury situation for the Los Angeles Chargers isn’t getting any better.
We’ve already asked if the Chargers should just sit Herbert for the rest of the season . The Mike McDaniel-led offense is a mess. The offensive line and overall offense constructed by general manager Joe Hortiz is subpar. And Jim Harbaugh looks straight-up lost at the controls now.
It begs questioning whether anyone not named Herbert will even be back with the Chargers next season.
So, sitting Herbert seems like it would be on the table. But given some new roster moves for the Chargers over the holiday, the injury might be taking their decision out of their hands anyway.
Tucked into a handful of roster moves over the holiday, the Chargers announced that they have signed quarterback Jake Browning to the active roster.
That would seem to say it all about Herbert’s status for his team’s Week 12 game against the New England Patriots.
After all, primary backup Trey Lance is already on injured reserve. That puts DJ Uiagalelei in line to start against the Patriots, but the team didn’t have a backup to him ready if Herbert can’t even be active as an emergency backup.
So, against the Patriots, Herbert will likely sit. Uiagalelei, who has completed two of his seven attempts as a pro, should get the nod as a starter. Browning, suddenly off the practice squad and on the 53, hasn’t completed a pass since 2025.
McDaniel, the offensive coordinator, had this to say about Uiagalelei’s week of practice so far, according to Fredo Cervantes of The Sporting Tribune: “He’s done a great job in the day and a half of work we’ve had.”
Looking beyond Week 12, we’ll see if the Chargers even push Herbert to get all the way back for Week 13, either. That’s a road game at 1 p.m. ET timeslot against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
The bigger point is the status of the team around Herbert. He took six sacks in the loss against the New York Jets last week before entering concussion protocol after the game. He’s at 39, which was tops in the NFL. It’s a failure around him again, and nobody would blame anyone if the Chargers let Uiagalelei and Browning finish out this season.

title: Justin Herbert’s Disaster Season Overshadowing Another Major Chargers Problem
full_text:
It’s hard to keep track of all the problems surrounding the Los Angeles Chargers right now.
One could argue the top issue is the Justin Herbert injury . Others could argue that Jim Harbaugh looking and sounding lost at the podium about his own football team is top dog. There’s also that matter of Bud Dupree trying to force his way out of town , among many other issues.
Tack on a bad Mike McDaniel offense, a front office sitting on loads of cash while the roster crashes and burns and draft picks fizzling out, plus a failed deadline deal and so much more, just for the heck of it.
So, sure, Herbert’s injury is the top thing right now. But don’t overlook a big issue on defense that could impact the future in a big way.
Going into the season, first-year coordinator Chris O’Leary getting Khalil Mack, Tuli Tuipulotu and first-rounder Akheem Mesidor as the staple of his pressure-creating edge presence seemed great.
Tuipulotu has 34 pressures over 10 games this year, but he hasn’t followed through on his 13-sack campaign all that well. He’s registered just three sacks so far. Mesidor has 2.5 and Mack has three.
Sacks aren’t the only metric that matters, of course. But Mack and the rest probably shouldn’t be only just outdoing names like Troy Dye and Dalvin Tomlinson.
It creates big issues looking into the future. One has to wonder if Mack will want to come back at all to the NFL yet again, never mind whether he wants to take another chance on the Chargers. And that annual $18 million price tag might go up.
There’s the issue of Tuipulotu’s contract too. It sure seemed like he and the Chargers didn’t agree on his price last offseason when they had a chance to do a deal. Is he going to hit the open market and get a deal that resets the position? Or are we looking at a costly franchise tag situation or something else?
Don’t forget the overlooked factor with Mesidor: He was an “older” rookie who could be pushing 30 by the time his fifth-year option discussion comes up. He’s shown some flashes, but there are some concerns with the long-term, given his age. So goes the cost of trying to find a quick fix after simply refusing to pay a departing free agent like Odafe Oweh.
We could shrug and say this is a quick fix on the second day of next year’s draft. But there are so many deep issues on this roster that what was expected to be a strength simply can’t be this needy right now.
Instead, pressure-creating edge rushers are a top need, it seems, right next to quality offensive linemen, skill positions weapons who fit the offense (no matter who is on the coaching staff next year), defensive line depth, improved linebacker play, better cornerbacks and a refresh at safety.

title: Chargers Get Back Preseason Star: What Does This Mean for Donte Jackson and the DBs?
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers may be 1-9 and looking toward the offseason for a rebuild, but some positive news found its way to the mass media, giving Chargers fans a small boost of hope for the future.
Prior to the NFL season, the Chargers signed undrafted rookie cornerback Avery Smith out of Toledo . This was viewed as one of the best undrafted rookie signings across the league, with the hope that Smith would make the Bolts' roster.
As a prospect, Chargers draft expert Thomas Martinez described Smith as: "a well built defensive back but is on the shorter side at just over 5'10. He relies on instincts and route recognition to make plays on the ball and does an excellent job at preventing wide receivers from stacking him on deep routes. His tackling could use some technique improvement but he is unafraid and willing to get in the mix."
During the offseason and preseason, Smith was constantly being brought up as one of the flashy players who was making a real case to make the final 53-man roster. During the preseason, Smith recorded 15 tackles and a pass deflection, showing good downhill tackling ability and the competitive nature needed for playing defensive back, especially as an undersized player at the position.
With Smith trending to make the roster, the Chargers instead decided to hear out a phone call from the Seattle Seahawks, another team that had interest in the now proven-preseason standout for trade offers.
A trade went through , with the Seattle Seahawks giving the Chargers a 2027 sixth-round pick in exchange for Smith.
While Chargers fans were sad to see the standout star go, they were happy to see the team essentially get a sixth-round pick for free, since they did not draft or spend major cap space on the Toledo product.
A couple of short months later, the Chargers seem to have won the trade even more after recent events transpired.
Smith played six games with the Seahawks, recording five tackles and 56 special teams snaps. On Nov. 24, the team released Smith to make way for offensive tackle Chase Lundt . In one of the best moves the Chargers have made all season, the team saw their struggling and injured defensive back room and a former preseason standout who knows the system, and decided to sign Smith back to their roster.
Chargers claimed CB Avery Smith off waivers Wednesday, per the transaction wire. They had traded Smith to Seattle on cutdown day in August for a 2027 6th round draft pick. Seahawks waived him Tuesday.
With this addition, the Chargers essentially got a free sixth-round pick from the Seahawks. Joe Hortiz has not built a winning roster, but getting a sixth-round pick for free is a good addition to his resume.
With the addition of Smith, the Chargers depth chart will look to be:
CB1: Tarheeb Still CB2: Donte Jackson CB3: Cam Hart CB4: Deane Leonard CB5: Isas Waxter CB6: Avery Smith IR: Rodney Shelley
With Smith just coming back to the team, it should be expected for him to be relegated to special teams and reserve defensive roles, but in time, he could be promoted to as much as CB4, with the team obviously not loving what they have seen from Leonard and Waxter.
It should also be noted that Donte Jackson has been struggling mightily since his return from injury and if the team eventually fully commits to rebuilding, they could look to play the young DBs over a veteran on an expiring deal like Jackson.

title: 3 Things the Chargers Should be Thankful For This Thanksgiving
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 1-9; 2026 has been rough. Let's not pretend there is much for fans of the Chargers to be thankful for that is football-related this Thanksgiving, at least not in regards to the 2026 results.
The 2026 Chargers season has gone off the rails. All of the top players have been hurt at one point or another, the offensive line has been a constant game of musical chairs for the second season in a row and the offense has gone through multiple identity crises. But, the good news is, through the dark days of 2026, there have been several lighthearted moments and bits of news to find some thanks for Thanksgiving.
The Chargers' main connection to the fan base whether on social media platforms or content sources like YouTube is driven by one of if not the best social media team in the NFL. The time spent on schedule releases, fun videos and even post-game responses are fun and engaging.
To find a lighthearted moment, look no further than the announcement of Daiyan Henley's trade to the Broncos being followed up with the announcement the trade had been canceled. The reunion from the failed trade was going to be awkward for everyone and simply crossing out the "thank you" and handwriting "Welcome back" was a lighthearted twist from the social media team.
https://t.co/Ewbs7j6Yga pic.twitter.com/QzaZ40ZFF7
The Chargers may not be winning games but at least they still look good doing it. Despite the yellow uniforms still being around, at least when they debut later this season, the pants will be white instead of the full color rush style yellow.
ur favorite uniforms' favorite uniforms pic.twitter.com/O1QvxR0B3j
The silver lining with the terrible year on the field is that the Chargers will end up with a very high draft slot and pick high in every round in which they have their own picks. Going through a terrible season is not ideal but the top draft position does at least bring some level of hope for the future and the offseason ahead.
The Chargers are on track for a top three pick in the 2027 draft. Depending on where they ultimately pick, a draft slot that high can net a course-altering draft and in this upcoming class, all eyes will be on Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith.

title: Chargers' Joe Hortiz Pulls Off Savvy Move, Reacquiring Avery Smith
full_text:
Joe Hortiz brought Avery Smith back to the Chargers . This was a very smart decision , and it’s refreshing knowing Hortiz still can make the right moves.
Earlier in the season, the organization moved Smith and received a sixth-round draft pick. Now Smith is back, and the cost to reacquire him was no additional compensation. So essentially the Bolts got a free draft pick.
The original move brought a draft choice into the picture. A sixth-round selection may not sound like a major return, but every pick has value .
At the time, turning Smith into an extra selection gave the team another chance to add young talent.
The front office has recovered a player it knows while keeping the draft compensation it received earlier. The transaction gives the team a chance to benefit from both decisions , although the real value will depend on what Smith contributes.
I like the thinking behind this move because a roster decision does not always have to be permanent.
Teams make changes because of roster limits, immediate needs, player evaluations, and the value of draft picks. Circumstances can look different later. If a familiar player becomes available and still fits, bringing him back can be sensible.
There is no guarantee Smith will make a major impact. He still has to earn his place and turn this opportunity into production. The transaction itself does not promise playing time or success of course. Reacquiring him without spending another pick gives the coaching staff another option while protecting a future draft opportunity. That flexibility matters during a season. Injuries, performance, and changing roles can expose needs that were not obvious earlier. Another player can create competition and give the staff more choices when setting the lineup. Even if Smith’s role is limited, he could provide useful depth when it matters.
The next step belongs to Smith. He has a fresh chance to show he can help, while the team can evaluate whether the fit works this time. If he contributes, the organization may gain useful depth while holding on to the pick it collected earlier. If it does not work out, the team has not surrendered another selection to find out. That balance makes this reunion an interesting piece of roster management.
It is a reminder that roster building means recognizing when a previous decision can be revisited without paying twice for him again.

title: Chargers Still Hoping Quentin Johnston Shakes Bust Label is Another Big Problem in LA
full_text:
It took a series of big missteps and overall mismanagement to put the Los Angeles Chargers in their current hole.
The weird misalignment between a thrifty front office and a poor coaching staff is a big part of it.
Look at former first-round pick Quentin Johnston.
The Chargers took Johnston in the first round back in 2023 and drop issues have been the major defining thing about his tenure, even overshadowing the fact he scored eight touchdowns apiece in 2024 and 2025.
Despite this, the Chargers and general manager Joe Hortiz took the obvious “bargain” by picking up Johnston’s fifth-year option.
Now 1-9, the Chargers have 15 catches for 275 yards and one touchdown from Johnston.
Let Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh tell it, the offense just needs to get Johnston the ball more.
“We’ve got to get the ball to Quentin,” Harbaugh said . “I’d like to see the ball in Quentin’s hands. Blocked extremely well, but more targets, more opportunities, I think, would really help us. … You can’t force (targets) … but yeah, I’d like to see the ball in his hands more.”
It’s a pretty wild idea, considering Johnston has caught just 15 of his 32 targets. A Mike McDaniel offense that seems to need speedier options doesn’t really feel like it has a place for what Johnston brings to the table.
Making matters all the worse is that pesky fifth-year option. The Chargers are on the hook for a fully guaranteed $18 million salary next year. Nobody is walking through that door to trade for Johnston based on what he’s put on film.
So, looking ahead to 2027, what’s the play? Keep McDaniel and the bad fit? Start over with a coordinator who better fits a wideout who has caught 159 of 275 career targets from a quarterback like Justin Herbert? Let the $18 million player ride the bench?
The Chargers’ cheap front office isn’t helping. Johnston should be on an expiring contract right now, opening up their offseason options. It’s a problem that extends throughout the roster. They cheaped out on guards yet again and it shows. Not paying Odafe Oweh led to using a first-round pick on Akheem Mesidor when the answer was already on the roster. Don’t forget the “can’t-miss offer” for Daiyan Henley at the trade deadline to a rival after proclaiming they wouldn’t trade anyone, then failing that trade anyway.
Four seasons in now, Johnston’s time with the Chargers is pretty much up. Except, of course, for that pesky front office that values good deals more over actual production and winning. Until that front office proves otherwise, anyway.

title: Omarion Hampton is Perfect Example of Everything Wrong With Chargers
full_text:
Los Angeles Chargers running back Omarion Hampton is a fantastic football player.
The problem is, he plays for the Chargers.
Amid the 1-9 disaster, the Chargers boast emerging players to watch . Yet somehow, Hampton isn’t one of them, not really, because of a coaching and organizational approach that borders on malpractice.
Look right at the top with the listless Jim Harbaugh , who had some pretty shocking quotes about Hampton this week.
“Yeah, in hindsight, we should have done that sooner,” Harbaugh said . “I’m glad we’re doing it now, glad he’s certainly responded like the really good player that he is.”
Harbaugh was talking about making Hampton the workhorse back. He rushed for 105 yards and a score on 22 carries in a Week 10 win over Baltimore. He averaged 6.4 yards per carry on 14 chances in the loss to the New York Jets last week.
Before those games? Hampton was lost in a three-back rotation and he played fewer snaps than Kimani Vidal and Keaton Mitchell in weeks 4, 5 and 8. They went 0-8 over that span and are only just figuring out that Hampton might be the key.
How the heck did the Chargers get here?
Start back in 2025, when the Chargers decided that a running back was a good value in the first round at No. 22 overall. A wild decision, given the value debate around taking that position so early. And that’s to say nothing of the many premium spots on the offensive line, at wideout or across the defense they could have filled instead.
Hampton then struggled as a rookie at times due to injuries. He ended his rookie year with 124 carries, 545 yards and four scores on a 4.4 average over nine games. But the vision and obvious first-round stuff were there. The future was bright.
Then arrived Mike McDaniel this year and his weird insistence on running three-back looks. Keeping everyone fresh for the entire season is a nice idea, but when the record hits 0-5 or 0-6, maybe it’s time to step back and admit that making Hampton the workhorse everyone knows he can be might be the only way to pick up some wins.
That’s to say nothing of Joe Hortiz’s mediocre roster building. They knew the guard positions were an issue and signed an obvious dud in Cole Strange and had five guys competing for the other guard spot, including a second-round center Jake Slaughter asked to learn a new position in the pros.
It’s really just Chargering the whole thing. It was questionable to draft Hampton at all, they then failed to build the trenches in front of him properly, brought in a “good” coordinator who decided not to use him and are only just realizing near December that maybe the first-round running back should be playing more.
It would be funny if it weren’t so predictable and bordering on malpractice, really. Now, they’ll use Hampton as a workhorse in meaningless games, risk injury and top draft slotting the rest of the way, too.

title: Don’t Overlook These 3 Chargers Emerging Through Jets Loss
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 1-9 and coming off a loss at home to the New York Jets. The loss significantly moved the Chargers towards locking down a top-three pick in the 2027 draft but several players stood out in their efforts.
The Chargers are finally starting to get some consistency and players have carved out roles amidst injuries and the volatility associated with a 1-9 season. The Chargers will face significant questions heading into 2027 regarding roster construction and depth. Let's discuss three players who played or have been playing well enough to enter into 2027 considerations.
The Chargers have been featuring a heavy rotation of three edge rushers throughout most of the season with a fourth occasionally joining the mix. Veteran Bud Dupree has not played a snap on defense since week five with Caleb Murphy, now back with the Chargers for his second stint, taking over the role behind Khalil Mack, Tuli Tuipulotu and rookie Akheem Mesidor.
Murphy's role has slowly grown over the past few weeks and he had a monster sack negated by a penalty Sunday against the Jets. The play that was called back featured Murphy bull rushing the left tackle Olu Fashanu into Jets quarterback Geno Smith and Murphy reached through Fashanu to ensnare Smith and drag him to the ground along with the blocker.
Khalil Mack may not be back in 2027, and the Chargers and Tuli Tuipulotu have yet to come to terms on an extension leaving the edge rusher room thin heading into the offseason. Murphy, since returning to the Chargers, has shown significant development as an edge rusher as both a pass rusher and run defender. Paired with his effective play on special teams he should at the very least be considered a lock to be edge number four heading into next year.
Logan Taylor earned the starting left guard role, head coach Jim Harbaugh confirmed it during the week leading up to the Jets game. Taylor still has plenty of rookie wrinkles to smooth out but he has improved every week in the starting lineup. Taylor's ascension makes the rotation at left guard throughout training camp all the more confusing and frustrating in how that process played out only for it to naturally get figured out months later.
If Taylor can continue developing and head to the offseason with a solid foundation in the NFL, a full offseason of position-focused training, as opposed to combine preparation, should set him up to challenge for the starting job going forward.
Cole Strange: Unnecessary roughness Kayode Awosika: Very acceptable and necessary roughness pic.twitter.com/vUjTDZ9ovx
The Chargers signed Kayode Awosika this past offseason as a low-cost veteran guard to potentially compete for playing time in the reworked offensive line. He became the frontrunner for the starting left guard job almost instantly and despite the frustrating efforts of the coaching staff with questionable rotations, Awosika eventually won the starting job but was hurt with what was described as a fibula injury in week two against the Raiders, his only unopposed start before this past Sunday against the Jets.
Awosika was finally off the injury report following the Chargers victory over the Ravens and the Chargers plugged him into the starting lineup over Cole Strange who has been struggling. Inserting Awosika into the starting lineup immediately raised the floor of the unit and Awosika's physical presence helped rookie center Jake Slaughter and rookie tackle Travis Burke.
The Chargers will need to address their interior offensive line in the offseason and search for upgrades, but Awosika's presence should be strongly considered as an option to return to compete if he can stay healthy and keep performing down the stretch. The free agent guard class in 2027 may be light again and as history has shown, the Chargers need capable depth.

title: Justin Herbert Injury Updates: Latest on Chargers QB for Week 12 vs. Patriots
full_text:
Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert has a new injury to manage , this time ahead of his team’s Week 12 game against the New England Patriots.
After dealing with a finger issue in prior weeks, Herbert is now in concussion protocol.
Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh told reporters early this week that Herbert “reported symptoms to the trainers and the doctors” after the loss to the New York Jets.
Here’s a look at Herbert injury updates before the Chargers play the Patriots in Week 12.
This story will be updated with more information as it becomes available .
At 1-9, the Chargers don’t have much hope without Herbert on the field. Primary backup Trey Lance is on injured reserve with an issue of his own.
Harbaugh provided a course of action if Herbert needs to miss Week 12: "Uiagalelei would be the next man up, and then we would bring Jake Browning up as well," Harbaugh said.
That’s DJ Uiagalelei, who has attempted seven passes this year, his only regular-season reps since entering the league. The Chargers also have Jake Browning on the practice squad, a journeyman backup who hasn’t attempted a regular-season pass since 2025.
At this point it should go without saying, but the Chargers and Mike McDaniel are a fantasy football disaster no matter who is out there. Herbert has completed 62.4 percent of his passes with eight touchdowns and 11 interceptions. His leading receiver has just 28 catches (Tre Harris) and lead back Omarion Hampton only just crept past the four-yards-per-carry mark on the season behind an offensive line battling various injuries.
With how things have gone, it’s now worth questioning whether the Chargers simply shut Herbert down for the season. But they certainly won’t rush him out there against the Patriots.
