title: Raiders Players Reveal What They’re Thankful for This Thanksgiving
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-7) will take on the Cleveland Browns (6-4), and ahead of that trip, we celebrate the glorious American holiday of Thanksgiving.
The Raiders have plenty of reasons to be thankful as an iconic franchise, without a doubt. This team is loaded with terrific young men who value the important things in life, and they aren’t afraid to talk about that, and of course the food.
DT Adam Butler told me in the locker room, “For family. I am thankful for family, this Raiders family, and life in general.” Does he have a go-to food on this day? Of course he does; he’s a lineman. “Turkey wings. Sounds typical, but the way we do it in the South, when I tell you the way it falls off the bone is good.”
Delmar “DJ” Glaze, The Mule, was straight to the point: “First, I am most grateful for God. My Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and my family. For getting to not just play here in Las Vegas for this organization, everyone. It has been the season we wanted so far.”
So I asked the big fella what his go-to food is on Thanksgiving. “Turkey, but it’s my parents’ turkey cooked in an infrared fryer, real crispy on the outside and juicy on the inside, and of course my mom’s mac-n-cheese.” Can you have Thanksgiving without mac-n-cheese? Wouldn’t that be almost un-American on this quintessential American holiday? “Of course, for real, man.”
DT Thomas Booker is an amazing young man who has a lot to be thankful for. “My family and support system. From my teammates to my coaches, to my immediate family. “So what is his go-to food? “It has to be stuffing. It is a combo: stuffing, mac-n-cheese, cornbread, and I have to have ham.”
Connor Heyward, the Raiders fullback, and I have known each other since 2016, and we have discussed this holiday many times. He loves it. He told me again from the Raiders locker room for this article, “It means everything to me to be able to spend that time with my family and close family. Thanksgiving, holidays, those are the best moments of my life, everyone's life. When I get back out there (to his family), we will have a feast. So glad I got my teammates and family here to spend the day with!”
Mac-n-cheese, some stuffing, and mashed potatoes and gravy.” Now I am a strictly fake potatoes guy, and finally my fellow Michigan State Spartan and I found something we disagree on. “Oh now, they have to be real.” Despite this obvious flaw, I assure you that Heyward is a great young man.
TE Ian Thomas, a proud Indiana Hoosier, said, “I am thankful for everything. First, God, and that really opens your eyes to the small things; then I start thanking him for the big things—friends, family, and the things we take for granted. Thanksgiving is a time you think about all the things that God has allowed you to do. Appreciation means so much to me, and this time reflects it, and then it just takes you into the holidays.”
Then he shocked me. When I asked him his go-to food, he said, “Deviled eggs.” What?
When Thomas saw my shocked look, he asked what my go-to was. I explained my grandmother’s homemade stuffing with walnuts.
His shock at that echoed my shock at deviled eggs, to which he jokingly exclaimed, “That’s white guy. As soon as you say walnuts, which is white guy.” He then added, “I could just eat deviled eggs along for Thanksgiving.”
When Connor Heyward heard Thomas’s comments on deviled eggs, he jumped into the conversation to say, “One thing, everything on the plate has to be touching, all of it. Just mixed in.”
For the record, in nearly thirty years of doing this almost every year, no player has ever said deviled eggs like Thomas.
The pride of the Ohio State Buckeyes, Tommy “Freaking” Eichenberg, may not be the most loquacious, but he said, “It means family, and football.” Which is a great thing, but his one food may be suspect: “It is a casserole of some sort, has pecans on top.”
Dareke Young heard Eichenberg and said, “That is a bad answer. So what is Young’s go-to? It won’t surprise anyone: “Mac-n-cheese, and yams.”
The Raiders have the best punter in the NFL, and AJ Cole knows exactly what he wants on Thanksgiving. “Got to be cranberry sauce. Turkey is too dry, and I can’t eat it without cranberry sauce.”
Fernando Mendoza knows what this holiday means to him. He has a lot to be thankful for, and he was warm and open to share it. “Thanksgiving is a season, not just a day of thanksgiving. Thankful for my family, my teammates, the beautiful Raiders organization for giving me this opportunity, and I can’t thank Jesus Christ enough for all that he has done for me.”
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: 3 Biggest Reasons Raider Nation Has Plenty to Be Thankful For
full_text:
LAS VEGAS, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-7) are headed for the cold wind and gorgeous view of Lake Erie this weekend, and ahead of that trip, today we celebrate the glorious American holiday of Thanksgiving.
A day set aside to reflect and ponder all that we have to be thankful for.
Around the world, the reputation of the Silver and Black legacy is firmly rooted in the iconic foundation laid down by the legendary American Al Davis: the "Commitment to Excellence" and "Just Win, Baby" ethos, delivered across three Super Bowl championships and a roster full of Hall of Famers.
Today, the amazing fan base (Raider Nation) holds on to those long-ago roots that established football's ultimate outlaw identity—a gritty, rebellious brand wrapped like a Christmas present in silver and black.  The first professional franchise to embrace misfits with open arms, shatter racial barriers with historic coaching hires, and remain globally recognizable from Oakland and Los Angeles to Las Vegas.
But while I am neither advocating nor suggesting they should shed, or shy away from that, after over twenty years of mediocrity, this historic franchise is back on course, a true reason for celebration on this Thanksgiving holiday.
This franchise, and the present Raiders rebuild , has a litany of things to be thankful for, but today, we will look at the four biggest, in my opinion, and what stands out.
For all that Al did in establishing this franchise, Mark is a far superior businessman, and he has taken what his father did and, with superior business acumen, set up the future with the best stadium and facilities in the NFL.
Mark is not a sterile owner who sees the franchise as a cash cow; he is emotionally invested, and in my opinion, the only owner in the NFL who identifies more as a fan, the Raider Nation, than the billionaire owners, with whom he shares the commonality of wealth.
Who knows if he will ever hoist a Lombardi Trophy in Las Vegas, but as someone who respects him and holds him in high regard, I can tell you the fire to win burns no brighter inside him than anyone else's.
While both men are vastly different, Al established it, but Mark has laid the foundation for the future, with the love for an organization that allows him to make decisions and embrace what he knows and doesn’t.  That is character.
The brilliant young coach, Klint Kubiak , leads the Raiders locker room with a genuine love of his players and for the game; the Raiders have found a perfect mix of football acumen and passion.  What makes Kubiak who he is is that while he loves the game, both its strategy and preparation, he stays centered.  Football is his profession, but it isn’t who Kubiak is.
He is honest, a man of faith and integrity, and he has seized the locker room with his blunt honesty and compassion for people.  Kubiak is a rarity.
Let’s be honest, the odds are against him being successful, but in this town, a town built on those who ignore the long shots and win.  I believe in Kubiak, and if I were a betting man, I would go all in on him.
Kubiak is the real deal, and the Raiders organization, after years of trying to solve the coaching carousel, have their guy.
The Silver and Black have finally got their franchise QB, Fernando Mendoza .  A young man who, as I have gotten to know him, intrigues me like Kubiak.
Similar to his head coach, the young man loves football, but it isn’t what defines him.  He loves the nuances, the minutiae of football, the learning, the preparation, and the game.
The odds, like Kubiak's, are against him succeeding; that is the life of the NFL, where anyone’s success is a long shot.  But if you have to pick someone to bet on, he is your kid.
The Raiders have a young franchise QB, with the next 15 years ahead of him, and he is rooted, caring, and appreciative to be part of this organization.
Mendoza is the real deal, as a player and a person, and Raider Nation is fortunate to have such a bright spot as the face of your franchise, the future, and the work ethic to keep leading and improving on the field.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Raiders First Injury Report Presents Interesting Outlook on Brock Bowers
full_text:
Despite losing both games, the Las Vegas Raiders have made progress in several areas on both sides of the ball. It hasn't been pretty, but compared to their 3-14 campaign in 2025, Las Vegas has undeniably taken strides in the right direction. Those strides have come at a cost.
After a grueling stretch against some of the league's best teams, Las Vegas is a week away from its Bye Week, which falls on the latest possible week that league rules allow Bye Weeks to be scheduled. Las Vegas heads into its Week 12 road matchup against the Cleveland Browns, nursing multiple injuries.
The Raiders' Week 11 loss to the Denver Broncos gave the world a peek into the future of a young and talented team that is still thin at several critical positions. Las Vegas' offseason moves have helped significantly, but unexpected losses have begun to chip away at a rebuilding roster.
Las Vegas fell behind on the road early in Week 11, as Fernando Mendoza and the offense found their footing. After crawling back from a 17-point deficit shortly before halftime, the Raiders' roster and inexperience eventually gave way to a deeper, more established Broncos team.
The Raiders and Broncos have another date soon, but for now, Las Vegas has turned its attention to a Browns team that is in the thick of the playoff race. After originally receiving zero primetime games this season, Sunday's slate against the Browns was flexed to Sunday Night Football.
Las Vegas has analyzed its Week 11 loss and begun working on the many improvements they quickly need to make. However, their roster may be the most significant concern ahead of their second straight road game.
Many of the same players who have been listed on the injury report in recent weeks were listed on the first injury report of Week 12. Las Vegas sustained several injuries along an interior defensive line that entered Week 11 thin, with Tonka Hemingway on the mend.
Hemingway and Brock Bowers were limited participants on Wednesday. Klint Kubiak said he is optimistic Bowers will play on Sunday. This would be a huge swing for the Raiders' offense.
Defensive linemen Tim Keenan and Adam Butler didn't practice on Wednesday. Patrick Johnson fully practiced on Wednesday. The Raiders could use contributions from all three.
Michael Mayer, JJ Pegues, and Dareke Young were also all listed on Wednesday's report as full participants.
Bowers' return cannot be overstated, as Las Vegas' offense found a spark in Week 11 without him. It will be interesting to see if they can have even more success with Bowers on the field and Mendoza with more than one start . He is a massive part of the offense.
However, the fourth quarter of Week 11 also confirmed the importance of Las Vegas finding answers along its interior defensive line. The Raiders lost multiple interior defensive linemen against the Broncos, adding to the importance of Hemingway's return.
The second half of Week 11 witnessed the Raiders' interior defensive line eventually give way to the Broncos' ground game. The injuries they sustained along the unit quietly changed the momentum of the game. As the Raiders lost defensive linemen, the Broncos were more successful on the ground.
The interior defensive line has gone from one of Las Vegas' deepest positions to one of its thinnest, in a matter of weeks. As the Raiders progress through the season's final six games, they will need a stroke of luck on the injury front. Kubiak explained how the Raiders plan to address the position.
"Well, we got guys on the practice squad that are going to have to step up. We're going to have to take a look outside and probably bring some guys in, but that's where we're at right now. So, we got to make sure that the guys that are coming in from the practice squad are ready to roll," Kubiak said earlier this week.
Las Vegas will face another challenge this Sunday night against a stout Browns team. It will be yet another tough road game for the Raiders' ailing roster. However, Week 11 proved that these Raiders cannot be counted out, even if they are down by 17 without their best offensive weapon.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Rookie, Sophomore Power Rankings: What Stands Out
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered the season planning to spark their rebuild by depending upon several of their young players to play pivotal roles this season. As the season has progressed, even more young players have been forced into action, as Las Vegas searches for the right mix of players.
“We have a roster of a lot of young guys, and it's our job as coaches to develop them and make sure they're a huge part of our future,"  Klint Kubiak said on Monday.
“The expectation is for these young guys to play and these young guys to contribute. Those guys definitely have stepped up really all season. Fernando [Mendoza] is making his second start, but we have a roster of a lot of young guys, and it's our job as coaches to develop them and make sure they're a huge part of our future."
After 11 games, Las Vegas is all in on its group of young contributors . Below are our power rankings for the Raiders' rookies and second-year players who impacted Week 11.
Mendoza played well in the first road start of his career. The pick-six was unfortunate, but several other things could have been done better by others around the rookie. Overall, the Raiders are likely not competitive in that game without Mendoza under center.
The rookie made several plays that simply would not have been made earlier in the season. Tough completions and timely runs have opened up the Raiders' offense. It will be interesting to see how Mendoza does over the final six games, especially if Las Vegas keeps running the ball well.
Jeanty finished Week 11 as the team's leading rusher and its leading receiver. He still leads all running backs in receiving yards this season. Once the Raiders improve the roster further, performances like that from Jeanty will lead to wins.
Regardless, outings like the one he had on Sunday are why Las Vegas' front office was comfortable using the No. 6 overall pick on the running back. Now, they need more games like that from Jeanty.
Las Vegas has needed Bech to step up for some time, but injuries kept the second-year player out for weeks. The Raiders' receivers have had their ups and downs this season, especially without Brock Bowers, but on Sunday, the unit stepped up, largely behind Bech's solid contribution.
Bech caught eight of his nine targets for 88 yards, leading Las Vegas' receivers in yards on Sunday. Kubiak explained the connection Bech has already formed with Mendoza in just two starts with the rookie quarterback.
“Well, I think a quarterback and receiver relationship builds when there's adverse times and the guys are making plays. So, those plays that Jack [Bech] made last night, those are things that he's done in practice with Fernando [Mendoza]. He has the trust of the quarterback,” Kubiak said.
Las Vegas' coaching staff to its time with McCoy, gradually bringing the rookie along as he recovered from a significant injury before entering the league. After shuffling through other young corners, the Raiders were forced to lean on McCoy more heavily in Week 11, and he responded well.
McCoy did dodge a major bullet that could have swung the game. However, even on that play, things worked as they should, as Las Vegas' pass rush helped force a throw that was just off target enough.
It has only been a few games, but the Raiders have run the ball better since Zuhn became a starter. He isn't the sole reason for the improvement, but he is the only change the Raiders have made along the starting lineup in recent weeks.
If Zuhn keeps developing, that would be huge for Las Vegas' offseason plans and their future. The Raiders' front office will likely thoroughly address the offensive line this summer. Zuhn's ascension could mean the Raiders need one less offensive guard.
Stukes remains a pivotal player in Las Vegas' defensive backfield. The rookie shows progress with each game and seems to make fewer mistakes by the week. The final six games will be critical for Stukes ahead of what will be an even more vital second offseason in the league.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Raiders' Week 11 Performance Confirmed Areas of Improvement
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 11 outing against the Denver Broncos will go down as a loss, but it featured many of the positives the Raiders hope will one day become mainstays of Klint Kubiak's tenure. The Raiders have lost three in a row, but gained valuable experience at the same time.
That experience has come with its bumps in the road, as the Raiders have struggled for weeks in several areas, on both sides of the ball. Yet, the past two losses have felt like building blocks for the future. Las Vegas is a rebuilding team facing many of the league's best teams in consecutive weeks.
The overall results have been about as expected, as Las Vegas' roster is still a work in progress. That unfinished product has given two of the league's more polished teams competitive games with a rookie quarterback.
Rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza started his first career road game in Week 11. The Raiders' supporting cast stepped up. Las Vegas' ground game exploded for its best outing of the season and, technically, one of its best games on the ground in the past two seasons.
Las Vegas entered Week 11 with the second-fewest rushing yards in the league, but ran for 143 yards against the Broncos. It was the most rushing yards they have had in a game this season. It came against one of the best teams in the league, and without Brock Bowers on the field.
Las Vegas' Week 11 success on the ground was a surprise, to say the least. That success helped the Raiders' offense get going after weeks of struggles. Klint Kubiak shared his thoughts on Las Vegas' improved ground game.
"I just think over the season, as it's gone on, our guys are getting more familiar and comfortable with the scheme, and the more time on task that you have, you anticipate improvement, and it was a step in the right direction,” Kubiak said on Monday.
“Obviously, you get to shorter third downs. In the fourth quarter is when you normally get bigger runs. So, when you're able to run the ball in the fourth quarter, that has a big effect on the outcome of the game. It helps the defense. It helps the whole organization when you're running the football well."
Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty ran for 79 yards on 11 carries. Mike Washington added 42 yards on nine carries, and Mendoza added another 22 yards on the ground. Kubiak noted how the running backs' success, combined with the threat of Mendoza running the ball, helped open things up.
“I think plays like that are successful when there's the threat of the run. Then on third-and-two, when there's a threat of the run, that's when you can get the edge like that. Play fake or no play fake, early in the game when you're running the football, that's when those play actions and those keepers really come to life. But you got to be able to run the ball first," Kubiak said.
Las Vegas needs much more than one good game on the ground to confirm they have figured out their issues. However, for a team that has struggled to run the ball for as long as the Raiders have, Sunday's outing could be the turning point for the long-standing issue that has plagued Las Vegas.
Las Vegas finished with the fewest rushing yards in the league in two of the past three seasons. In the third of those three seasons, they finished with the third-fewest rushing yards in the league. Along with their issues at quarterback and elsewhere, finding a consistent ground game has been elusive.
Las Vegas has one of the toughest schedules in the league this season, but has made it through the hardest part of the schedule. The remaining six games give the Raiders a chance to make the most of the struggles they've had this season in an attempt to end the season on a high note.
The Raiders have a manageable final quarter of the season. The past two weeks have solidified that they are headed in the right direction . The next six weeks may give an idea of how soon they can realistically reach their destination.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How the Dolphins List of 2027 Opponents Is Rapidly Coming Together ... And Is Thanksgiving Back on the Table?
full_text:
With one of the big questions surrounding the Miami Dolphins about exactly how high they'll pick in the 2027 draft, it's almost being taken for granted they will finish with one of the worst records in the NFL this season and that would include being last in the AFC East.
It sure looks like that's the way things are headed with the Dolphins standing at 1-9, tied for the Tennessee Titans and L.A. Chargers for worst record and two games behind every other team in the league.
With their starting quarterback and top three defensive tackles on injured reserve, it's not an insult to make that assumption, just as the same applies for the Titans in the AFC South and the Chargers in the AFC West.
In fact, based on how the standings look right now, we have a very good idea of what the Dolphins' 2027 schedule will look like in terms of their opponents because it's predetermined on the basis of rotation and the previous year's division standings.
The Dolphins will face in 2027 the entire AFC South and the entire NFC East, with home games against the Houston Texans, Indianapolis Colts, Philadelphia Eagles and Washington Commanders, and road games against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Tennessee Titans, Dallas Cowboys and New York Giants.
In addition, the Dolphins will play host to the team that finishes in the same place in their division standings in the AFC North and NFC South (the 17th game) and will go on the road against the same-place finisher in the AFC West.
At this time, the Chargers look like front-runners to finish last in the AFC West, which would mean a trip to SoFi Stadium and the AFC North last-place team at the moment is the Baltimore Ravens, who trail Cleveland and Pittsburgh by two games and continue to operate without star quarterback Lamar Jackson.
The NFC South final standings very possibly won't be determined until the final week of the season considering Atlanta, New Orleans and Tampa Bay currently all are tied for second at 3-7, two games behind division leader Carolina.
If you were paying attention, you would have noticed the trip to face the Cowboys next season, which immediately opens the possibility of playing on Thanksgiving. Sure, the recently added Thanksgiving night game provides another option to be selected without a road game against Detroit or Dallas, but those slots are reserved for teams usually coming off a strong season — and that obviously doesn't apply to the Dolphins like it did in 2024 when Miami was selected to play at Green Bay for the Turkey Day night game.
The Dolphins have been regulars on Thanksgiving, including five previous games at Dallas. Those games took place in 1973, 1993, 1999, 2003 and most recently in 2011. Miami is 3-2 in those games, winning in 1973 (14-7), 1993 (16-14) and 2003 (40-21).
Overall, Miami is 5-3 on Thanksgiving.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Poup's Perspective: What the Dolphins (and I) Should Be Thankful For
full_text:
It's Thanksgiving Day, so of course we have to go the obligatory column regarding anything, everything, anybody for whom we're thankful.
It's not just tradition, it's basically a law for every journalist.
And who am I to ignore this obligation?
So here it is, separated into three parts, first the things for which I think the Miami Dolphins should be thankful, second the things for which I think the team's fans should be grateful, and lastly my own personal list (if you'll indulge me).
It's obvious a painful season for the organization, but it's not been a total waste, certainly not like, say, the 2004 or 2007 seasons that seemed like an ending point because this one feels like the start of something.
-- The Dolphins should be thankful that by all appearances they seemed to have nailed the two key hirings of the offseason, that of GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and head coach Jeff Hafley. The jury hasn't returned the verdict yet, but the early signs absolutely are encouraging.
-- The Dolphins should be thankful that they appear to have landed some foundational pieces among the NFL-high 13-member draft class, with that list right now consisting of Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez and Caleb Douglas. Landing four multi-year starters alone would make it an all-time draft class for the Dolphins.
-- The Dolphins should be thankful that Chop Robinson emerged in his third season as a bona fide impact player as defensive end/edge after a really disappointing 2025 performance.
-- The Dolphins should be thankful about Ollie Gordon II's emergence after De'Von Achane went down with his knee injury because they can go into the offseason confident about having a good 1-2 tandem at running back.
Well, we should start here with everything the team should be thankful for because if it's good for the team, then it's good for the fans as well.
-- Dolphins fans should be thankful there aren't that many games left in the 2026 season because it's no fun watching the team lose week after week.
-- Dolphins fans should be thankful for the knowledge that spending to get the team back to contender status won't be an issue because it's never been under owner Stephen Ross — say what you want about his tenure as owner, but he never could be accused on being cheap.
-- Dolphins fans should be thankful that the team will have one of the top picks in the 2027 draft because it's likely (hopefully) to bring an exciting new player.
I close with my own personal list, which is more about covering the team than the team itself.
-- First and foremost, I'm thankful that I've been able cover the NFL for my career, after I first had visions of working in the sports field as a kid. My mother often joked with me about me "doing play-by-play" into those very old (antique, really) recorders when I was young. I have been covering the Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 and that picture of the top of this column shows me accepting a prize from the legendary Don Shula at the annual golf/tennis tournament the team used to hold every summer.
-- I'm thankful I've been able to add podcasting over the past few years to my writing work because the different platform offers a unique and different way to dissect the Dolphins.
-- I'm thankful that the NFL — to an extent greater than other sports — offers the possibility that the Dolphins could become contenders within a couple of years, whereas a rebuilding project like the one they've undertaken would take longer in other sports.
-- I'm thankful for all the Miami Dolphins On SI readers and all the viewers and subscribers of the All Dolphins Podcast and the Dolphins Collective, and especially thankful to a solid group of fans with whom I've developed a great rapport. You guys know who you are, but I do want to give a shout-out — and preface with apologies to anybody I forget — to good folks like Noel, Craig, Dana, Dave, Mike, Toby, Bret, Steve, Marcus, Lu, Ashley, Jason, Kevin, Jonathan and more.
-- I'm thankful for my Dolphins beat peers, which I would describe as a talented and good group of folks.
-- Lastly, and most importantly, I'm thankful for my wonderful wife and children, family and friends.
-- Happy Thanksgiving everyone!

title: Brents, Jackson Highlight First Dolphins Week 12 Injury Report
full_text:
Three players on the Miami Dolphins active roster missed their first practice ahead of their Week 12 game against the New York Jets, but it was a limited participant who stood out on the list.
That would be right tackle Austin Jackson, who was a limited participant as he nurses elbow and knee injuries. This, of course, is significant in a week where Jackson's job security was called into question, though head coach Jeff Hafley said before practice Wednesday that Jackson would remain in the starting lineup if he's healthy enough to play Sunday at Hard Rock Stadium.
The three players who did not practice included starting cornerback JuJu Brents, who is dealing with neck and shoulder issues. If he can't play, his place in the starting lineup logically would be taken by Jason Marshall Jr., with Darrell Baker Jr. likely to get more snaps in that event.
Also not practicing Wednesday were punter Bradley Pinion (right groin) and wide receiver Jared Wayne (quad), who both missed the 26-9 loss against the Buffalo Bills because of their injuries — Wayne actually has missed the past two games.
Pinion looks like he'll be out another game considering the Dolphins signed Jack Browning to the active roster before practice Wednesday.
Linebacker Ronnie Harrison Jr. practiced Wednesday for the first time the week of the season opener. He was listed as questionable with the hamstring injury that's kept him on IR since early September.
Safety Dante Trader Jr. was back at practice after missing the Buffalo game with shoulder and groin issues, though he was a limited participant.
The other two players who were limited participants Wednesday were edge Rodney McGraw (shoulder) and linebacker Jackson Woodard (hand).
Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez is nursing a knee injury and was on the injury report, though he was a full participant in practice Wednesday.
The Dolphins will not practice on Thanksgiving, therefore their Thursday injury report will be based on an estimation of the players' status had there been a practice.
The Jets' injury report featured seven players, including two who didn't practice.
One was rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr., who is dealing with ankle and groin injuries and missed the Jets' 27-24 victory against the Los Angeles Chargers last Sunday. Cooper burned the Dolphins for five catches for 115 yards and a touchdown in the Miami-Jets game at MetLife Stadium in October.
The other was starting defensive lineman Harrison Phillips, who is dealing with an ankle injury but had a sack against the Chargers.
A significant development for the Jets had defensive tackle T'Vondre Sweat returning to practice for the first time since sustaining a knee injury against the Dolphins in Week 7. Sweat, who is eligible to be activated for the game Sunday, was a full participant in practice Wednesday.
Sweat was injured late in the first half in the first meeting.

title: Should Anderson Stay in the Starting Lineup? And Other Players We Want to See
full_text:
Zayne Anderson's remarkable stat line in the Miami Dolphins' Week 11 game was all the more remarkable considering it came after he had played a grand total of 18 defensive snaps the previous five games.
The question now is what that performance could do for Anderson's status with the defense.
Back in the starting lineup because of the injury to Dante Trader Jr., Anderson became the NFL first defensive back since at least 2000 to finish a game with at least 11 tackles, one sack, one interception and three passes defensed.
This was quite remarkable in and of itself, but even more so when you consider the reason Anderson played so little on defense since the beginning of the season was his performance simply wasn't up to par.
So the question is whether his work against Buffalo was an outlier or a sign of more good things to come.
And that's not insignificant considering Anderson, like so many of the offseason free agent pick-ups, signed a one-year contract when he joined the Dolphins.
Now, we're not suggesting that Anderson suddenly is an All-Pro-caliber safety just because he filled the stat sheet against the Bills, but it certainly was a step toward getting himself an extension in Miami.
And in the short term, logic says he should earn him more snaps on defense even if Trader can return to action against the Jets because Trader's performance hasn't necessarily been top notch either.
Beyond Anderson, there are some other young players who we feel should be getting more snaps on offense or defense as we head into the final seven games of the regular season.
RB Kaytron Allen — Allen did some get work, albeit very limited, at running back against the Colts in Week 10, but it says here maybe the Dolphins should give him the backup carries because it's just not happening for Jaylen Wright and it would be nice to see what Allen can do.
TE Justin Joly — The Dolphins claimed him off waivers from the Denver Broncos as a rookie fifth-round pick based mostly on his receiving ability, and the Dolphins could use that at tight end. Now, with Joly and everybody else, we should mention that usually there's a good reason coaches aren't using certain players, whether it be knowledge of the offense or being fundamentally sound enough, so we get it if certain lineup decisions are being made.
TE Will Kacmarek — The rookie third-round pick is playing 38.1 percent of the offensive snaps, which is the exact same percentage as rookie free agent fullback DJ Herman, and quite frankly we'd like to see Kacmarek a bit more involved.
CB Darrell Baker Jr. — Baker definitely was noticeable in his limited action on defense against Buffalo in his Dolphins debut and has earned more playing time from where we sit.

title: Examining the New Complication on the Dolphins Offensive Line
full_text:
Kadyn Proctor will not be moving to right tackle this week for the Miami Dolphins this week, and that might not happen at all this season.
But there still is a question about the status of Austin Jackson, not so much in terms of keeping his starting job but rather an injury issue that has popped up.
Head coach Jeff Hafley indicated before practice Wednesday that Jackson would be limited in practice on this day, though he didn't disclose the nature of his injury.
Hafley did add that Jackson would be at his spot at right tackle barring an injury forcing him out of the game against the New York Jets at Hard Rock Stadium on Sunday.
Jackson played every snap in the 26-9 loss against the Buffalo Bills on Sunday and it's unclear when or how he got injured, but if he ended up being physically compromised for the Jets game, it could give Hafley the opportunity to look at somebody else at right tackle without having to bench Jackson.
Since Hafley made it clear Proctor isn't an option at right tackle right now, the other logical choices if not Jackson would be Chukwuebuka Godrick or Caedan Wallace.
Godrick started three games for the Kansas City Chiefs last season; Wallace has two career starts on his resume, both in 2024 with the New England Patriots but one came at left tackle and the other was as a sixth offensive lineman.
Whoever plays right tackle will face the difficult task of trying to contain rookie pass rusher David Bailey, the second overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft who is tied for third in the NFL with 9.5 sacks.
The Dolphins held Bailey in check in the teams' first meeting in Week 7 as part of their best offensive performance of the season, with Bailey finishing with half a sack and four tackles in 61 snaps.
While there's now a little bit of mystery at right tackle because of Jackson's injury, the Proctor topic appears closed.
And it appears Hafley doesn't care to revisit it.
When he was asked about Proctor and practice time at right tackle, Hafley kind of shut down the discussion by saying, "I respect the question, guys. I'm not going to sit up here and talk about what could happen in hypotheticals. If we get to that, if we ever get to that point, we'll discuss all those things. But I'm not going to live in a world of what if this, what if that. I mean, it's not the time or the place to do that right now because I don't see it (Proctor going to right tackle) happening right now."

title: Why Sieler Returning to the Dolphins Always Figured To Be a (Near) Slam Dunk
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' rebuilding project will revolve around their young players moving forward, certainly as we head into the 2027 season.
But there also will be a handful of key veterans who will be counted on to lead the way with what they do on and off the field, and one of those always figured to be defensive tackle Zach Sieler.
His agent, Drew Rosenhaus, indicated as much on his most recent appearance on South Florida TV station WSVN.
“I expect Zach to be back with the team next year,” Rosenhaus said. “I don’t think there’s going to be much debate about that. I’m pretty confident in talking to the team that he’s in their plans. I don’t ever speak for the team. I’ll let them say when it comes to announcing whether a player will be back.
"But I’ll just say from my perspective, based on conversations with the team, I’m confident Zach will be back. We don’t have any reason to think otherwise.”
That this would be even be in question is because of the combination of Sieler's age and contract.
Sieler will be 32 at the start of the 2027 regular season and the contract extension he signed in September 2025 has three years remaining with cap numbers between $21 million and $24 million annually.
That's not an egregious figure, but maybe a bit high for what still might be a rebuilding team in 2027.
As it was, Sieler's cap number of $11 million this year is far ahead of that of any other player still on the roster, surpassing the second-place cap number of $6.7 million for tackle Austin Jackson.
There's also the issue of the structure of Sieler's contract, which has no guaranteed salary remaining.
If the Dolphins were so inclined, they could release Sieler and save $8 million off their cap for 2027 or they could make it a post-June 1 release and save $16 million by spreading the dead cap hit over two years instead of one.
But what we would expect is a contract restructure where his base salary could be converted into a signing bonus to lower his cap number — and keep him on the roster.
The Dolphins probably tipped their hand in regards to Sieler when they reportedly refused to entertain trade offers for him around the deadline.
And why would they do that if they weren't planning on having him around for the foreseeable future.
Before he landed on injured reserve with a biceps injury, Sieler was the Dolphins' most productive interior defensive lineman because of his all-around ability against the run and as a pass rusher — and the gap between him and the rest of the position group was not insignificant.
Beyond that, there always is the leadership aspect, with Sieler again serving as a team captain as well as having been selected by his teammates as their representative with the NFL Players Association.
Perhaps more important than anything, the Dolphins do have some cap space available next year, so they don't need to be getting rid of quality players.
And Sieler clearly qualifies.

title: Why the Dolphins Finally Gave Up on a Rookie Draft Pick
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' churning of the roster is still going, and two end-of-the-roster players were waived Monday.
The day after the 26-9 loss against the Buffalo Bills in Week 11, the team announced it had waived edge defender Max Llewellyn and linebacker Shaka Heyward.
This is the second time Llewellyn has been waived since the Dolphins made him their seventh-round pick in the 2026 NFL draft. He made the initial 53-man roster before being cut when the team added players from other teams after the "final cuts," then was re-signed to the practice squad and re-signed to the 53-man roster after he exhausted his three allowed practice squad elevations.
But in his fourth game, and first on the active roster, Llewellyn again was an afterthought. He played a total of 18 snaps, nine on defense and nine on special teams, in those four games.
He clearly didn't show enough to keep a spot on the 53 in a season where the Dolphins are looking to identify young players to keep around for the future.
Since he can't play for the Dolphins again in 2026 unless he's re-signed to the active roster because he's out of practice squad elevations, it's likely Llewellyn is done with the Dolphins. This isn't a failure because he was a seventh-round pick and the Dolphins still have done very well with their 2026 draft class.
Everybody else is on the roster, though Trey Moore currently is on injured reserve and DJ Campbell is on the practice squad.
As for Heyward, he was strictly a special teams contributor after the Dolphins signed him off the Cincinnati Bengals practice squad.
With Llewellyn and Heyward gone, the Dolphins now have two roster openings, one of which might go to kicker Daniel Carlson after he went 3-for-3 on his field goal attempts against the Bills.
Keeping up with all the roster moves this month:
November 23 — Waived EDGE Max Llewellyn and LB Shaka Heyward
November 21 — Activated Darrell Baker Jr. off Reserve/PUP
November 18 — Signed EDGE Max Llewellyn to the active roster off the practice squad ... signed P Jack Browning to the practice squad
November 17 — Placed DL Zeek Bigger and Jordan Phillips on injured reserve ... signed QB Brady Cook, DL Jordan Jefferson and EDGE Eric Watts to the active roster off the practice squad ... signed WR Brady Boyd, DL Matthew Butler, K Daniel Carlson and DL Chris Smith to the practice squad
November 16 — Waived K Zane Gonzalez and EDGE Jamree Kromah
November 11 — Signed DT Keith Cooper Jr. off the Carolina Panthers practice squad
November 10 — Placed DT Zach Sieler and QB Malik Willis on injured reserve ... waived CB Reese Taylor

title: Dolphins QB Malik Willis Health Update and Why We Should Want Him Back in the Lineup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins now have played two games without starting quarterback Malik Willis, and the question remains how many more beyond the next two required after he was placed on injured reserve.
The latest update from head coach Jeff Hafley regarding Willis' status remain as positive as they can be, though we might not know until after the Week 13 game against the Denver Broncos when Willis will be ready to return to the lineup.
And, make no mistake, the Dolphins need him back in the lineup.
"I would say right now, as of today," Hafley said Monday, "I would say that he does not need the surgery right now, just to try to clear that up for you. I don't foresee him needing the surgery leading up to that time. Once we get to the four weeks, we'll re-evaluate that to see how he feels and if he's ready to go. But as of today, I would not say that, yeah, he's going to have the surgery before that time period."
Now, this wasn't exactly committing to Willis being ready to return for the Week 14 game against the Chicago Bears, though it beat the alternative of Willis definitely needing surgery, which likely would sideline him for the rest of the 2026 season.
Backup quarterback Kyle McCord had a dreadful statistical performance in the 26-9 loss against the Buffalo Bills, completing only 12 of 33 passes for 102 yards with no touchdowns, one interception and a 32.6 passer rating.
The 36.4 completion percentage was the worst by a Dolphins starting QB since 2022 when Tua Tagovailoa went 10-for-28 (35.7) in a loss against the Los Angeles Chargers and the passer rating was the lowest since Tua's 31.6 against the Cleveland Browns last year.
But as we wrote after the game Sunday, McCord's performance wasn't anywhere near as bad as the numbers when you factor in all the dropped passes, particularly Chris Bell failing to catch a perfectly thrown deep pass down the left sideline.
That said, it's clear there are limitations to Kyle McCord's game, but then again we should have known that given his background (sixth-round pick on his third team before throwing a regular season pass).
It's not like McCord can't have a future in the NFL and maybe he could become a dependable backup on a good team, but let's just say it looks an awful lot when Quinn Ewers was in the game last year.
There certainly wasn't anything terrible about McCord's work, it just was fairly uninspiring and, again, this is what should have been expected, though some fans got carried away by his work at Syracuse and some glowing scouting reports.
Willis, for his part, remains more of an unknown quantity and he showed enough flashes before landing on IR to remain an intriguing player.
No, the results haven't been good enough and there were times when he didn't make the right decisions in the first nine games, but the reality is the number of games when he was totally healthy was very small.
So it would be nice to get more of an evaluation on Willis to maybe determine just how urgent the need to get a quarterback in the 2027 draft will become. In a best-case scenario, Willis performs well down the stretch this season and the Dolphins can be more selective in the draft.
If Willis doesn't come back and doesn't show enough promise, then it could be that the Dolphins' hands will be tied and they'll have to go quarterback if they hope to have success next season.
Regardless of whether Willis or McCord plays quarterback down the stretch, the Dolphins still aren't likely to win many games. It's just better for the player evaluation process that it be Willis running the offense in those final weeks.

title: (Overdue?) Offensive Line Changes Could Be Coming for Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins offensive line probably stands at the top of the most disappointing position groups for the team this season, and it might be time for some changes on the underperforming unit.
Head coach Jeff Hafley brought up the possibility during his weekly day-after-the-game media session Monday, one day after backup quarterback Kyle McCord was constantly harassed by the Buffalo Bills pass rush — much the same way Malik Willis was harassed every game before he landed on injured reserve.
Hafley was asked specifically about possibly benching starting right tackle Austin Jackson, who has struggled in pass protection all season, but offered a broader-view answer.
"Yeah, I would say we'll look at the offensive line hard this week," Hafley said. "We sat down this morning. We're going to do more this afternoon, and we'll look at everything to see you what we need to do to help him more, and what we need to do overall. Like I said to you guys yesterday, we'll take a look at what we can do better to help, and then we'll take a look at what we can do overall to play better on offense. So I would say that with all the positions."
While Hafley made it more about the whole group — actually everybody on offense — it's pretty clear to anyone watching Dolphins games this season that the right side of the line has been the weak line, with guard Jonah Savaiinaea's play slipping after he got off to a decent start this season.
And, yes, the Dolphins have issues on offense that extend beyond the offensive line, which is how they rank last in the NFL in scoring and 31st in total offense.
But good offensive line play can mask a lot of deficiencies, and what's happening with the Dolphins is just the opposite.
And that's a major problem.
And it's gone on long enough.
It's why it's high time for a change.
So who could come in and come out of the lineup on the offensive line starting Sunday in the rematch against the New York Jets at Hard Rock Stadium?
Obviously the two players in danger of being benched are Savaiinaea and Jackson, and it's probably easier to bench Jackson considering he's in the last year of his contract and probably won't be back in 2027.
It also would be painful to bench Savaiinaea before the end of his second season as a second-round pick, but at some point the Dolphins might be forced to accept the reality he's just not the answer at right guard.
If the Dolphins do make a move at guard, then the easy solution for a replacement is Jarrett Kingston, who started against Cincinnati when rookie first-round pick Kadyn Proctor was out with a concussion and has taken over from Caedan Wallace as the sixth offensive lineman whenever the Dolphins use the jumbo package.
The right tackle spot is a bit more complicated because of the Proctor factor.
And this is where Hafley's answer Monday whether there have been conversations about moving Proctor to right tackle certainly was interesting.
Remember that Proctor played left tackle at Alabama and the thinking by many folks when the Dolphins selected him 12th overall in the 2026 draft was that his long-term future in Miami was at right tackle on the opposite end of left tackle Patrick Paul.
Neither Hafley nor GM Jon-Eric Sullivan ever have made definitive statements about Proctor's position for the entire season, only saying in the spring that they were going to start him out at guard.
"I would say conversations have been had because there's a lot of conversations, and I say that to be honest with you," Hafley said. "As of right now, I don't see him playing tackle this week. So yeah, that's how it answers your question."
Of course, the "as of right now" means that Hafley could change his mind before the start of practice Wednesday, which is when preparations for the Jets game will begin with the first practice of the week.
If the Dolphins indeed keep Proctor at guard, then the logical choice to replace Jackson if Hafley and his staff decide to do so would be Chukwuebuka Godrick, who they signed as a free agent after the final cuts to 53 after he had been released by the Kansas City Chiefs.
Godrick started three games at right tackle for the Chiefs late last season. He would seem the logical choice even though he's listed as the second-team left tackle on the depth chart and Wallace is listed as the second-team right tackle ... considering Wallace was inactive the last two games.
Of course, it's possible that Hafley ultimately decides to maintain the status quo for the Jets game, but in this season of evaluation there's no reason to keep going with players who don't fit into the long-term plans.
So it says it's time. Let's make a change.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 11 Loss
full_text:
Chilly weather, broken tables, and the Miami Dolphins falling to the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park. It's been a common theme since 2016, the last time the Dolphins won a game in Western New York. They didn't come close to breaking that streak Sunday.
While the Dolphins have lost as many games as they have, a good chunk of them had been by a touchdown or less. That wasn't the case against Buffalo, as after the Bills went up 13-0 with 13:23 to go in the second quarter, the deficit never went back down to less than eight points.
Against a team looking to compete for a spot in Super Bowl LXI, the youth and inexperience of the Dolphins reared their ugly head in a way that hasn't been seen since maybe the San Francisco loss. That said, you can find positives if you look hard enough, and there was especially some good from the defense.
As you'll probably come to find out, the entire offense looked shaky in this game. McCord got no help from his offensive line, and a lot of his wide receivers forgot to wear their extra-sticky gloves. He's playing the Bills in Buffalo, for crying out loud.
He looked like someone who hadn't played many games of professional football, with a generous number of passes that either sailed over receivers or were underthrown. He rarely went for the long ball, and when he was under pressure, he equally struggled with check-downs or anything that required him to scan the field. He only threw one interception, which in itself feels like a win.
At no point in this game did it look like he could take over by himself, which is justified because that was always going to be impossible given the circumstances.
Back-to-back weeks for Chop being one of the biggest winners on these lists. Numbers-wise, his performance doesn't stand out with three tackles, a pass deflection, and a QB hit. If it were any other quarterback, he probably would have also recorded at least two sacks, but Josh Allen did what he does best and escaped an impossible situation.
The one time he couldn't make magic happen, though, was on that Robinson pass deflection, leading to an errant throw that sailed right to Jacob Rodriguez for an interception. He's not a one-dimensional player, as he was also solid in managing the run game, helping the defense limit the Bills to 95 rushing yards, an astronomically low number for a team with Allen and James Cook III.
The rookie sensation had a hard time establishing himself. He was targeted 10 times, and while a fair number of the throws were off the mark, he was only able to haul in two receptions for 30 yards. More than anything, though, this will be the game that showcased perhaps his biggest issue — the drops.
There were four in this game for Douglas, with none bigger than the one on third-and-goal early in the third quarter. It forced their third field goal of the day, and it was the closest they ever got to a touchdown the rest of the game.
Filling in for Dante Trader Jr., Anderson made the most of an extended workload and recorded 12 tackles, a sack, three pass deflections, and an interception. It's easily his best performance of the season, considering how red-hot Buffalo's offense was entering this game. The sack was critical, as it forced a 54-yard field goal attempt from Tyler Bass that sailed wide left in the third quarter.
The interception, meanwhile, was the first of back-to-back picks thrown by Allen and McCord toward the end of the first half. It wasn't all perfect for Anderson, as DJ Moore's touchdown was assisted by both Anderson and Michael Taaffe blowing the coverage, and forcing us all to watch Moore pretend to be a seal for two full seconds.
Just when you thought maybe Jackson was improving after a clean stat sheet with no pressures, sacks or penalties against Indianapolis, things got ugly against Greg Rousseau and Buffalo. He was responsible for two sacks by Rousseau, and every time he didn't pressure McCord, it felt like a small victory.
Jonah Savaiinaea also had a rough game, but it seems clear that one of the positions where Miami needs a fresh face at is right tackle. Jackson's best attribute this season isn't blocking, but rather how he's stayed healthy, and that's not good enough. It doesn't matter who the quarterback is; the right side of the line of scrimmage is always a battleground that they'd better avoid being near.
It sure is great not to have a small panic attack every time a kicker is brought on the field. Carlson set the tone in the second quarter with back-to-back 52-yard field goals, then added a 27-yarder in the third quarter for good measure.
Yes, it's only one game for Carlson, but it's refreshing to see someone provide consistency to Miami's special teams, as it's been anything but that this season. No one will find long-term reasons to remember this game from a Dolphins perspective, but at least it looks like Miami has one less problem to worry about on their roster for the time being.
Here we go again. Wright can't catch a break; the jokes about him being a magnet for defenders in the backfield have unfortunately aged well. He recorded 10 yards on five carries, and this is somehow an improvement from his games against the New York Jets, New England and Indianapolis.
Wright actually was decent on kick returns with 79 yards on three returns. Once he gets a full head of steam, he tends to be hard to bring down, but he never gets that opportunity on offense. That's why it's puzzling that he's been given this many carries up to this point as opposed to anyone else.
In fairness, it would have been hard to beat what Washington was able to cook up against the Colts as a receiver, runner, and ... thrower. But even in a bad game for Miami's pass offense, he was serviceable enough for 30 yards on three receptions, with four fewer targets than Douglas.
Surprisingly, it's his ability to run the ball that might be something Bobby Slowik and the offense should look into moving forward. Any way to get him the ball more is welcome, especially when the rookies struggle in games like this against a tough defense, and teams like Denver and Chicago are still to come.

A native of Homestead, Florida, Jake grew up a South Florida sports fan and has currently attended five Super Bowls in person.

title: Ryan Van Demark’s Vikings Future Could Be on the Line in Week 12 vs. Falcons
full_text:
Week 12 is in full swing, and the Vikings are just days away from a must-win matchup against the Falcons . The NFC North is tighter than ever in late November, and the Bears' win over the Lions on Thanksgiving furthered their divisional lead, putting pressure on the Vikings to leave U.S. Bank Stadium victorious this weekend.
Much like what most teams are forced to do at this stage of the season, the Vikings will likely be shorthanded when they host the Falcons. Although no one has been ruled out at the time of writing , several veterans are banged up at the moment, including starting left tackle Christian Darrisaw, who missed Wednesday and Thursday's practices with an ongoing shoulder injury .
Thursday’s #Vikings injury report pic.twitter.com/YqAqCuYuHz
Barring a miraculous recovery, Darrisaw will likely miss the Falcons clash, meaning Ryan Van Demark is probably in line for just his second start of the season. What happens next could make or break what the 28-year-old blocker's future in Minnesota looks like.
Looking to add some tackle depth in the offseason, the Vikings inked Van Demark to a one-year, $4.2 million contract in March. The former UConn blocker played 558 offensive snaps in 43 games (6 starts) during his three-year run with the Bills, offering the type of experience the Purple and Gold wanted behind Darrisaw, who missed a total of 17 games between the 2024 and 2025 seasons.
While the experience is there, the results haven't been, so far. Van Demark's pass protection has been far from reliable, as he's allowed eight pressures across the 130 offensive snaps he's played so far. Pro Football Focus is giving him an abysmal 34.7 pass protection grade , and it's safe to say that mark is where it is because of the putrid performance Van Demark displayed against the 49ers in Week 11. His 21.2 pass-block grade and 30.3 overall grade were easily the worst among Minnesota's offensive linemen in the defeat.
With the regular season winding down and Darrisaw nearing his return with each passing day, Van Demark doesn't have much time left to prove he deserves a significant role. In fact, Week 12 against the Falcons might be his final real chance to prove his worth.
Not only because Darrisaw might be back soon, but because the Vikings might decide they've seen enough of Van Demark and turn to rookie tackle Caleb Tiernan , whom they drafted 97th overall in April.  He's far from a finished product, but the Vikings used a Day 2 selection on him for a reason.
If they feel Tiernan is even closer to a bigger role in 2027, they'll have less incentive to bring Van Demark back—especially when Minnesota has 18 other pending unrestricted free agents to deal with and only $27.7 million to work with. Sacrifices will be made, and Van Demark could be one of them.
Assuming Darrisaw is inactive, Sunday's showdown against Atlanta could make or break what happens next with Van Demark. A strong performance will likely keep him as the starting left tackle as long as Darrisaw is out, while potentially strengthening the odds of a 2027 re-signing. However, a weak performance against the Falcons could tell the Vikings all they need to know.
That said, Week 12 should be a favorable matchup for the Wayne, N.J. native. Unlike when they finished 2025 with the second-most sacks in the NFL, the Falcons' pass rush is a shell of its former self and is currently tied for the eighth-fewest sacks (21). Their 82.2 PFF pass-rush grade is the second-best mark, but it's clear that they aren't efficiently taking down opposing quarterbacks.
Hopefully, Van Demark takes advantage of the matchup to silence any doubts that the Vikings and their fans have moving forward. If not, don't be surprised if we see less of him and more of Tiernan (or a potential free-agent addition) until Darrisaw is healthy enough to return .

title: Vikings Could Test the Caleb Tiernan Waters Again vs. Falcons in Week 12
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings' offensive line has had an up-and-down season. At times, they look like a capable unit in both run blocking and pass protection. At other times, they struggle to block opposing defenders. Minnesota allows fewer quarterback pressures per snap than average, ranking 12th at 29.8%. They also rank 13th in sacks allowed, giving up 27 in 10 games this season.
On Wednesday, Pro Football Focus ranked every offensive line based on grades and put extra weight on pass blocking. The Vikings were ranked 19th, and the report noted an injury to starting left tackle Christian Darrisaw. Against the 49ers , he had an 89.8 PFF pass-blocking grade and didn't allow a pressure on 28 pass-blocking snaps. Darrisaw's backup, Ryan Van Demark, didn't fare well in his place. His 21.2 PFF pass-blocking grade was fueled by allowing three pressures on 19 pass-blocking snaps.
Darrisaw has not practiced yet this week and is on the team's injury report with a shoulder issue . If he can't play, Van Demark would be expected to start in his place, but head coach Kevin O'Connell should consider getting rookie offensive tackle Caleb Tiernan some snaps at left tackle.
Minnesota is already starting guard Joe Huber at left guard after the season-ending torn meniscus of Donovan Jackson in Week 4. Although Huber has held up well , having another new starter next to him could make things difficult.
Van Demark has a 47.1 PFF grade this season and a pass-blocking grade of 34.7. If he is forced to start, the purple and gold will want to give him as much help as possible. On the other hand, Tiernan has a 59.9 PFF grade with a 75.7 pass-blocking grade.
Although Tiernan has only played 14 offensive snaps this season, the small sample size looks good for Minnesota's third-round draft pick. He has not allowed a single pressure or sack but has been flagged for one penalty.
It is understandable why Demark is above Tiernan on the depth chart. The fourth-year offensive lineman signed a one-year, $4.27 million contract to be a solid swing tackle for the Vikings. However, experience and a healthy contract shouldn't put a player on the field.
If Tiernan has a solid week of practice leading up to Sunday's game against the Atlanta Falcons and Darrisaw is ruled out, the team should consider at least splitting snaps between Van Demark and Tiernan to give the rookie some more experience and get a bigger sample size of his potential.

title: Breaking Down Vikings’ Week 12 Injury Report: Who’s Hurt and Who Could Return vs. Falcons
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings are dealing with some significant injuries heading into Week 12. The team is preparing to take on the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday and will want as much talent as possible on the field at U.S. Bank Stadium.
Last week against the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday Night Football, the Vikings were without multiple players who could have been contributors, and hopefully at least one of them will return to action this weekend.
Who could return for the Vikings against the Falcons, and who might need more time to recover before they are ready for action? Let's dive into the injuries for Minnesota.
In a game-time decision against the 49ers, Isaiah Rodgers was out in Week 11. Minnesota's secondary was toasted by San Francisco in that game, so getting him back would be a huge boon for the defense.
Rodgers has not practiced this week while allowing his thigh injury to heal. Giving him some time to rest will increase the chances of him being able to suit up against Atlanta, but it is still a situation to watch.
Leaving the game against the 49ers with a shoulder injury , starting left tackle Christian Darrisaw has not practiced this week. He is considered day-to-day, so there is a chance he could play against the Falcons.
If Darrisaw can't play, backup tackle Ryan Van Demark will likely start in his place. That's not a good sign for an offensive line that has struggled to protect its starting quarterback, especially with a pocket passer like Kirk Cousins at the helm.
The Vikings are hoping that WR2 Jordan Addison will heal from his thumb surgery and be able to return to the team without having to place him on short-term injured reserve. However, that return will likely not be against Atlanta.
Addison is a great weapon for Minnesota, and the offense should be more explosive when he is able to come back. In the meantime, players like Jauan Jennings, Tai Felton and Myles Price will need to pick up the slack.
Even if Kyler Murray is fully recovered from his hamstring injury , the Vikings are in no rush to get him back. He lost his starting job to Cousins and now will serve as a backup. Having him inactive isn't a problem for head coach Kevin O'Connell, since he is rolling with Carson Wentz as the backup.
Murray has been a disappointment for Minnesota this season. He hasn't been able to command the offense, which led to the Purple and Gold trading for Cousins. Now, he may not play another snap for the team this season.
No additional players were lost for the season against the 49ers on Sunday Night Football. The Vikings already have seven players on injured reserve this season, including left guard Donovan Jackson, safety Jamal Adams, tight end Josh Oliver and running back Demond Claiborne.

title: Jalen Redmond's Breakout Could Prove Costly for Vikings
full_text:
Jalen Redmond is having a fantastic season for the Minnesota Vikings. The 27-year-old defensive lineman has been one of the most consistent and reliable players in defensive coordinator Brian Flores' unit.
Over 11 weeks, Redmond has played 500 defensive snaps, the fourth most of any qualifying defensive lineman. He has 32 tackles, seven quarterback hits, five tackles for loss, four passes defended, and two sacks.
After this season, Redmond is scheduled to become a restricted free agent . The Vikings can't allow him to sign with another team, making re-signing him a priority . Getting an extension done before the end of the season would be even better.
The problem is that Redmond's excellent play , combined with the trending increase in NFL salaries, could mean that an extension will be expensive. His 80.6 Pro Football Focus grade is fantastic, and his 85.7 run defense grade ranks him second among all qualifying defensive linemen.
Finding a comparable player to estimate his potential contract isn't easy. However, one good comparison might be DaVon Hamilton of the Jacksonville Jaguars. Hamilton is in his seventh season and has a 74 PFF grade. Although he has played considerably fewer snaps this season, he has a longer track record of solid play.
Hamilton is on a three-year, $34.5 million deal that averages $11.5 million per year. That seems like a good amount to not only reward Redmond for his play to this point, but also keep him under contract through the 2029 NFL season.
However, the longer the Vikings wait to extend Redmond, the more likely it is that the price tag will increase. In fact, there would be plenty of leverage to hold out for around $17 million per year, like Buffalo Bills defensive lineman Ed Oliver, who has two more quarterback pressures than Redmond this season.
Although the focus of the team right now is being competitive for a potential playoff push, preparing for the future is wise. Minnesota drafted Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange this year to be the future of the defensive line, but having Redmond play so well has forced him into the long-term picture.
Honestly, a fair and reasonable extension for Redmond is around a three-year, $39 million deal. If the Vikings can lock him down on a deal similar to that, it would be a win for both Minnesota and the young standout defensive lineman.

title: Vikings Could Be the Biggest Losers of the Aaron Rodgers-Mike McCarthy Drama
full_text:
From J.J. McCarthy to Kirk Cousins, the Vikings haven't been short on drama in 2026, but another franchise may have just taken the crown .
Aaron Rodgers is no stranger to leaving teams on less than friendly terms, and after departing the Packers and Jets with a grudge, he's now out of Pittsburgh, leaving a trail of destruction behind him.
Rodgers' reunion with his former coach Mike McCarthy ended in another ugly divorce , and the Steelers' former starter is now searching for a new team. And while the Steelers have publicly supported McCarthy since Rodgers' scathing claims, if even half of what was said is true, Pittsburgh may be in the market for a new head coach in 2027—and that's pretty bad news for the Vikings.
Rodgers claims that McCarthy was falling asleep in meetings and breaking down huddles with the wrong team's name among other embarrassments. Some reports have corroborated those accusations, and while it's generally looked down upon to spill locker room beans, it may be too hard for McCarthy to reinvent his image.
If the Steelers ultimately decide that McCarthy isn't the man for the job, the next man they turn to could very well be Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores.
Flores has familiarity with the franchise after serving as a defensive assistant in 2022, and interviewed for their head coach opening earlier this year after Mike Tomlin's departure. Obviously, it's hard to know how close Flores was to getting the job over McCarthy, but it's reasonable to expect that he'd be in the running again should the Steelers opt for a change this offseason.
Clearly, losing Flores to a head coaching job would be a devastating loss for Minnesota, which boasts of the NFL's top defenses. Through Week 11, the Vikings' defense ranks first in points allowed, first in sacks  and second in yards allowed per game. Some, as ridiculous as it is, have even speculated that the Vikings should move on from Kevin O'Connell in favor of Flores after carrying the Vikings through the first half of the season.
Any other assistant with that kind of resume would be a surefire head coach in 2027, but Flores' situation could make things messy. His time as a head coach in Miami ended unceremoniously after a 24-25 record with no playoff appearances. Flores is also currently suing the league for discrimination, which could also complicate his path towards another shot as the head man.
The Vikings have already made Flores one of the highest-paid assistants in the NFL, but the allure of a head coaching job is still very obviously on his mind. There may not be much Minnesota can do if the Steelers come knocking.
Assuming Pittsburgh looks to make a change, they remain a logical landing spot for Flores, and the Vikings may be looking to replace someone irreplaceable next season.

title: 3 Most Important Things Vikings Fans Must Watch for When Falcons Visit in Week 12
full_text:
Sometimes in life, you get knocked down. Other times, you get absolutely steamrolled.
That’s what happened to the Vikings last week against the 49ers in Mexico City. Now, they’ll return home looking to turn over a new leaf against the 3-7 Falcons.
With seven games remaining in the regular season , head coach Kevin O’Connell’s squad will need to be at their best going forward, and Sunday should provide plenty of chances to get back on track.
Here’s what matters most as Minnesota looks for its eighth win of a confusing 2026 season.
It’s not often that the head coach of a 7-3 football team is under scrutiny , but this season has been anything but ordinary for O’Connell and the Vikings. Despite their record, the offense has been wildly disappointing for much of the season. With Kirk Cousins making his return home in his third game back in purple against a shaky Atlanta pass defense, the excuses are few and far between for another dud on Sunday.
The Vikings have scored less than 20 points in six of their ten games so far this season.
O’Connell will need to be at his best over the next two months if the Vikings are going to be seen as a serious threat in the playoffs. Avoiding turnovers, establishing the run, and gaining chunk yardage via play action may be the keys to unlocking the Vikings' offense once again.
Luckily for O’Connell, Cousins has proven capable of doing just that throughout his career.
The Kirk Cousins era in Atlanta was always… odd, to say the least.
Cousins left the Vikings in 2024 seeking long-term security, signed a massive deal with the Falcons, and was blindsided when they drafted Michael Penix eighth overall just over a month after he signed. Then, he was benched for the rookie in December of 2024. He would stick around in 2025, stepping in after Penix was injured, but the relationship between player and team was clearly shattered.
Penix on Kirk Cousins: I'm excited to see him out there. #Falcons
After a short tenure in Las Vegas, Cousins is back in Minnesota with a chance to prove his former team wrong in his first home game back as a Viking. Ironically, Cousins’s last appearance at U.S. Bank Stadium was as a Falcon in 2024.
With a friendly crowd and personal motivation, Cousins may be set up for a big game this weekend .
Last Sunday’s loss in Mexico City may have season-defining implications for the Vikings, especially if they are unable to hit their stride over their remaining seven games. ESPN ’s football power index still gives the Vikings a 92.1% chance to make the playoffs , but only a 26.2% chance to win the NFC North.
The Vikings will need to be close to perfect over the final month and a half of the season if they want to host a home game in the playoffs.
Sunday begins a three-game stretch that should allow the Vikings to sort through their struggles before hosting the Lions for a massive Sunday Night Football meeting on Dec. 20. They’ll host the Falcons this weekend, the Panthers in Week 13, and travel to face a depleted Patriots team for Thursday Night Football in Week 14.
If the Vikings are going to make a run, they’ll need to show up against the “lesser” opponents left on their schedule.
Still, the Falcons certainly should not be ignored, as they managed to do one thing the Vikings couldn’t: beat the 49ers.
